title: Trump signs proclamation declaring Oval Office a national monument
summary: The action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that President Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself.
story: President Trump on Thursday signed a proclamation that he says will preserve the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument, his first official action after his party was swept aside in midterm elections on Tuesday.

But the action does not prevent future presidents from restyling the iconic office that Mr. Trump has filled to the brim with gold flourishes, nor does it prevent a successor from rolling back the proclamation itself. Mr. Trump himself has reversed national monument designations made by his predecessors.
Mr. Trump, however, described the Oval Office order in expansive terms.

"It will not be allowed to be touched by anybody, destroyed, ripped down by stupid people, in order to build something in a slightly different shape," Mr. Trump said. "We like the Oval Office, and it's a symbol, like the White House itself."

It was the third day this week that the president, a real estate mogul, delivered remarks fixated on his pet projects in Washington. On Wednesday, a day after Republicans suffered defeats in key races across the country, Mr. Trump gathered reporters to see the final beam being raised during construction of his opulent ballroom project. On Monday, he went to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool to talk about his renovation of the landmark.

The proclamation, released after Mr. Trump's remarks, says that nothing in it will "restrict the President's authority to redecorate the monument, select furnishings, or make ordinary operational and security modifications that do not substantially impair the monument's historic structure or architectural character."

It orders the Interior secretary to manage the Oval Office and requires "documentation, review, and consideration of alternatives before any action that would substantially alter or demolish the monument." Mr. Trump separately said any major changes would need review from Congress, though such a requirement is not in the document's text.

"If they want to say, 'Let's not have oval anymore, let's make it square,' what happens is they have to go back to Congress and hopefully the Congress, the people in Congress, will be smart enough not to let that happen," said Mr. Trump — who notably demolished the East Wing of the White House to make room for his ballroom.
A red baseball cap with "VETO" on the front was sitting on the Resolute Desk as Mr. Trump signed the document, a not-so-subtle nod to the shifting of powers in Congress.

His effort to preserve changes at the White House comes as Democrats gear up for new scrutiny of Mr. Trump. Connecticut Sen. Richard Blumenthal, the top Democrat on the Homeland Security Committee's Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, sent a flurry of letters Thursday to known donors to Mr. Trump's ballroom, demanding that they provide information or face "alternative measures to obtain compliance."

Since returning to the White House, Mr. Trump has overseen numerous design changes to various rooms, including the Oval Office, where he has filled the wall space with portraits, a copy of the Declaration of Independence and numerous golden accents.

As he talked about his interior decorating decisions, Mr. Trump highlighted new chandeliers that he says were installed in the Cabinet Room to address "very bad lighting." His other additions to the Oval Office include numerous gold wall appliqués and gold-framed portraits.

Mr. Trump did not elaborate on precisely what he was hoping to prevent but suggested that the Oval Office might face some threat in the future. Mr. Trump himself has faced several lawsuits alleging that his Washington beautification projects were done without the necessary approval.
"If anybody ever decides to come and start knocking down walls, you call me wherever I may be," Mr. Trump said, "and I'll come back here and I'll make sure it never happens."

Late Thursday, the National Capital Planning Commission gave final approval for the president's 250-foot triumphal arch, which will be constructed between the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.

The NCPC, which acts as the federal government's planning agency for the region and is stacked with Trump allies, voted 8-4 to greenlight the project after almost 9 hours of public comments from members of Congress, veterans, architects and Washington, D.C., and Virginia residents.
However, a federal judge is weighing whether to temporarily block construction of the arch.

title: Nithya Raman ousts incumbent Karen Bass in LA mayor's race, CBS News projects
summary: Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.
story: Councilmember Nithya Raman will be Los Angeles' next mayor after defeating incumbent Karen Bass in the November general election, CBS News projects.
Raman's win comes after resounding victories for Democrats across the country on Election Day.
On Thursday night, Raman stood among supporters in the Fairfax District and pledged to restore Angelenos' "faith in City Hall."

"My goal is to earn your trust. My goal is to make sure that we're doing the work to actually have a City Hall that is capable of delivering on the promises that I made during the campaign," she said. "That is my commitment to every single person, whether you voted for me or you didn't, or you sat out this election completely. I want to make sure that we can restore your faith in City Hall."

Bass released a statement on Thursday morning conceding to Raman, saying she called her to congratulate her on the victory. The last time a challenger ousted a sitting LA mayor happened in 2005, when Antonio Villaraigosa defeated incumbent James Hahn.

"While this is not the outcome we hoped for, the people of Los Angeles have spoken. I have called Councilmember Nithya Raman to congratulate her on her victory, and I have committed to ensuring a smooth and seamless transition," Bass wrote.
Bass thanked her supporters and other leaders who helped during her campaign. She added that she will continue to "ensure the promise of a better life belongs to all of us."
During her Thursday night speech, Raman thanked Bass for "her decades of service to the city" and for her work to make LA "the epitome of the American Dream."

"I know her service is something that people across America have gratitude for, and certainly every person across Los Angeles," she said. "We committed to working together on the smoothest possible transition for Angelenos. We love this city. We want to make it an incredible, incredible place."
After Bass' concession, Los Angeles Police Department Chief Jim McDonnell congratulated Raman and thanked Bass for her time in office.

"As Chief of Police, I remain committed to leading a department that delivers professional, constitutional, and compassionate policing to all Angelenos," McDonnell wrote in a statement. "By working together, we can meet the challenges ahead and continue building a safer Los Angeles for everyone."

Raman, a Democratic socialist, has been riding her momentum after pushing past Spencer Pratt in the June primary, but suffered a setback with voters a week before the election, according to the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the Los Angeles Times.
A survey released by the UC Berkeley Institute of Governmental Studies and the LA Times shortly before the election showed Bass and Raman tied, with 40% support among likely voters.
Bass and Raman became frontrunners after the primary election when they rallied ahead of third-place candidate Pratt.

"I want to tell every single Angeleno out there, I am going to work so hard, and everyone behind me is going to work so hard to earn your trust," Raman said. "To earn the trust of everyone across this city and to make people believe in Los Angeles again."
Councilmember Nithya Raman
Raman announced her surprise bid for mayor in February after previously endorsing Bass' reelection bid.
During the primary, Raman called her campaign a "long shot" before ultimately overtaking Pratt to face Bass in the general election.
Before being elected to Los Angeles City Council in 2020, Raman served as the co-chair of the Silver Lake Neighborhood Council Homelessness Committee and co-founded a homeless advocacy nonprofit.

One of her most notable acts in office came in 2025, when she introduced a motion capping maximum annual rent increases for tenants in rent-stabilized apartments built before 1978. It eventually passed 13-2. She said she hoped to undertake similar work to help small businesses.
Mayor Karen Bass
After serving more than two decades in public office as a congresswoman and as LA's 43rd Mayor, Bass said this race will be her last campaign for office.

Bass was raised in LA with her three brothers. She began her professional career as a nurse and physician assistant, where she later founded the Community Coalition to help underserved residents of South LA battle substance abuse, poverty and crime.

She kickstarted her career in politics in 2004 as a member of the California Assembly, where she became the first Black woman to serve as Speaker of a state legislative body. She left the Assembly in 2010 to run for Congress, where she served in the House for 12 years.

Leading up to the primary election, Bass received endorsements from notable politicians including California Gov. Gavin Newsom and former Vice President Kamala Harris. Nearly a week before the November election, billionaire Rick Caruso threw his support behind his former rival in the 2022 mayoral race and vowed to vote for her in November.
"For the love of LA, I must put the past behind me because this election must be about our future," Caruso said in a post to X. "I will be casting my ballot for Mayor Karen Bass."
He also said in the video that he had concerns about Raman that were not "much about ideology, but about competence."

title: Democrats have flipped over 40 House seats. Here's the breakdown.
summary: Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday by flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red.
story: Democrats won control of the House of Representatives on Tuesday by flipping more than three dozen Republican-held seats, picking up perennial swing districts and seats that were once considered deep red. The party's wins ranged from suburban areas in the northeastern United States to areas of South Texas that were once viewed as increasingly GOP-friendly.

The 2026 midterm elections were also shaken up by last year's nationwide mid-decade redistricting gambit, with Texas Republicans shifting several districts rightward at President Trump's behest, California Democrats moving districts to the left and several other states tweaking their House maps for partisan purposes. Democrats notched several wins under the new maps, while the GOP's pickups have been more limited so far.
Winners in dozens of races have yet to be projected by CBS News.
So far, 43 districts have shifted to Democrats and two have shifted to Republicans. Here's a look at the seats that swung:
Upsets
In several districts, Democrats ousted GOP lawmakers who won by double digits two years ago.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019. Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.

New Jersey's 2nd District: Republican Rep. Jeff Van Drew lost to Democrat Zack Mullock in a South Jersey district that was widely seen as solid red. Van Drew, who won by 16.9 points in 2024, is known for switching from the Democratic Party during the first Trump impeachment saga in 2019.

Ohio's 10th District: GOP Rep. Mike Turner was ousted by Democrat Kristina Knickerbocker, ending Turner's nearly quarter-century tenure in Congress just two years after he won reelection by more than 18 points.

Missouri's 2nd District: Democrat Fred Wellman unseated GOP Rep. Ann Wagner, who won by 12 points in 2024. Republicans tried to make the St. Louis-area seat slightly redder last year, but the new maps were tossed out in the courts. As recently as September, the Cook Political Report viewed it as solid-red.
Indiana's 5th District: Republican Rep. Victoria Spartz lost to Democrat J.D. Ford in one of several election night surprises. Spartz won reelection by just over 18 points in 2024.

Kentucky's 6th District: The race between Democrat Zach Dembo and Republican Ralph Alvarado for the open seat was not expected to be competitive, but the election forecasters moved the GOP-held seat toward Democrats in recent weeks. Outgoing Rep. Andy Barr won it by 26 points two years ago.

Wisconsin's 1st District: Republican Rep. Bryan Steil, who was first elected in 2018, lost his race to Democrat Mitchell Berman. A Democrat has not represented the district in more than 30 years. Steil won his last reelection by just over 10 points, outperforming Mr. Trump, and the Cook Political Report rated it "Likely Republican" until late September.

Nevada's 2nd District: Teresa Benitez-Thompson will be the first Democrat to represent Northern Nevada in decades, after she defeated Republican David Flippo. The seat was left open by the retirement of longtime GOP Rep. Mark Amodei, who won by a nearly 19-point margin in 2024.
Ohio's 15th District: Democrat Don Leonard defeated GOP Rep. Mike Carey, who won reelection by 13 points in 2024.
Rematches
A few Democrats won against Republicans who they'd faced before — in one case, multiple times.

Pennsylvania's 10th District: Democrat Janelle Stelson beat GOP Rep. Scott Perry in a rematch in the district, which is centered on the state capital of Harrisburg.Virginia's 2nd District: Former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria defeated GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in a rematch. Luria lost to Kiggans in 2022 after redistricting made the area more favorable to Republicans. The military-heavy district — which includes Virginia's Eastern Shore and Virginia Beach — has flipped parties four times since 2008.Wisconsin's 3rd District: Democrat Rebecca Cooke ousted two-term Republican Rep. Derrick Van Orden in a rematch in the highly competitive district that covers parts of the western and central areas of the state. Iowa's 1st District: Republican Rep. Mariannette Miller-Meeks lost to Democrat Christine Bohannon in their third consecutive rematch. Miller-Meeks has a history of close races since she was first elected to Congress by a six-vote margin in 2020.
Pennsylvania's 10th District: Democrat Janelle Stelson beat GOP Rep. Scott Perry in a rematch in the district, which is centered on the state capital of Harrisburg.

Virginia's 2nd District: Former Democratic Rep. Elaine Luria defeated GOP Rep. Jen Kiggans in a rematch. Luria lost to Kiggans in 2022 after redistricting made the area more favorable to Republicans. title: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carry out 3 U.S. executions on the same day
summary: This marks the second time this year that three people in the U.S. were put to death on a single day.
story: For the second time this year, three executions by lethal injection were carried out on the same day, this time in Indiana, Florida and Alabama.

An Indiana man who admitted killing his girlfriend's two children was executed in the early morning hours Thursday. Jeffrey Weisheit killed the children, ages 8 and 5, by setting fire to his girlfriend's house in the Evansville area in 2010.

Weisheit died at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City. The lethal injection started just after midnight and he was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. local time, according to Noelle Russell, Indiana Department of Correction chief communications officer.
She said Weisheit's final meal was barbecue ribs and he had no final words. Weisheit was Indiana's first execution of the year.
Early Thursday evening, Florida carried out its record-tying 19th execution of the year.
Jesse Guardado, 64, was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. local time following a three-drug injection at a state prison in Starke.

Guardado had pleaded guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman inside her Walton County home in 2004 before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other valuables to buy drugs. The woman had helped him get a job and housing.
A federal appeals court in 2024 said Guardado, now 64, had received a "full and fair" hearing during the death penalty phase of his case.
In Alabama, 54-year-old Michael Taylor received the last lethal injection of the day for his conviction in the killing of an elderly man and woman in a 1991 home robbery.
Taylor was pronounced dead at 6:10 p.m. local time. The execution got underway shortly before 6 p.m. as Taylor replied "no sir" when asked if he had any final words.
He appeared to mouth "thank you" toward his attorneys seated in the witness room. Taylor's spiritual adviser approached and prayed with him, and he closed his eyes, never opening them again.
This marked the second time this year that three people in the U.S. were put to death on the same day. Alabama, Tennessee and Oklahoma conducted executions on Aug. 13.

The death penalty has faced renewed scrutiny following the September failed execution of Christa Pike in Tennessee, although courts have rejected efforts to halt other executions since she survived two lethal doses of pentobarbital.

Pike said in a statement dictated to her lawyers and released a month after the botched execution that she's been in pain every moment since she woke up confused in a hospital. "I had not contemplated life beyond that night," she said.

Lawyers had wanted Indiana Republican Gov. Mike Braun to allow Weisheit, 50, to undergo brain scans in an effort to reinforce their argument that he has a history of head injuries and mental health problems. Braun declined, and he also turned down a request to reduce the sentence to life in prison.

Weisheit's latest objection centered on the state's planned use of lethal drugs purchased from a pharmacy that is facing a disciplinary hearing next week at the Indiana Pharmacy Board. The Indiana Department of Correction said it's confident "in our ability to humanely carry out" the execution.
Following the execution, Braun issued a brief statement noting Weisheit's case was reviewed many times by state and federal courts.
"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," he said. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said that the execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty."

Florida, meanwhile, has carried out more than half of the 34 executions so far this year in the U.S. Outgoing Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis has made aggressive use of the death penalty like few other governors.

Taylor was executed by Alabama 35 years after fatally beating an older couple with a metal bar during a robbery in their Gadsden home. Police arrested the 19-year-old Taylor with the victims' Cadillac, an hour away in Birmingham. The execution was the state's third this year.
Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to reduce Taylor's sentence to life in prison, noting his age and immaturity at the time of the killings.

"If the state kills Michael, it is not the 19-year-old who made the worst mistake of his life who it kills. But the mature, well-respected, God-fearing man sitting in that cell today," said Esther Brown of Project Hope to Abolish the Death Penalty.

Ivey declined, however. She called Taylor's actions "reprehensible" in a statement following his execution, adding the couple had opened their home to him and "Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry."
She also took a jab at California's Gov. Gavin Newsom for planning to commute all death sentences there.
"California may let their criminals escape justice, but not Alabama. Here, we enforce the law and always will," Ivey said at end of the statement.

The state executed Taylor by lethal injection after a judge declared a nitrogen gas method unconstitutional. His attorneys objected to the last-minute switch to lethal injection since he selected nitrogen gas as his method several years ago, but a judge ruled against Taylor.

The defense attorneys said Taylor "knew the depth of the harm he caused" and "grieved it for the rest of his life," adding he became a changed person in prison and that "Michael's life was proof that God isn't finished with any of us."

title: Trump agenda likely to be curbed with Democrats in charge
summary: Investigations, a struggle to confirm nominees and maybe some bipartisanship lie ahead for President Trump.
story: Washington — President Trump seems to be reconsidering his approach to Democrats after Tuesday's massive Republican election losses and has so far made contradictory comments about how he plans to deal with them as they take control of the Senate and the House in January.

"We're going to work with the Democrats," the president told Politico as GOP defeats were beginning to stack up Tuesday night, though in a phone call with CBS News' Robert Costa before polls closed, he had said, "I have the ultimate power — it's called 'veto.'"
By Wednesday afternoon, he had merged the two approaches.

"I'll get along, probably, with the Democrats, unless they want to be destructive, but I have the power of the veto," the president told reporters at the White House ballroom construction site Wednesday. On Thursday, a red hat that said "VETO" sat on the Resolute Desk in the Oval Office.

But Democrats may not be the only source of friction ahead. After two years of working in lockstep with Mr. Trump, some Republicans may prove more willing to defy the term-limited president to try to salvage their political careers.
Here's what the newly empowered congressional Democrats may have in store for Mr. Trump in 2027 for the last two years of his presidency.
Oversight and investigations
The committee chair's gavel comes with subpoena power, and Democrats plan to wield it.

"Lawyer up," warned Rep. Robert Garcia of California, the incoming chairman of the House Committee on Oversight and Government Reform. He has been mapping out the panel's investigative agenda for months.

New probes will focus on the Trump family's business dealings, corporate corruption, Department of Homeland Security and Immigration and Customs Enforcement actions and the Jeffrey Epstein scandal, Garcia said.

Garcia wants to know more about Donald Trump Jr.'s Bahamas wedding festivities that were partially paid for by a Russian oligarch, a $2 billion investment that Jared Kushner's private equity fund received from Saudi Arabia's sovereign wealth fund, the Trump family's crypto ventures, companies linked to the president's sons that have received Pentagon contracts, allegations of a pay-to-play scheme and other kickbacks related to DHS contracts and White House ballroom donations.
"Folks that need to be concerned first are administration officials that have caused real harm. We're going to investigate the abuses," Garcia said at a news conference in California on Wednesday.
He singled out White House deputy chief of staff Stephen Miller, former DHS official Corey Lewandowski and former DHS secretary Kristi Noem, as well as Trump family members, as possible targets.
"There's a lot of folks that need to understand that we are going to ask them to testify in front of the U.S. Congress," Garcia said.

He acknowledged that the Trump Justice Department is unlikely to take any enforcement action against those who don't cooperate. But he said that in the majority, Democrats will have the power to sue on behalf of the House.
"We have the power of contempt charges. And contempt charges not only go to the DOJ; there's also a civil contempt process that goes to the courts," he said.

Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin of Maryland, who will lead the House Judiciary Committee, has his own lengthy list of investigative targets, some of which overlap with the oversight committee, like the Justice Department's handling of the Epstein probe and Ghislaine Maxwell's transfer to a low-security prison.

Raskin also plans to scrutinize what Democrats have characterized as "slush funds" — an international initiative called the "Board of Peace;" the "anti-weaponization" fund created from a settlement of a Trump lawsuit against the IRS and Treasury Department and White House ballroom funding.
"There are private entities that we can subpoena to come in," Raskin told Punchbowl News, regarding other avenues to gather information from outside of the Trump administration.
Rep. Adam Smith of Washington, the top Democrat on the House Armed Services Committee, said he plans to conduct "vigorous oversight" of the Defense Department.

The "illegal war against Iran is top of mind for me and the American people," Smith said in a statement Wednesday. He said he also plans to look at "sweetheart deals" and waste, fraud and abuse in government contracts.

Smith also wants to investigate the "unauthorized military strikes in the Caribbean and Latin America, the deployment of the military to U.S. cities, and the blatant and corrosive politicization of our Armed Forces and purging of the ranks based on loyalty and ideology."

Douglas Kriner, a professor in Cornell University's Government Department, said "there's always been greater investigatory activity in divided governments than when the president's party controls Congress." He said the House has always been more aggressive in its investigations than the Senate.

A White House official said that if Democrats want to "abuse their power and politicize the process of investigations, subpoenas and destroying lives, they should be reminded that we still control the federal government and all of its powers."

"As the president has said, he's willing to work with anyone to continue delivering victories for hardworking Americans," said White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis. "If Democrats choose to pursue sham investigations and radical left policies, they are choosing to work against the American people."
Not inclined to impeach Trump at this point

During the campaign, Mr. Trump often predicted he'd be impeached if Democrats took control of Congress, but for now, they've shown no sign that this is on their agenda. On Wednesday, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries told reporters, "I haven't had a single member of the House Democratic Caucus talk to me about impeachment."
Mr. Trump was impeached twice during his first term when Democrats controlled the House. Both efforts ended without a conviction in the Senate, which requires a two-thirds majority vote.

Even those on the far left, like Rep.-elect Melat Kiros of Colorado, who is among the contingent of democratic socialists joining Congress next year, told CBS News in a recent interview that the party should focus on legislation that could make a material difference in the lives of working-class people.
"I'm not convinced that there is a path forward for impeaching the president that would lead to removal," she said.
Asked whether he would support impeaching the president, Rep.-elect Chris Rabb of Pennsylvania, another democratic socialist, told CBS News that the question was "too broad" for him to answer.

Some Democratic leaders like Raskin agree there are more important issues to address than pursuing impeachment, even though they believe that Mr. Trump has committed impeachable offenses. Raskin was the lead House manager for Mr. Trump's second impeachment.
The president also perceives that there's currently little appetite for a third try.

"Not even a little bit," Mr. Trump responded when asked if he was worried about being impeached again. "I think it would destroy the Democrat Party if they did that. 'Cause impeachment for no reason — what, for having a successful country? Our country is more successful now than at any time in its history."
Taking back power of the purse

Democrats will also be taking back Congress' power of the purse from Mr. Trump, who often bypassed the Senate and the House, and Republicans in the Capitol, who usually went along with the president's budget priorities. But their much slimmer House majority often slowed down the process.
Democratic Rep. Rosa DeLauro of Connecticut, who's expected to lead the House Appropriations Committee, said she plans to use "what tools are available" to rein in the Trump administration.
In a recent interview, DeLauro said she wants to address cost-of-living issues but also said, "I will fight Donald Trump and the Cabinet secretaries as well."
"I'm going to hold the Trump administration accountable for the corruption," she said. "I'm going to rein in corruption at the highest level of government. I would do that through appropriations."
"We will build in guardrails in the appropriation bills," DeLauro added.
Asked whether she would consider zeroing out funding to enforce accountability, DeLauro said all options "will be reviewed."

Although congressional Democrats plan to ratchet up the pressure on the Trump administration, they know they'll need to work with Republicans on major legislation, like funding the government because of the Senate filibuster. The majority of measures need to reach a 60-vote threshold of support in the Senate to overcome a filibuster.

With a few exceptions like the One Big Beautiful Bill Act, "most of what Congress has done in the first two years of the Trump administration has required bipartisan support because it's had to overcome the filibuster," said Molly Reynolds, vice president and director of governance studies at the Brookings Institution. "So, in that sense, we would still be looking at bipartisan legislating."

Kriner suggested Democrats may try to use the appropriations process, limitation riders and other tools at their disposal to influence what Mr. Trump's agencies can and can't do. And more than once, the White House Office of Management and Budget has unilaterally made spending decisions about funds that were already appropriated by Congress. The OMB has tried to make the case, Kriner said, that presidents have exclusive powers under Article II to decide how money is spent.

"That's been the central front of an institutional battle over the first two years of the Trump administration, and it has really big, lasting implications for what the balance of power across the branches is going to look like," Kriner said.
In contrast with the White House's pugnacious tone, Mr. Trump has been more conciliatory and said he may work with Democrats.

"My message is congratulations to the Democrats, and I look forward to working with you for the good of our country," the president told CBS News senior White House correspondent Weijia Jiang on Tuesday night.
What will happen to Trump nominees?
Democratic control of the Senate will make it difficult for the president to get his nominees confirmed.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly said he doesn't plan to fire Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. But he also told ABC News' Jonathan Karl on Wednesday that it would be easier to confirm a new defense secretary before the new Congress is seated in January.
The president will likely have to rely on acting officials for roles that need to be filled, unless he nominates candidates who can win bipartisan support.
Power of the pen
The president has relied on executive authority for much of his second-term agenda, even under the unified control of government he enjoyed during his first two years in office.

Brandon Rottinghaus, political science professor at the University of Houston, said, "That's been his M.O. He likes it as a streamlined way to pursue his objectives in a way that aren't checked typically by Congress."

Rottinghaus noted that President Barack Obama increasingly relied on executive actions after Republicans won back the House in 2010, especially on his immigration priorities, many of which were challenged in court and rolled back by the Trump administration.
"Legislative constraints will encourage presidential unilateralism, but the courts will definitely limit those kinds of actions," Rottinghaus said.

The president picked up his pen Thursday to sign an executive order designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room national landmarks, saying future presidents won't be able to make major changes. But a future president could also sign a new executive order to undo it.
Trump's relationship with Republicans
Before the elections, most Republicans in Congress supported, defended and voted for Mr. Trump's priorities. Now, Mr. Trump is looking at what Rottinghaus called a "ticking clock."

"The last two years are going to be the hardest of his political career," Rottinghaus said. "His leverage over members of Congress, especially Republicans, will diminish as lawmakers think about their own political futures rather than the president's."
"Republicans are going to have to figure out a way forward," he continued. "You know, they're going to have to figure out a way forward around Donald Trump."

title: Did GOP efforts to redistrict the House turn into a dummymander?
summary: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House.
story: Republicans undertook a historic effort to redraw several states' Congressional districts mid-decade in an attempt to maintain control of the House. That effort was rebuffed on Tuesday night as the GOP was on track to lose all of the districts it tried to gerrymander.

There were several reasons that states undertook what had previously been a rare practice of mid-decade redistricting. Republican efforts started when President Trump ordered Texas lawmakers to redraw their map to net up to five seats for the GOP.
But despite the all-out effort, Democrats won control of the House on Tuesday, with CBS News estimating Democrats could end up with 251 to 268 House seats.

With the House decisively swinging toward Democrats and Democrats undertaking measures in a few states to counter the GOP's efforts, Republicans are faced with the possibility of having created a so-called "dummymander," a situation in which a party tries to gerrymander, but ends up benefiting the other party.
Here's a state-by-state breakdown of how the redistricting efforts panned out:
Texas

Texas Republicans went into Election Day controlling 24 seats, while Democrats controlled 13 seats and there was one seat in a GOP-leaning district that was vacant. In redrawing the map, Republicans sought to emphasize Mr. Trump's gains in South Texas to win five more seats.
Republicans won 24 seats and Democrats won 14 seats in the midterms, making Texas a dummymander.
Ohio

A commission comprising mainly Republicans hand-picked by GOP lawmakers redrew Ohio's map to net two more seats for their party. Republicans heavily targeted longtime Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur's district in the northern part of the state and Rep. Greg Landsman's Cincinnati-area district.

Heading into Tuesday night, Ohio Republicans controlled 10 seats and Democrats controlled five. Eight Democrats, including Kaptur and Landsman, won Tuesday night. Republicans only won seven districts, making Ohio a dummymander.
North Carolina
Although North Carolina has a Democratic governor, Republican lawmakers have a veto-proof majority in the statehouse and pushed through a new map that attempted to oust Democratic Rep. Don Davis.

North Carolina Republicans controlled 10 House seats going into Election Day, while Democrats controlled four, including Davis' district. As of Thursday, nine Democrats had won — including Davis — and CBS News estimated five districts with Republican incumbents were toss-ups, making the state a dummymander.
Louisiana

Louisiana lawmakers redrew their districts after the Supreme Court ruled in June that compliance with Section 2 of the Voting Rights Act could not justify the state's use of race in redrawing its House district lines.

Louisiana went into Election Day with four House seats controlled by Republicans and two controlled by Democrats. The new map aimed to eliminate one of the majority-Black districts that currently has Democratic representatives.

As of Thursday, Republicans had won three districts, while Democrats had won one. CBS News estimates Louisiana's 6th District is a toss-up and the 5th District race will go to a runoff. If Democrats win either of those districts, Louisiana will be a dummymander.
Alabama

After the same Supreme Court decision, Alabama Republicans sought to eliminate the state's two majority Black districts, both of which are represented by Democrats. Both incumbents won reelection on Tuesday, so Republicans did not net any more than the five they already controlled, making Alabama a dummymander.
Tennessee
Tennessee lawmakers also redrew their map after that Supreme Court decision to target the lone Democratic district in Memphis.

Going into Election Day, Republicans had eight seats, and Democrats had one. As of Thursday, Republicans had won eight seats, including the newly drawn 9th District that includes Memphis, and one seat is estimated as a toss-up. If Democrats win the remaining toss-up race, the state's House delegation will remain the same.
Florida
Led by Florida's Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis, GOP lawmakers redrew their map to net up to four more seats for their party.

Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled 20 seats and Democrats controlled eight. As of Thursday, Republicans had won 17 seats, Democrats had won seven and there were four districts that CBS News estimated were toss-ups. If Democrats win any of the toss-up races, Florida will be a dummymander.
Missouri

Missouri's GOP-led legislature last year redrew its map to make one of the state's two Democratic-held districts more friendly to Republicans. But the map's legality was challenged, and a state court ruled the map could not be used unless it was approved by voters. The Supreme Court three times blocked Missouri from using the new map, leaving the 2022 congressional districts in place for Tuesday's election.
Heading into Election Day, Republicans controlled six districts while Democrats held two. Democrats flipped another district, giving them three seats to the Republicans' five.
Indiana

Mr. Trump had also pushed lawmakers in Indiana to pass a map that would edge out the state's two Democratic lawmakers and make it a 9-0 Republican delegation. Despite pressure from Mr. Trump, the GOP-led state Senate rejected the new map.
Using the same boundaries as the last two cycles, Democrats held onto their two seats and flipped a third, making the state's representation 6-3.
South Carolina

South Carolina Republicans also sought to redraw their map after the Supreme Court decision in an effort to edge out powerful Democratic Rep. Jim Clyburn and make the state's representation 7-0 for Republicans. But the measure failed in the state Senate, and Clyburn won reelection on Tuesday. Two other races are considered toss-ups.
California

In response to Texas' redistricting efforts, California's Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom put forth a ballot measure to redraw the map to gain five seats for Democrats, which was decisively approved by voters.

Heading into Election Day, Democrats held 43 districts and Republicans held nine. As of Thursday, Democrats won in 44 districts, while CBS News estimates another four are likely Democratic. Republicans have won two districts and another two are likely Republican.
Since Democrats picked up seats in California, it is a successful gerrymander for Democrats.
Utah

A judge in 2025 rejected Utah's congressional map that favored Republicans in all four districts, and then a district court rejected the redistricting map selected by the GOP-controlled legislature and instead selected a map that would create a Democratic-leaning congressional district in Salt Lake City.
Under the new map, Democrat Ben McAdams won the 1st District in Salt Lake City by 47 points.
Virginia

Virginia voters decisively approved a ballot measure in April to redraw the congressional map to favor Democrats in 10 districts and Republicans in one. But the map was thrown out by the Virginia Supreme Court, putting back in place the map drawn in 2021.
Heading into Tuesday, Democrats held six seats while Republicans held five. Using the same boundaries as the past two cycles, Democrats won eight seats and Republicans won three.
Maryland

Maryland's state constitution requires that congressional districts be compact and connected, and Democratic Gov. Wes Moore and other Democratic lawmakers championed a ballot initiative to remove those restraints on redistricting.
The ballot initiative, known as Question 3, passed by 20 points on Tuesday, so Democrats are likely to redraw their map now to edge out their sole GOP representative.

title: Lawler defeated in New York battleground district
summary: Democrat Cait Conley won the crucial 17th Congressional District seat.
story: Washington — Democrat Cait Conley defeated two-term Republican Rep. Mike Lawler, winning a highly competitive seat in New York's Hudson Valley region, CBS News projected.
Lawler's loss is another setback for Republicans. CBS News has projected that Democrats will take control of the House in January with a wide majority.
Lawler called Conley to concede Tuesday, though vote-counting continued for longer than expected due to issues at polling precincts in Westchester County.

"I have never been afforded in any of my elections a concession on election night and I fundamentally believe it's the right thing to do," he said. "And so I congratulate Cait on her win and wish her well as our next member of Congress."

Before redistricting shuffled the boundaries in several states for the 2026 election, Lawler was one of just three Republicans who won districts carried by Democratic presidential nominee Kamala Harris in 2024.

A West Point graduate, Conley served six tours overseas before joining the National Security Council and the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency during the Biden administration. Though she grew up in a neighboring area, she moved to the 17th District months before announcing her campaign.

In their Sept. 30 debate, Conley said she supports continued military aid to Israel and did not believe that Israel's actions in Gaza constitute a genocide — positions at odds with many in her party, but which could be crucial given the district's demographics.

Lawler has held the lower Hudson Valley seat since 2023 after narrowly ousting Democratic incumbent Sean Patrick Maloney, who served as House Democrats' campaign chief. In 2025, Lawler considered running for New York governor, but opted to run for a third term as Republicans sought to hang on to the crucial battleground seat.

Lawler has cast himself as a moderate who has been willing to buck his party, including on immigration protections for Haitians and on extending the now-expired enhanced Affordable Care Act tax credits. Lawler also played a central role in securing a temporary increase to the cap on state and local tax deductions — a bipartisan issue on the East and West coasts — as part of President Trump's sweeping tax and spending package, the One Big Beautiful Bill Act.
In the recent debate, Lawler tried to appeal to voters on both sides, claiming that he ranks "among the most bipartisan and effective members of Congress."
But Lawler has also embraced Mr. Trump, campaigning with him in May even as he risked alienating swing voters who are pessimistic about the president's handling of the economy and Iran war.

title: CBS News exit polls show how Democrats won in the midterms
summary: Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
story: Note: Poll percentages may have updated since this was published.
Economic issues helped propel President Trump to victory in 2024, and those same issues dragged down his party in 2026.
Fueled in part by economic frustration, parts of the Democratic coalition that Mr. Trump made inroads with in 2024 swung back toward Democrats this year.
Persistent negative views of the economy turned against the party in power. Those who said the economy was bad voted for Democrats for the House, according to CBS News exit polls.

This was the second straight election most voters told us inflation was a hardship for them, and more said their finances are worse now compared to two years ago — these voters backed Democrats over the Republicans for the House.
This election was clearly a referendum on Mr. Trump and largely a rejection of his policies.
Nationally, most said his tariffs hurt the economy, his administration's immigration efforts went too far and the decision to take military action against Iran was the wrong one.
Groups coming back to the Democrats

In 2024, Mr. Trump made gains nationally with young voters, Latinos and women, but majorities of all these groups backed Democrats for the House this year. Democrats' margins with women were similar to what they were in 2018 when Democrats won control of the House during the president's first term.
And majorities of each of these key groups said the cost of living was crucial in their vote.
Democrats made inroads with Republican-leaning groups
Historically, men have generally backed Republicans in both presidential and midterm elections, but they largely split their votes this year.
Mr. Trump won men by double digits in 2024. Today, most disapprove of the job he is doing, and those who do backed Democrats.
White women historically mostly vote Republican, but they narrowly backed Democrats in this election, according to exit polls.

The national electorate was slightly more Democratic than the most recent two elections, which helped Democrats. But their lead with independents was critical in putting them over the top. They also led with those who did not vote in the 2024 presidential election.
This electorate was a pessimistic one — unhappy about the state of the country and the economy and not very hopeful for the next generation.
So the Democrats may have their work cut out for them.
Just over half of voters had an unfavorable view of the party. Voters did give the Democrats an edge over Republicans on the economy, so they likely expect results.
Joe Williams contributed to this report.

title: Rob Sand's runway modeling past resurfaces after Iowa gubernatorial win
summary: Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew the Iowa governor-elect once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, who was previously elected to the Iowa state auditor's office, replied affirmatively in the comments.
story: Iowa Gov.-elect Rob Sand, who won Tuesday's election, walked runways for Prada and other fashion houses while he was in college, according to Vogue.

Vogue asked on Instagram whether followers knew that Sand once modeled for Prada. A verified account for Sand, @robsandia, replied in the comments Thursday: "Yes, I knew that." The comment had more than 700 likes about 20 minutes later, and many replies were congratulatory.
"From runway to run USA ✨," one comment read, while another enthused, "THE biggest flex EVER for a politician plus 2 words: Italian Vogue. YES SIR! 👏 🔥"

Vogue reported that the modeling past surfaced on social media after his win, when a user reposted a video of Sand with a caption expressing disbelief that he once modeled in the early 2000s. A Google search confirmed it, Vogue said.

WCCO has reached out to Sand's campaign for confirmation and are awaiting response. However, the New York Times earlier reported, in a 2019 profile, that Sand briefly modeled in Paris and Milan while in college but does not like to talk about it.

Sand began modeling while attending Brown University, which Vogue described as a successful side hustle that took him to Milan. He walked for Prada, the Japanese label Number (N)ine and Giuliano Fujiwara, and appeared in editorial spreads, including a fall 2002 AnOther Magazine spread titled "Adolescents," Vogue reported.
Sand told Newsweek, according to Vogue, that he missed a chance to caucus in 2004 in his hometown of Decorah, Iowa, because he was in Milan.
Sand, who was previously elected as Iowa's state auditor, defeated Republican Zach Lahn in Tuesday's race for governor.

title: Why did Republicans lose the midterms?
summary: Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong, and a brewing blame-game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.
story: Washington — Widespread Republican losses in the midterm elections are roiling the GOP, prompting soul-searching over what went wrong and a brewing blame game that's expected to heat up as the party looks toward the next election.

From House and Senate races to governors' mansions, Republicans saw striking losses, both in battlegrounds and in places where the party saw significant support just two years ago. The victories dramatically shifted the balance of power in Washington, delivering Democrats a sizable majority in the House far beyond what was expected heading into Election Day, as well as a Senate majority larger than what the GOP has enjoyed for the last two years.

As Republicans process the results, including some GOP officials who have ambitions of their own in 2028, they're offering frank assessments of the shortcomings — and laying the groundwork for where the party heads next.
The war in Iran

Throughout the country, as Republicans tried to rally support around their accomplishments over the last two years, the president's war in Iran loomed large. And in this week's elections, its impact on the economy and prices appeared to overshadow most everything else.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vice President JD Vance said in a candid post on social media that was among the first efforts from a top Republican to unpack the party's losses.

"If you'd like to argue it was worth it, that losing the Senate for the next 6 years was worth it, then do so. Argue it was a worthwhile cost to pay," said Vance, who is widely seen as a possible presidential contender in 2028. "But everyone knows why we lost. And any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Asked about the comments, President Trump told reporters that it's "largely true" that Republicans lost the House and Senate because war led to higher energy prices, agreeing with Vance. But he also argued that the war has been worthwhile.
"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," Mr. Trump said.

Early in the war, Mr. Trump acknowledged that the vice president was "philosophically, a little bit different than me," and was "less enthusiastic about going" into Iran. Still, Vance has largely stood by Mr. Trump on Iran.
GOP Sen. Ted Cruz of Texas, who called the midterms a "Watergate-level repudiation," also cited the war, saying, "the Iran war has dragged on too long."
"It should have been brief, decisive, and over — it needs to end," said Cruz, who has vocally supported the war.
But Cruz pointed more broadly to the war's impact on prices, citing gas and diesel, along with the impacts of the president's trade policy, saying, "Tariffs have made everything too expensive."

Former Vice President Mike Pence also criticized Republicans' handling of the Iran war, but from the opposite direction, writing that the "unfinished war against Iran became an albatross around the necks of Republicans because Washington stopped short and pursued appeasement rather than allowing our troops to finish off the threat posed by the Iranian regime, once and for all."
Cost of living takes center stage
More so than the war in Iran, voters nationally said cost of living was a major factor in their vote, according to CBS News exit polls.

Cruz said many GOP candidates this cycle seemed "like they didn't understand or they didn't care" about the cost of living. He said there's a "very real economic disconnect: Our K-shaped economy is a yawning divide," referring to the idea that some Americans' fortunes are on the upswing while others are pointing downward.

The Texas Republican cited Elon Musk becoming the world's first trillionaire, while at the same time, millions of Americans struggled to feed their families. And as data centers were constructed and the wealthiest people became even wealthier, he said Americans saw their electricity bills go up significantly in recent years.
"Understandably, people were pissed off," he said. "And elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain."

Democrats hammered Republicans over the cost of living, as economic populism became a key tenet of the cycle, while some candidates, like James Talarico in Texas, billed the fight as top-versus-bottom, rather than left-versus-right. Texas Republicans suffered one of the most striking routs of the midterms: Starting next year, Cruz will be one of the only Republican statewide elected officials in a state that was once viewed as almost imperviously red.

GOP Sen. John Cornyn of Texas, whose seat Talarico will take in the new year after Cornyn lost his primary to Texas Attorney General Ken Paxton, lamented that after voters trusted Mr. Trump and the GOP to "protect their pocketbooks" in the 2024 elections, the president "misread his mandate."

"Voters wanted to retool our trading relationships, but got arbitrary 'Liberation Day' tariffs that raised prices without creating incentives for long-term reshoring," Cornyn wrote in a Wall Street Journal op-ed. "Voters wanted secure borders and peaceful streets, but got hyperaggressive immigration enforcement. The Iran conflict came with no attempt to persuade the public. And Mr. Trump signaled disconnection by focusing on sideshows like swimming-pool liners in the Reflecting Pool."
Cornyn added, "Americans elected the Donald Trump who put on the apron of the Golden Arches and got a plan for a Triumphal Arch instead."

Cornyn, who was formerly the No. 2 Senate Republican, also pointed to how corruption surged to a top issue for voters, "thanks to flawed midterm candidates and a parade of unsavory headlines out of Washington."

Democrats like Talarico worked hard to tie corruption to cost-of-living concerns expressed widely. And roughly nine in 10 voters nationally said government corruption was a major factor in their vote.

"Voters won't trust Republicans to cut fraud and scams out of government programs until we cut them out of our own ranks," Cornyn wrote. "Party leaders have to stop excusing the inexcusable and police our side of the aisle — or voters will continue to police it for us."
Focus on culture wars
Beyond the cost-of-living concerns, some Republicans also pointed to an over-emphasis on culture war issues.

Outgoing Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis, who called the midterm outcomes as "close to an extension-level event for Republicans as we have seen probably in the last hundred years," said he knew Republicans were in trouble when he saw they were spending hundreds of millions of dollars on ads centering transgender issues.
"That was not the issue motivating voters, and it was kind of like an attempt to just scare Republicans to vote," DeSantis said at a news conference.

By late October, more than $180 million had been spent on ads that centered transgender-related attacks against Democrats, according to The Associated Press, reminiscent of the "Kamala is for they/them, Trump is for you" ads that blanketed the airwaves in the 2024 presidential election.

DeSantis — who has staked out conservative positions on transgender issues — argued the issue is no longer as potent, saying: "Four years ago, we were in the peak-woke era." But now, he argued, "the issues are different."
"Republicans, it seemed like — in some of the ads I was seeing, with how much money they were spending — they really were fighting yesterday's battles," he said.

As Republicans turned their attention to transgender and other culture-war issues, Democrats didn't give the attacks traction, shifting the focus at nearly every turn to affordability concerns. Some moderate Democrats in battleground states also voiced opposition to transgender athletes' participation in girls' sports, which may have neutralized some attacks.

But DeSantis also argued the election wasn't the result of voters having positive views of Democrats — exit polling shows voters had unfavorable opinions of both parties, though Republicans' favorability (40%) was lower than Democrats' (47%).

Instead, DeSantis said, it was a "rejection of Republicans in Washington." And that rebuke wasn't only aimed at the president, he argued, but also the GOP-controlled Congress, as voters became "frustrated with the lack of productivity from Republicans in the House and Senate."
"So it's really both sides of Pennsylvania Avenue," DeSantis said. "It's not just one."

title: Trump's lawyers argue appeal in "hush money" case
summary: President Trump was convicted in 2024 of 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to adult film star Stormy Daniels.
story: President Trump's lawyers on Thursday urged a New York appellate court to throw out his conviction on 34 felonies tied to a 2016 "hush money" payment to an adult film star.

They argued that the jury was given flawed instructions, allowing them to consider violations of federal election law as part of their determination in the case, calling it an "obvious ground for reversal." Mr. Trump has long argued that the federal law, known as FECA, preempts state prosecution.

"All of the payments that are issued in this case, whether it be the payments to [adult film star Stormy Daniels], other payments to two other folks, those were payments that were deemed to be illegal contributions or expenditures under FECA," said Mr. Trump's attorney, Robert Giuffra.
Steven Wu, a lawyer for Manhattan District Attorney Alvin Bragg, countered that a federal court has twice rejected the claim that FECA preempted New York's prosecution of Mr. Trump.
"This court should reach the same conclusion here," Wu said.
Giuffra and Wu were interrupted frequently by a five-judge panel that pelted them with questions picking apart their arguments.

A unanimous jury convicted Mr. Trump in May 2024 for his part in a scheme to falsify business records related to reimbursements made to Michael Cohen, his attorney at the time. Cohen had paid $130,000 to adult film star Stormy Daniels, days before the 2016 election, in exchange for her silence about an alleged sexual encounter with Mr. Trump years earlier. Mr. Trump has denied the allegations.

The jury was asked to consider if Mr. Trump falsified business records, counts that by themselves would have been misdemeanors, and if he intended to commit any other crime in doing so, including bank fraud, tax fraud or the violations of FECA — any of which elevated the charges to felonies. They did not have to be unanimous in what other crimes they thought he intended to commit.
Giuffra, the powerful co-chair of the white-shoe firm Sullivan & Cromwell, argued that they should have been required to be unanimous on that element of the felony.

Wu noted that the trial judge in the case asked Mr. Trump's defense attorneys about that, and they indicated they did not believe it was required under the law. Instead, they asked the judge to include that directive "in his discretion because of the importance of the case," Wu said, paraphrasing Emil Bove III, who was one of Mr. Trump's trial lawyers.
The trial judge, Juan Merchan, declined.
"What you're asking me to do is change the law, and I'm not going to do that," Merchan said at the time.

Mr. Trump's attorneys in the case have changed since the 2024 trial — one former defense attorney, Todd Blanche, is now U.S. attorney general, and Bove is now a federal judge — but his new team of personal lawyers has continued to echo the arguments he made throughout the trial.
An Oct. 16 filing by Giuffra began with a line that Mr. Trump himself frequently said and posted on social media: The case, "should have never been brought."

A spokesman for Mr. Trump's legal team said a 2024 Supreme Court decision related to presidential immunity, "the federal and New York state Constitutions, and other established legal precedent mandate that the Witch Hunt perpetrated by the Manhattan D.A. be overturned and dismissed."
"President Trump will continue defeating Democrat weaponization at every turn," the spokesperson said.
Lawyers for Bragg have characterized the 2016 "hush money" plan as "a conspiracy to defraud the American public and government regulators."
"The criminal charges here arose from [Mr. Trump's] unofficial, non-presidential conduct—as multiple courts have already found," they wrote in a July brief.
The arguments came a week after the death of a judge who was presiding over a yearslong parallel effort by Mr. Trump to move the case from state to federal court.

The judge, Alvin Hellerstein, repeatedly rejected Mr. Trump's arguments, and was particularly scathing in his response to Mr. Trump's claim that the reimbursements to Cohen were related to his official work as president.

"Reimbursing Cohen for advancing hush money to [Stormy Daniels] cannot be considered the performance of a constitutional duty," Hellerstein wrote. "Falsifying business records to hide such reimbursement, and to transform the reimbursement into a business expense for Trump and income to Cohen, likewise does not relate to a presidential duty."
On Thursday, the two sides also argued over whether tweets shown at trial and testimony of former White House communications director Hope Hicks fell under presidential immunity.

One judge on the panel said Hicks' testimony, which described a conversation about the Stormy Daniels allegations after they became public, may have fit in the "gray area of what's in the outer sphere of presidential duties."
Asked for his thoughts after the arguments, Giuffra said, "I think it went well."
"We should definitely win," he said.

title: Midterm elections could zap the data center buildout, experts say
summary: Democratic victories in several gubernatorial races are likely to slow data center development across the U.S., according to tech analysts.
story: The Democrats' sweeping victories in the midterm elections on Tuesday could buoy opponents of data centers in some parts of the U.S. and slow the spread of the controversial facilities, according to Wall Street analysts.

As of Wednesday afternoon, voters had approved 38 ballot measures restricting data centers in communities across California, Illinois, Maine, Ohio, New York and other states, according to an analysis from political research firm Redbud Consulting. Residents in Harwood, North Dakota, were the only voters to approve a data center.
The election also elevates a number of state and gubernatorial candidates who made stricter regulation of data centers a key part of their campaigns.

The rapid development of data centers around the U.S. to help power artificial intelligence has provoked widespread public backlash. By a margin of more than 2-to-1, more Americans oppose than favor building a new data center in their area, a CBS News poll found this summer.
Focus on Texas

Franklin Templeton chief market strategist Stephen Dover predicted that the election results will lead to a "slowdown in data centers being built," bringing new regulations and costs for their developers.

"For tech investors, the big focus is will these midterm elections slow the pace of the planned 800 to 1,000 data centers across the U.S. fueling the AI Revolution," Yorkville Ives & Co. technology analyst Dan Ives said in a report. "The answer in our view is a clear YES."

Ives pointed to Texas, which accounts for 25% to 30% of the data center capacity expected to come online by 2030, as one state that could be affected. Democrat Gina Hinojosa, who defeated Republican incumbent Greg Abbott in the race for governor, proposed a temporary ban on data center construction during her campaign.
"Texas is the foundation of the AI buildout in the U.S.," Ives told CBS News.
Hinojosa's win over Abbott could stall the addition of 13 gigawatts of data-center power in Texas, according to Gordon Johnson, CEO and founder of the investment adviser GLJ Research.
Abbott had already suspended data center approvals, which makes it easy for Hinojosa to extend the moratorium.
"Texas already has a moratorium — Abbott built it. All the new governor has to do is keep it in place. She doesn't need a new law to keep data center permits frozen," Johnson told CBS News.
Keisha Lance Bottoms' gubernatorial victory in Georgia, the third-largest data center market, also has significant implications for the infrastructure buildout.

Bottoms, who campaigned on pausing new data center construction in the state, told CBS Mornings on Wednesday that she would immediately "sign an executive order for that pause, and then we will determine what else we need to do administratively to take that pause into effect."
Bottoms also said she plans to review tax incentives offered in Georgia that have spurred data center development.

"So, of course, we are going to have to take a look at what those agreements entail and determine what our remedies are to enact that pause, but I don't think we're going to get a lot of pushback across the state," she said. "Many local governments have already taken that first step."
Cooling an overheated sector

Market analyst Adam Crisafulli of Vital Knowledge noted that semiconductor, hardware and other stocks associated with data center construction fell sharply on Wednesday amid investor concerns over permitting delays.

Seema Shah, chief global strategist at Principal Asset Management, thinks data center developers could face additional requirements to invest in electrical grids and potentially lose tax incentives, thereby raising their costs. She added in a research note that higher development costs for new facilities could "increase the value of existing infrastructure that is already powered, permitted, and operational."

Massive investment in data centers and the artificial intelligence sector more broadly has helped propel U.S. economic growth and drive stock market gains. In the long term, however, a slower data center buildout is unlikely to hamstring the economy, Dover of Franklin Templeton told CBS News.

"It's possible to argue that the AI trade and data center buildout was getting overheated, and this could dampen some of the excessive investment that might not have a good return on capital, which investors have questioned anyway," he said. "So unbridled expansion will be tempered a bit, but probably not a lot."
Although data center moratoriums may delay construction, they're unlikely to torpedo capital spending on AI or short-circuit broader growth, according to economists.

"A more restrictive stance toward data centers would stretch the timelines of future projects, and slower construction in the medium to long term wouldn't necessarily be a bad outcome for the macroeconomy," analysts with Oxford Economics said in a report.
