title: 'The Pitt' star Noah Wyle does 100 push-ups a day ‘come rain or come shine’ at 55
summary: Noah Wyle reveals his daily push-ups routine and chin-up bar goal with his accountability partner while filming the demanding medical drama "The Pitt."
story: The 55-year-old actor told Fox News Digital that he does 100 push ups every day on set and hopes to be able to do 10 pull ups by the end of season three.
Noah Wyle is sharing how he manages to stay fit while filming the hit medical drama, "The Pitt."

During a recent interview with Fox News Digital, the 55-year-old actor shared what it means for the Cedar Sinai Board of Governors to honor the show with the Hollywood Leadership Award, and how he stays fit enough to keep up with filming the physically demanding HBO Max show.

"I have an accountability partner and a guy named Dash Land who's the on-set dresser and he and I do a hundred push-ups every day, come rain or come shine. That's the base," Wyle said about his fitness routine. "We try to add a little bit on top of that if we can, if we remember to. That's base. We also installed a chin-up bar recently. I have a goal to be, I'm going to embarrass myself, to do ten by the end of the season. I'm at six right now, solid six."
The actor stars in "The Pitt," an intense medical drama which follows emergency nurses and doctors over the course of one shift, with each episode showcasing one hour of a 12-hour shift.
Wyle shared he stays fit by doing 100 push-ups every day. (Warrick Page/HBO Max)
NOAH WYLE, MATT DAMON, LEONARDO DICAPRIO STILL CAPTIVATING AUDIENCES WELL INTO THEIR 50S

Wyle portrays Dr. Robby on the show, who is the chief attending physician and head of the emergency department at the fictional Pittsburgh Trauma Medical Center, and is dealing with the emotional toll years of working on the frontlines of medicine can take on a person.

When speaking to Veja+ in January, Wyle said that the cast has to "take very good care of ourselves" almost "out of necessity," because while filming they "work 14 hours a day, five days a week, for nine months straight."
WATCH HERE: NOAH WYLE WORKS OUT EVERYDAY ON THE SET OF ‘THE PITT’ WITH AN ACCOUNTABILITY PARTNER

"At the beginning of filming I asked all the actors to do an exercise, and it was just standing on your feet for 15 hours," he said. "And as you stand, every hour begin to note where your fatigue is coming in – where do you get stiff, where's painful, when do you have to use the bathroom, when do you get hungry. Write all that down and then work it into the appropriate hour of your shift, and it'll give you the physicality that you need."

Men's Health referred this exercise as NEAT, which stands for non-exercise activity thermogenesis, which takes into account everyday activities which aren't necessarily considered exercise, but get the heart rate up, such as mowing the lawn or vacuuming the floor.
Wyle previously detailed the 14-hour workdays on set of "The Pitt." (Jesse Grant/Variety via Getty Images)

Wyle was named People Magazine's "Sexiest Man Alive" in 2026, and the internet has mixed emotions about it. (Gilbert Flores/2026GG/Penske Media via Getty Images)

The cast of "The Pitt," which also includes Emmy Award winners, Katherine LaNasa and Sean Hatosy, were recently honored by Cedar Sinai Medical Center at the Sunset Soiree, for the series' authentic portrayal of emergency medicine, a moment Wyle called "incredibly gratifying."

"Cedars is like the crown jewel of Los Angeles health care, and being a third generation Angelino, I'm extremely gratified to be recognized by them as an institution," he said. "They were where my first son was born. I've said goodbye to many a friend there. The work that they've given to the people that I've known on both ends of life has been stellar, exemplary, heroic, beautiful. I'm really happy to come out tonight to support them and to try and raise money for them by opening up my rolodex."
Prior to landing the role of Dr. Robbie on "The Pitt," Wyle starred in a different medical drama playing Dr. John Carter in "ER" alongside George Clooney.

title: Miranda Lambert says fan told her ‘I did shoot him’ after being inspired by ‘Gunpowder & Lead’
summary: A fan's shocking confession about "Gunpowder & Lead" left Miranda Lambert in tears and forever changed how she viewed the domestic abuse anthem.
story: The singer told Fox News Digital the best way to heal sometimes is to "face those things that you've been running from," and that's what she did with her new album.
Miranda Lambert is reflecting on a fan encounter that left her in tears.

During an appearance on the "And the Writer Is..." podcast, Lambert discussed the powerful impact "Gunpowder & Lead," her 2007 song about a woman confronting an abusive partner after he is released from jail, has had on her fans.

"It's such a huge staple for me in my catalog, just the subject matter, and how I got to that and who I got to write it with, and the stories I’ve heard from women over the years who have come up to me and said, ‘That song saved my life,’" Lambert said of the hit, which was released on her album "Crazy Ex-Girlfriend" and was co-written with Heather Little."At some meet-and-greets, I've heard some crazy things."
TRACE ADKINS SURVIVED EX-WIFE'S 'KILL SHOT' AFTER BULLET PASSED THROUGH HEART AND LUNGS
Miranda Lambert opened up about the impact her 2007 song "Gunpowder & Lead" has had on fans. (Getty Images)
She recalled one woman who approached her in Indianapolis and said she didn’t want a photo.
"She's like, ‘I just want to tell you that I finally had enough, and that song gave me the courage, and I did shoot him — and I got off,’" Lambert said.
"I was like, ‘OK,’" she continued. "She was dead serious. She was hardcore. And then we cried together."
Lambert said the woman’s story left her overwhelmed.

"When someone tells you something like that about something you wrote that didn’t actually happen to you, it’s very intense," she said. "She was like third in line at the meet-and-greet, and I had like 85 people, and I was like, ‘I’m going to need a minute.’ I needed to take a breath, hug her and recover from what that is."

Lambert previously explained how she drew on her unconventional upbringing when writing the song.
In a 2014 interview with SPIN Magazine, Lambert said her parents sometimes took in abused women and their children while she was growing up.

"When I was younger, my parents took in abused women and children, and their kids, to live with us from time to time, and I saw firsthand what abuse can do to a family, multiple times," she said.
Lambert's upbringing inspired the hit. (Brenton Ho/Dick Clark Productions via Getty Images)

"That song is from a real place — it’s not just a girl writing about something where she has no idea what the subject is about," Lambert continued. "I wrote it with a girl who experienced abuse herself."

title: ‘Back to the Future’ star Christopher Lloyd confesses he was ‘hooked’ on cocaine during ‘Taxi’ years
summary: Christopher Lloyd reveals in his memoir how cocaine and alcohol became "entrenched" in his life, leading to a dramatic rehab escape in Arizona.
story: Our "To Be Continued..." interview with Bob Gale as we talk longtime fandom, creating a treasured classic, inventions predicted like flying cars, releasing his "Complete Screenplay"

Christopher Lloyd is opening up about his decades-long struggle with alcohol and drug addiction, revealing how substance abuse became "entrenched" in his life before he ultimately sought treatment and found sobriety.
The 88-year-old actor detailed his battle in his new memoir, "In My Own Time," and discussed his recovery during a recent interview with his "Back to the Future" co-star, Michael J. Fox.
In the book, Lloyd recalled that his cocaine abuse began after a woman approached him at a Los Angeles nightclub and asked if he wanted to "do a snort."
BRAT PACK ICON ANDREW MCCARTHY SAYS DRINKING 'DERAILED MY CAREER ENTIRELY'
Christopher Lloyd shared details about his battle with addiction in his new book. (Getty Images)

"She meant cocaine, which at that point I had never tried," Lloyd wrote. "I hadn’t been out looking for it, but I said all right. We went out to her car and did a couple of lines. That was all it took. I was hooked almost immediately. I loved it, and that was where my cocaine abuse began."

"Within a couple of years of my arrival in Los Angeles, cocaine, alcohol, and pot had become woven into my life in a serious way," he continued. "It wasn’t just the occasional weekend indulgence. It got entrenched."

title: Even occasional marijuana use linked to higher stroke risk, study finds
summary: A study of nearly 450,000 adults found that both casual and heavy marijuana users faced higher odds of stroke and cardiovascular disease than non-users.
story: American Heart Association expert Robert Page warns that cannabis use may increase cardiovascular risks, even in younger adults who don't smoke tobacco. He urges patients to discuss cannabis use with their doctors.
A new study of nearly 450,000 American adults links cannabis use to an increased risk of stroke and cardiovascular disease.

The findings, scheduled for presentation at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 in Chicago Nov. 6–9, show that both casual and heavy marijuana users have higher odds of heart conditions compared to non-users.
Researchers analyzed survey responses collected between 2020 and 2024 through the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention's Behavioral Risk Factor Surveillance System.
SHARON STONE'S TERRIFYING WEED WITHDRAWAL SPARKS WARNING ABOUT TODAY'S POTENT MARIJUANA

People who reported using cannabis between one and five days per month had 23% higher odds of reporting a history of cardiovascular disease than non-users. Those using it 16 to 30 days per month had 21% higher odds.

"This study raises important concerns about cannabis use and cardiovascular health, particularly stroke," Dr. Kristen "Nicke" Worth, an Ohio-based physician and medical adviser at NuggMD, a telehealth platform for medical marijuana evaluations, told Fox News Digital.
A study of nearly 450,000 U.S. adults found that cannabis use is linked to significantly higher odds of cardiovascular disease, especially stroke. (iStock)

"One finding I found particularly interesting was that people who used cannabis just one to five days per month had somewhat higher reported odds of a previous stroke than people who used it more frequently," added Worth, who was not involved in the study.
Low-frequency users had 40% higher odds of a reported stroke, while heavy users had 25% higher odds. The study found no statistically significant link between cannabis use and heart attacks.
MARIJUANA USERS MAY FACE HIDDEN DRIVING DANGER THAT STANDARD TESTS CAN MISS

"That isn't what we'd necessarily expect from a straightforward dose-response relationship, where greater exposure is associated with greater risk. But we shouldn't interpret this as evidence that heavier use is safer," Worth said.
The method of consumption did not change the outcome. Whether participants smoked, vaped or consumed edibles like gummies, the risk remained consistent, according to the researchers.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

"We were surprised to find that the link between cannabis use and cardiovascular disease was not straightforward," said lead author Dr. Aabha Divya, an assistant professor of cardiothoracic surgery at Tulane University School of Medicine, in an AHA press release.

"We expected that the chances of heart disease would gradually rise as people used cannabis more often, but that wasn't the case. Both low-use and heavy-use groups had higher odds of developing heart disease."
While the study showed a strong correlation with strokes, researchers found no statistically significant link between cannabis frequency and heart attacks. (Getty Images)

The study comes amid growing commercial availability and use of the drug across the country. According to the research team, about one in six adults reported past-month cannabis use in 2024, up from one in 10 in 2020 — a 51% increase over four years.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Dr. Robert L. Page II, a professor of clinical pharmacy at the University of Colorado and an American Heart Association volunteer expert who was not involved in the study, said the findings challenge common assumptions about the drug's safety.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"In patients who use both, cannabis has always been considered an innocent bystander; however, this is not the case," Page said in a press release.
"Overall, cannabis is beginning to emerge as a major contributor to premature heart disease in young and older adults, which can lead to serious cardiovascular events."
"People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."
Page added that doctors should question patients about marijuana use just as they do with cigarettes and alcohol.

Researchers noted several key limitations to the findings. Because the study was observational and captured data from only a single point in time, it can only show a statistical link and cannot prove that cannabis causes heart disease or strokes.
Adult cannabis use has surged nationwide, rising 51% between 2020 and 2024 to reach one in six Americans. (iStock)

The data also relied on telephone surveys, leaving room for errors in participants' memory regarding their medical diagnoses and drug use. Additionally, the researchers did not track product strength, THC potency or total amounts consumed.
The findings remain preliminary until vetted through the full, peer-reviewed publication process.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"For patients, I wouldn't recommend making abrupt treatment decisions based on one preliminary study, but I wouldn't dismiss these findings," Worth said. "People should not discontinue prescribed cardiovascular medications because of this report."

"Anyone using cannabis, medically or recreationally, should discuss their cardiovascular history, existing risk factors, medications and treatment alternatives with their healthcare professional," she added.
Khloe Quill is a lifestyle writer with Fox News Digital. She and the lifestyle team cover a range of story topics including food and drink, travel, and health.

title: Wisconsin infant dies of measles as state sees first death from disease since 1990
summary: Wisconsin's health officials announced an infant's measles-associated death, marking the state's first in 36 years, amid 431 cases in 13 counties.
story: An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, according to state health officials.
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years, the state's Department of Health Services announced on Thursday.

The Department of Health Services said the child died in southwestern Wisconsin but did not provide a more precise location. The department said it would not release any additional details to protect the privacy of the family.
The coroner listed the immediate cause of death as measles.

"It is with a heavy heart we are reporting the first death of an infant connected with a measles outbreak in Wisconsin in many years. My heart is broken for the family," state Department of Health Services Secretary Kirsten Johnson said in a statement.
CHILD'S MEASLES DEATH MARKS NEW YORK STATE'S FIRST IN MORE THAN 30 YEARS AMID OUTBREAK
An infant in Wisconsin died of measles, marking the state’s first death linked to the disease in 36 years. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

"Any death of a child is a tragedy and even more so when it is related to a vaccine-preventable disease. Measles can cause serious illness and death, and it is important for all Wisconsinites to evaluate their risk and take steps to protect themselves and their family," she continued.

Measles can cause life-threatening complications, including pneumonia and swelling of the brain. The department said that while anyone can become seriously ill, children younger than 5, pregnant people and people with weakened immune systems are at increased risk of complications.

Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year, reflecting the highest number of cases seen in the state in more than 35 years. Among these cases, nine people required hospitalization for severe symptoms.

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine.
Wisconsin has reported 431 measles cases in 13 counties so far this year. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The U.S. Department of Health and Human Services previously told FOX News Digital that "Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles."
Earlier this week, a child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death.
"As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement.
NEW YORK DECLARES MEASLES DISASTER EMERGENCY AS CASES SURGE IN PENNSYLVANIA

State officials urged Wisconsinites to be proactive in preventing illness to protect themselves and their communities, saying the best way to prevent measles is with the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine. (Raquel Natalicchio/Houston Chronicle via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention has reported four measles-associated deaths across the country this year, although state health departments have reported higher figures.

In Pennsylvania, state health officials have confirmed six measles-associated deaths in 2026 and are investigating another reported death that has not yet met the state's criteria to be classified as measles-associated.
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Popular weight-loss drugs may prevent prediabetes from turning into diabetes
summary: A large study found GLP-1 medications like semaglutide and tirzepatide are linked to 41% lower all-cause mortality risk versus metformin in prediabetes.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a dietitian and diabetes educator, talks about important factors that affect blood sugar and gives an opinion on a recent study suggesting eating with a partner can decrease blood sugar levels.
Adults with prediabetes and obesity who took GLP-1-based medications had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death compared with those taking metformin.

Metformin is an oral medication used primarily to treat type 2 diabetes, widely considered the first-line treatment, combined with lifestyle modifications. It is also sometimes prescribed to people with prediabetes to help prevent or delay progression.

The findings, which come from a large observational study, are set to be presented at the American Heart Association’s Scientific Sessions 2026 this weekend in Chicago. They have not yet undergone the full peer review process.
DR OZ LINKS OBESITY TO CHRONIC DISEASE SURGE, SAYS GLP-1S CAN 'JUMPSTART' BETTER HEALTH
The study involved health records for 256,492 adults with prediabetes and obesity, averaging 52 years of age.
Approximately half of the group received GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) medications – including semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and dulaglutide – and half received metformin.
Adults with prediabetes and obesity who took GLP-1-based medications had a 31% lower risk of developing type 2 diabetes and a 41% lower risk of death compared with those taking metformin. (iStock)

Based on a three-year follow-up, in addition to the lower risk of diabetes and all-cause mortality, GLP-1–based medications were associated with 20% fewer strokes, 15% fewer heart attacks and 25% fewer cases of heart failure.

"The 41% lower risk of death from any cause surprised me most," study author Vinicius de Sousa Barzon Serra, M.D., a research fellow in the department of cardiovascular medicine at the Mayo Clinic in Scottsdale, Arizona, told Fox News Digital.
POPULAR DIET SLASHES LIVER FAT BY 67% WHILE REVERSING PREDIABETES IN SOME PEOPLE

"I expected GLP-1 medications to do better than metformin on blood sugar and diabetes risk, because they lead to much more weight loss. I was also struck that the benefit appeared across many outcomes, including heart attack, stroke, heart failure and atrial fibrillation."

Approximately half of the group received GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1 receptor agonists) medications – including semaglutide, tirzepatide, liraglutide and dulaglutide – and half received metformin. (iStock)

Nearly 40% of U.S. adults have prediabetes, according to statistics from the AHA. That condition is marked by blood sugar levels that are above normal but not yet elevated enough for a diabetes diagnosis.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
As many as 10% of those with prediabetes will go on to develop type 2 diabetes each year.

"Most earlier research on these medications focused on people who already had diabetes," Serra noted. "Our study suggests the prediabetes stage may be an important time to consider them, rather than waiting until they develop type 2 diabetes."

Nearly 40% of U.S. adults have prediabetes, according to statistics from the AHA. That condition is marked by blood sugar levels that are above normal but not yet elevated enough for a diabetes diagnosis. (iStock)

Dr. Bradley Serwer, an interventional cardiologist and chief medical officer at VitalSolution, an Ingenovis Health company that offers cardiovascular and anesthesiology services to hospitals nationwide, agreed that the study raises the possibility that GLP-1 medications could play a large role in primary cardiovascular prevention.

"We have long known the benefits of controlling blood pressure, cholesterol and urging smoking cessation, but now we should consider aggressively treating obesity and metabolic dysfunction," Serwer, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
Study limitations
While the study found a link between GLP-1 medications and better health outcomes, it does not prove that the drugs were responsible.
The findings are preliminary until published in a peer-reviewed journal, Serra noted.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"We matched patients by age, health conditions and other characteristics to make the groups comparable … even so, other differences between the groups may remain," he said. "We also grouped the GLP-1 medications together, so we could not tell whether individual drugs differ."

The study relied on patients' electronic health records, which may have contained missing or incorrect information. It is also possible that factors not measured in the study, such as medication dosage and compliance, could have influenced the results, the researchers noted.

Metformin is an oral medication used primarily to treat type 2 diabetes, widely considered the first-line treatment, combined with lifestyle modifications. It is also sometimes prescribed to people with prediabetes to help prevent or delay progression. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)
People with prediabetes and obesity should talk with their doctor about all their options and should not stop or change any medication on their own, Serra advised.

"Metformin is a safe, inexpensive option with a long track record, and lifestyle changes such as healthy eating, regular physical activity and weight management remain the foundation of treatment," he emphasized to Fox News Digital.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"For some patients, a GLP-1 medication may be worth discussing, depending on their overall health, other medical conditions, cost and access. The decision should be made together with their doctor."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Serwer emphasized the importance of identifying patients who would benefit most from aggressive treatment to prevent cardiovascular disease.

"Not everyone with prediabetes needs a GLP-1 medication," he said. "We need to identify those with obesity, insulin resistance and multiple cardiovascular risk factors who are most likely to benefit from early intervention."

title: College students discover new muscle attachment that could improve hip surgery
summary: Two Tulane University sophomores found a previously unknown muscle in the hip during a cadaver lab session that even their professor couldn't identify.
story: Tulane University students Dominic Roy and Cooper Bruce join anatomist and professor Dr. Shane Tubbs to discuss their discovery of a previously undocumented pelvic muscle and what it could mean for medical research.
Two undergraduate students at Tulane University in New Orleans discovered an anatomical feature that even their professor couldn’t initially identify.
Dominic Roy and Cooper Bruce were both 19-year-old college sophomores at the time of the finding in 2024.

In an interview with Fox News Digital, Roy said it had been an ordinary day volunteering in the cadaver lab with R. Shane Tubbs, Ph.D., professor of neurosurgery and director of surgical anatomy at Tulane School of Medicine.
5 HABITS THAT COULD HELP KEEP YOU OUT OF A NURSING HOME, FROM AN ORTHOPEDIC SURGEON
The students were dissecting several specimens’ hips to compare where the iliacus joins the psoas major, a muscle that runs from the lower back through the pelvis to the upper thigh.
Front view of a woman's thigh and knee muscles with anatomical labels. (iStock)
When looking for a particular muscle, the iliocapsularis, which sits laterally in the hip, Roy found something else instead.
"I spotted a similar looking muscle that was on the other side of the Iliac fascia, close to the inguinal region of the pelvis," he said.
WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS
"I called Dr. Tubbs over and asked, ‘What is this?’ We didn't talk about this in our morning meetings ... and I think he was as stumped as me."
After searching through extensive literature and textbooks to see if the muscle had been previously identified, the team came up short, which suggested it was a new discovery.
The new muscle attachment discovered by Tulane undergrad students is illustrated in a diagram. (Tulane University/iStock)
"It was kind of like a reserved excitement," Bruce reflected. "Especially if the great R. Shane Tubbs can't put his finger on exactly what it is."
Physicians from overseas and rising medical school students also assisted with the discovery.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE

"Everyone kind of huddled around the same specimen and we started draping and doing the pictures … I was in awe," Roy said. "I was like, ‘Oh, wow, this is happening so quick.’ It was seriously something special."
The findings were recently published in the journal Clinical Anatomy.
Tulane students Dominic Roy, left, and Cooper Bruce made a novel discovery while volunteering in the cadaver lab. (Dominic Roy)
Tubbs, who is also a co-editor-in-chief of the human anatomy reference textbook Gray's Anatomy, said Roy and Bruce’s discovery was "serendipity."
"[They] identified a different part of a muscle that we had not looked at yet," he confirmed to Fox News Digital. "It's deep in the pelvis and runs out to the front of your hip."
KNEE TREATMENT WITHOUT SURGERY OFFERS LASTING PAIN RELIEF FOR 80% OF ARTHRITIS PATIENTS, STUDY FINDS
Potential medical uses
Although the team has not yet determined the muscle’s function, clues suggest it may help stabilize the psoas major, a large muscle involved in bending the hip.
The next step is to determine whether MRI scans can reveal the muscle attachment, allowing researchers to study whether its presence is linked to more or fewer symptoms, according to the doctor.
Dr. Tubbs said his lab uses anatomical donors for education and research to identify clinical problems. (Tulane University)

"More research is needed for us to better elucidate what it does," Tubbs said. "Can you see it on imaging? Does it contribute to patients' problems? But I think this is the first step in identifying something."
As minimally invasive procedures become more common, Tubbs said awareness of this small muscle could improve care, particularly for patients undergoing hip surgery.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"They might use physical therapy to help rehab the muscle, because we did find that the fibers of this attachment directly attach into the front of the hip joint," he added. "So it may be that the muscle’s weak and causes symptoms, so you could rehab it."
Doctors could also use injections to weaken the new muscle if overactivity causes pain or other symptoms.
The muscle discovery could help improve future surgeries and hip pain, the professor said. (iStock)

"Surgeons are replacing hips and doing hip surgery on a daily basis, so if they see the muscle, potentially they could correlate the symptoms of the patient and whether or not maybe cutting the muscle would help the patient," Tubbs said.
Variations in anatomy
This muscle was not found in every cadaver, the researchers noted, as each human body is different.
"When you look beneath the layers of the skin, human beings have lots of variation," Tubbs said. "I tell our students that no two of you are built the same inside or out."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
The researchers found the same muscle attachment in gorillas, suggesting a possible evolutionary link.
Bruce said this raises the question of why this muscle would still be present in some humans and not others.
Tulane University School of Medicine is shown in New Orleans on Feb. 12, 2022. (iStock)
"Just by the nature of working with cadavers and not knowing a deep personal history of each individual … maybe this individual played soccer, or this person did a lot of rock climbing," he said.
"They might've had more need for this attachment ... It's difficult to make that connection."
Lessons beyond textbooks
Working with real cadavers has made a big difference in shaping future doctors, Tubbs shared, as the synthetic models that are now circulating in university labs are cookie-cutter.

"Many people have the notion ... that the entire form of the human has been worked out, and we know all the different parts. And they think we've known that for hundreds of years," he said. "But in actuality, people are still discovering things about human anatomy."
Medical students "need to experience that variation" and have the hands-on experience before dealing with real patients, Roy commented.

Although the new muscle attachment will have to be studied across geographic regions, Tubbs said he expects the students' discovery will eventually be added to anatomical textbooks.

The discovery inspired the students, now seniors, to further explore a career in medicine. Roy said he plans to enter a master’s program in anatomy.
"The bottom line is that anatomical discovery doesn't end when a textbook is published ... and discovery in the anatomical sciences continues on, even in the year 2026."

Rachel Apa, 24, died on Sunday, Nov. 1, while running the New York City Marathon after succumbing to complications from rhabdomyolysis, a rare muscle condition.

Apa made it to mile 24 – just 2.2 miles from the finish line – before collapsing. She received immediate medical attention and was taken to Mount Sinai Medical Center, where physicians worked to save her for more than six hours.

title: NYC marathon runner, 24, dies just 2 miles from finish line after sending dad chilling texts
summary: Rachel Apa's father says rhabdomyolysis killed the 24-year-old NYC marathon runner, who collapsed at mile 24 during her first-ever race Sunday.
story: Rachel Apa, 24, collapsed near mile 24 of the New York City Marathon. Her father says she died from rhabdomyolysis, a dangerous muscle condition. She was running to honor her late grandfather.
New York City marathon runner Rachel Apa died on Sunday after collapsing at mile 24.
Apa, 24, set out to run the world-famous race on Nov. 1 for the first time, along with more than 60,000 other runners.

The former Bucknell University Division I field hockey player had reportedly trained for the marathon for months. The New York Times reported details from the runner's parents, Michelle and Steve Apa, on Monday.
HEALTHY ATHLETE HAD NO SYMPTOMS BEFORE MANDATORY HEART SCREENING REVEALED HIDDEN DEFECT
Michelle Apa said she watched her daughter run by at mile 14 in Long Island City, Queens. She took a video of Apa looking strong, smiling and giving out high-fives before taking off again.

Rachel Apa, 24, died while running the New York City marathon on Nov. 1, 2026. (Instagram @rachelapa)

Rachel Apa reportedly texted her father back at mile 18, saying, "Ow." And once again at mile 19, "Ow ow."

At mile 23, Steve Apa texted, "Final stretch." Rachel Apa never responded again, according to The New York Times.

title: Bird flu kills US resident after dairy cow exposure, marking nation’s third death
summary: A Yakima County resident with underlying health conditions died after contracting H5N1 bird flu from infected dairy cows at a local dairy farm.
story: Dr. Tyler Evans, an infectious disease physician and founder of Wellness Equity Alliance in California, speaks with Fox News Digital about E. coli infections linked to a California pumpkin patch that closed just days before Halloween.
A resident of Yakima County, Washington, has died from complications of bird flu, public health officials confirmed, marking a rare fatal human case of the virus in the United States.
The individual, who had underlying medical conditions, was hospitalized with severe illness after contracting avian influenza through exposure to infected livestock at a local dairy facility.
Local officials declined to release the person’s name, age or gender, citing privacy concerns.
H5N1 BIRD FLU CONFIRMED IN AUSTRALIA FOR THE FIRST TIME, MEANING VIRUS HAS NOW REACHED EVERY CONTINENT
"Our hearts go out to the individual's family and loved ones during this difficult time," Dr. Dave Atteberry, health officer for the Yakima Health District, said in a statement.

"Avian influenza can cause severe illness, particularly among people who have underlying health conditions," he went on. "While this is a serious and heartbreaking outcome, the risk to the general public remains low."
Officials strongly urge dairy and agricultural workers to take precautions and contact health authorities immediately if they develop symptoms after exposure to infected cattle. (iStock)

Health officials on Monday also confirmed a third human case of avian influenza in Yakima County. That individual, who was also exposed to infected dairy cattle at a local farm, has not been hospitalized and has not experienced severe illness.
Public health teams are actively tracing and monitoring close contacts of both individuals for potential symptoms.
RARE TICK-BORNE VIRUS TURNS DEADLY FAST AS US CASES REACH RECORD HIGH, EXPERTS WARN

"People at greater risk include dairy workers and others who have close or prolonged contact with infected animals or environments contaminated with the virus," the health district said in an advisory.
"If you work on a dairy farm and develop symptoms after potential exposure to infected cattle, contact your healthcare provider or the Yakima Health District."
What is bird flu?

Avian influenza, or bird flu, is a disease caused by influenza type A viruses that typically spread among wild aquatic birds and domestic poultry, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
In recent years, an outbreak of the H5N1 strain has expanded beyond birds to infect various mammals, including domestic dairy cows and outdoor livestock.
The individual contracted the virus through direct exposure to infected cattle at a local dairy facility. (Dado Ruvic/Reuters)
Federal and state health officials emphasize that the overall risk to the general public remains low.
Person-to-person spread of bird flu is extremely rare and has not been identified in the U.S., according to the CDC.

Agricultural workers, veterinarians and people in close, prolonged contact with infected animals, raw milk or contaminated manure are at the greatest risk of exposure, the above agency states.
Commercial pasteurized milk and properly cooked poultry remain safe to consume, as heat kills the virus.

title: Child’s measles death marks New York state’s first in more than 30 years amid outbreak
summary: A child in Lewis County marks New York's first measles-associated death in over 30 years as Gov. Kathy Hochul urges people to get their vaccinations.
story: CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz joins Bill Hemmer and Dana Perino to discuss the growing measles outbreak and an early flu surge across the U.S. Schwartz also weighs in on the White House initiative on women’s health research.
A child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years amid an ongoing measles outbreak, officials announced on Monday.
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death.
"As a mother and grandmother, I cannot imagine what this family is going through. My heart goes out to everyone who knew and loved this child," Hochul said in a statement.

"Measles is highly contagious, and vaccination remains our best protection against this dangerous disease. This is New York’s first measles-related death in 30 years, a devastating reminder of what’s at stake when Washington deliberately erodes decades of progress in protecting Americans from preventable illnesses," she added. "In New York, we will continue to stand by proven public health measures and do everything we can to keep New Yorkers safe and healthy."
DEADLY MEASLES OUTBREAK HITS NORTHEAST AS STATE RECORDS FIRST DEATHS IN 35 YEARS
A child in New York state's Lewis County died in the first known measles-associated death in the state in more than 30 years. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

The Trump administration has made changes to federal vaccine policy, including revising the childhood immunization schedule and reviewing how vaccines are recommended. The CDC, however, continues to recommend two doses of the measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccine for children and says two doses provide the best protection against measles.

"Our hearts go out to the family mourning this tragic loss," a spokesperson for the U.S. Department of Health and Human Services said in a statement to FOX News Digital. "Following New York’s formal request for an Epi-Aid, CDC deployed epidemiologists and other experts to work alongside state health officials on the ground, providing surveillance, data analysis, strategic planning, and other outbreak response support. Secretary Kennedy and CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz continue to make clear that the MMR vaccine is the most effective way to prevent measles."

The child's death comes four weeks after Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states, expanding the pool of eligible people who can administer measles vaccines and providing quick access to additional resources if needed.
The governor said last month she planned to seek federal assistance to combat the outbreak.
TRUMP SURGEON GENERAL PICK BACKS MMR VACCINE, REJECTS LINK BETWEEN CHILDHOOD VACCINES AND AUTISM
Gov. Kathy Hochul said she was "heartbroken" to learn of the child's death. (Adam Gray/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The New York State Department of Health said it is working with county health departments and local partners to provide the MMR vaccine to any unvaccinated people who request it and to closely monitor and investigate all reported cases.
As of Oct. 24, New York had recorded 178 measles cases this year — 170 outside New York City and eight in the city.

State health officials urged New Yorkers to protect themselves by making sure they are up-to-date on their MMR vaccines and be aware of health advisories if traveling with unvaccinated people, especially young children.

"We are deeply saddened by the death of a child in Lewis County associated with the ongoing measles outbreak. We extend our heartfelt condolences to the child's family and loved ones and ask that their privacy be respected during this difficult time," the New York State Department of Health said in a statement.

The child's death comes four weeks after Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a State Disaster Emergency in response to the measles outbreak across areas of New York and neighboring states. (Adam Gray/Pool/Getty Images)

The department said measles is a highly contagious disease that can cause serious complications and death, stressing that vaccination is the "best protection against measles."

"The Department has offered resources to Lewis County to assist with community outreach and support local vaccination efforts – both in response to this case, and as part of our ongoing efforts to support counties that are facing this ongoing measles outbreak," the department's statement reads. "We urge New Yorkers to ensure they are up-to-date on measles, mumps and rubella (MMR) vaccinations and speak to their healthcare provider about immunizations."

title: Dangerous mosquito-borne virus surges in popular US state as cases reach highest levels in decades
summary: Florida's dengue fever outbreak has reached 485 locally acquired cases, with Tampa Bay accounting for 95% of infections and emergency declarations issued.
story: Florida is combatting its largest dengue fever outbreak in decades, with over 290 locally acquired cases reported. Former CDC Director Dr. Robert Redfield breaks down the risks of transmission and essential prevention measures. Meanwhile, Hillsborough County mosquito management teams deploy aerial spraying to target the mosquitoes carrying the virus.
Florida health officials have confirmed 485 locally acquired cases of dengue fever this year, as the state grapples with its largest outbreak in decades.

Between Oct. 18 and Oct. 24, state surveillance logged 60 new infections, with the Tampa Bay area accounting for roughly 95% of all locally acquired cases recorded statewide, according to the Florida Department of Health.

The surge prompted emergency declarations in Hillsborough, Pasco and Pinellas counties in late September, allowing for faster purchasing and spraying and requests for state and federal reimbursement. Hillsborough County has since extended its state of local emergency amid ongoing transmission.
DENGUE FEVER OUTBREAK TRIGGERS STATES OF EMERGENCY IN 3 SOUTHERN COUNTIES
The locally acquired infections are separate from more than 300 travel-associated dengue cases reported in Florida this year.
The Florida Mosquito Control Association said mosquito abatement teams are stepping up targeted ground spraying, aerial applications and localized property inspections.
Mosquito-control crews across the Tampa Bay area have increased surveillance and treatments as locally acquired dengue cases climb. (iStock)
What is dengue fever?

Dengue is a viral illness transmitted primarily through the bite of infected Aedes aegypti and Aedes albopictus mosquitoes. The virus can cause fever, severe muscle and joint pain, nausea, rash and, in severe cases, dangerous complications or death, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
Unlike many mosquito species that bite mostly at dawn and dusk, the mosquitoes carrying dengue feed aggressively during daytime hours and thrive in humid residential environments.
DEADLY MOSQUITO-BORNE VIRUS CLAIMS FIRST LIFE IN MAJOR US CITY AS CASES SPREAD

"The Aedes mosquitoes that can transmit dengue are active during the day and thrive in warm, humid environments like those found in Florida," an entomologist spokesperson at the SC Johnson Center for Insect Science and Family Health previously told Fox News Digital.
In addition to local spread, Florida has tracked more than 300 travel-associated infections this year, which continue to introduce the virus to domestic mosquito populations. (iStock)
"Staying aware of local mosquito activity and consistently protecting against bites are important steps people can take to help reduce their risk."

Public health officials emphasize that Aedes mosquitoes are "container breeders," requiring as little as a tablespoon of standing water to lay eggs. Officials urge residents to inspect yards weekly and drain or cover birdbaths, gutters, planters, discarded tires and outdoor containers.

title: New cancer treatment approach could help immune cells fight tumors longer
summary: UCLA researchers found that boosting p53 protein with navtemadlin helped T cells fight melanoma cancer cells longer, but dosing challenges remain.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel discusses an experimental melanoma vaccine breakthrough that reportedly lowers recurrence risk by more than 40%. Siegel also shares stories of healing from his book, 'The Angels Among Us.'
Scientists may have found a way to help the body's immune cells fight cancer for longer, potentially making some treatments more effective.

Researchers at the UCLA Health Jonsson Comprehensive Cancer Center found that temporarily boosting a protein called p53 helped specially prepared immune cells stay stronger and kill more melanoma cells in laboratory experiments.
The study, published in Frontiers in Immunology, focused on T cells, which are immune cells that help the body fight disease.
NEW CANCER VACCINE DELIVERS STUNNING RESULT AGAINST ONE OF THE DEADLIEST SKIN CANCERS
Some cancer treatments take a patient's T cells, modify them in a lab so they can recognize cancer, and then return them to the body to attack tumors.
One challenge is that these cells can eventually become "exhausted," making them less effective at fighting cancer, the UCLA researchers said.
Scientists at UCLA found that temporarily boosting a protein called p53 could help immune cells fight cancer more effectively in laboratory experiments. (iStock)

To address that problem, researchers treated human T cells with an experimental drug called navtemadlin, which temporarily increases the activity of p53, a protein known for helping to prevent cancer.

The treated T cells showed fewer signs of exhaustion, had more energy and developed characteristics that could help them last longer. When tested against melanoma cells in the lab, they were also significantly more effective at killing the cancer cells than untreated T cells, according to the research.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

Kien Vuu, a Los Angeles-based triple board-certified physician and former UCLA assistant clinical professor, confirmed that T-cell exhaustion is one of the biggest challenges encountered with these treatments.
"After repeated encounters with cancer, they become 'exhausted' and lose their ability to multiply and attack," Vuu, who was not involved in the research, told Fox News Digital.
Scientists tested an experimental drug called navtemadlin to determine whether it could help T cells resist exhaustion. (iStock)
Vuu said the approach could offer a relatively simple way to strengthen existing treatments.

"The practical appeal is simplicity," he said. "Rather than adding another genetic modification, this approach adds a drug during the manufacturing step, when a patient's T cells are being prepared in the lab."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
If the approach works in further research, Vuu said it could potentially help T cells remain effective for longer, particularly when treating solid tumors.
The findings are still preliminary, however.
The findings remain preliminary, with researchers emphasizing that the experiments involved human cells in a laboratory rather than patients. (iStock)
"This is early, laboratory-stage research," Vuu acknowledged. "The experiments were done with human cells in a dish against melanoma cells, not in animals or people."
Researchers will need to test the approach in animals and other types of cancer before moving into clinical trials, according to Vuu.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

The amount of the drug will also need to be carefully studied. The UCLA researchers found that higher doses caused more T cells to die, while lower doses produced the desired effects without substantially reducing the number of healthy cells.
"Dosing is especially important," Vuu said. "The researchers found that too much p53 activation actually killed more of the T cells, so getting the balance right will be critical."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Patients shouldn't expect this in the clinic soon, but it's a promising new direction worth following."
Fox News Digital reached out to the researchers for comment.

title: Type 2 diabetes patients 21 times more likely to achieve remission with intensive lifestyle changes
summary: A low-calorie diet paired with resistance training helped participants lose 18.5 pounds without shedding muscle, according to a new Lancet study.
story: Erin Palinski-Wade, a dietitian and diabetes educator, talks about important factors that affect blood sugar and gives an opinon on a recent study suggesting eating with a partner can decrease blood sugar levels.

A strict routine combining a low-calorie diet with supervised strength and aerobic training helped more than half of younger adults reverse type 2 diabetes within six months, according to a study published in The Lancet Regional Health - Americas.
The study, dubbed the RESET for Remission trial, found that 54% of participants under age 45 who completed the intensive lifestyle program achieved disease remission.
In comparison, only 4% of participants receiving standard medical care reached the same milestone.
VITAMIN SUPPLEMENT MAY DELAY DIABETES IN SELECT GROUPS, RESEARCHERS SAY
Type 2 diabetes diagnosed at a younger age is historically aggressive, according to medical literature.
Patients diagnosed before 45 face a faster loss of blood sugar control, earlier cardiovascular complications and a shorter overall life expectancy than those diagnosed later in life.
A strict routine combining a low-calorie diet with supervised strength and aerobic training helped more than half of younger adults reverse type 2 diabetes within six months. (iStock)

Researchers from McGill University in Canada and the University of Leicester in the United Kingdom enrolled 96 adults between the ages of 18 and 45 who were living with obesity and early-onset type 2 diabetes. None of the participants were using insulin.
The intervention group halted their blood sugar and blood pressure medications under medical supervision and began an intensive 800- to 900-calorie daily diet.
SIMPLE EXERCISE DONE JUST ONCE A WEEK COULD HELP LOWER BLOOD PRESSURE

For the first two weeks, patients consumed only meal-replacement products. From weeks three through 12, they were allowed one structured meal of lean protein and vegetables each day alongside meal replacements, before shifting into a weight maintenance phase for the final 12 weeks.
The program paired calorie restriction with supervised aerobic and resistance training twice weekly, plus one weekly solo workout.

To meet the medical standard for remission, patients maintained healthy blood sugar levels below an HbA1c threshold of 6.5% for at least 12 weeks while completely off all diabetes medications. (Peter Dazeley)

"Our study shows that it is possible to combine a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise in young adults with type 2 diabetes," lead author Dr. Kaberi Dasgupta, a professor of medicine and director of the Division of General Internal Medicine at McGill University, told Fox News Digital.
"There has previously been some concern about combining the two as being too much of a burden for people. However, people in our study stayed in our study."
"Our study shows that it is possible to combine a low-calorie diet with supervised exercise in young adults with type 2 diabetes."
Only 10% of participants failed to complete the final evaluations, and patients attended a median of 17 out of 20 scheduled supervised gym sessions.
The researchers emphasized resistance training to combat the loss of lean muscle mass, a major risk associated with rapid weight loss.
4 SIMPLE HABITS CAN HELP SLOW MUSCLE LOSS AS YOU AGE, FITNESS EXPERT SAYS

People who lose weight through crash dieting or appetite-suppressing medications may shed muscle along with fat, experts warn. If the weight returns, some research suggests it may come back disproportionately as body fat, potentially affecting muscle health and metabolism over time.
"In our study, we think the diet provoked the weight loss, and exercise helped make sure it was [not] from muscle," Dasgupta said.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"We were happy and surprised that not only did people lose fat from their organs and liver, our MRI studies indicated their muscle did not decrease at all and their handgrip strength went up."

Combining an 800- to 900-calorie daily diet with supervised exercise helped 54% of younger adults put their type 2 diabetes into remission within six months, compared with only 4% receiving standard care. (iStock)
Participants shed an average of 18.5 pounds over 24 weeks, while significantly boosting their treadmill endurance and overall cardiovascular fitness.
To meet the official standard for remission, patients had to maintain an HbA1c blood sugar level below 6.5% after going at least 12 weeks without any glucose-lowering drugs.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
After accounting for baseline health factors, researchers concluded that patients on the diet and exercise program were 21 times more likely to achieve remission than those receiving routine care.
Study limitations

Despite the promising outcomes, experts emphasized notable limitations. The trial was small, examining fewer than 100 individuals across medical centers in England and Canada over a relatively short six-month window.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
Dasgupta also noted that the study could not determine exactly what was responsible for each benefit.

"The main limitation is that we had to compare the diet plus exercise with usual care," he told Fox News Digital. "We would have liked to compare diet alone against diet and exercise to perfectly prove the point that the improvements in muscle and fitness were from the exercise."

Unlike crash dieting or weight-loss drugs that often strip away lean tissue, the regimen's strength training enabled participants to shed an average of 18.5 pounds, while preserving muscle mass and increasing grip strength. (iStock)

The strict routine also took a physical toll. Roughly 86% of the intervention group reported mild to moderate side effects, primarily during the early weeks, including headaches, fatigue, dizziness and constipation, though researchers noted that no severe medical complications occurred.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Health professionals cautioned that diabetes remission is not a permanent cure, and sustaining an 800-calorie threshold alongside supervised gym can present steep hurdles for busy adults outside a clinical setting.

Study authors noted that longer-term trials in real-world settings are still needed to determine whether patients can keep the weight off, preserve their muscle gains and remain medication-free once regular daily routines resume.

title: Your walking speed may hold a clue to how long you’ll live, study suggests
summary: A JAMA Network Open study of over 4,000 older adults found faster walking pace was linked to lower death risk over nearly 12 years of follow-up.
story: Dr. Courtney Conley and Dr. Milica McDowell, authors of "Walk," explain the extensive benefits of walking for physical and mental health. They join Steve Doocy to emphasize "Vitamin W" as an accessible activity, discussing how increasing daily steps from the current average of 5,000 to a brisk pace of 130 steps per minute can boost longevity. They also highlight "movement snacks" for overall wellness.
The speed a person normally walks could offer a simple clue about their overall health and longevity, new research suggests.
A study published in JAMA Network Open followed 4,067 adults in the U.K., who were about 69 years old on average, to see whether their usual walking pace was linked to their risk of death over time.
Participants completed a short walking test at their normal pace and also wore a wrist activity tracker for nine days to capture their walking speed during everyday life.
FORGET THE GYM: A 30-SECOND TEST MAY BE ONE OF THE BEST INDICATORS OF LONGEVITY

Over nearly 12 years of follow-up, faster walking in both settings was linked to a lower risk of death, even after researchers accounted for other health and lifestyle factors. A total of 739 participants died during that period.

Beth Templin, a board-certified geriatric clinical specialist and CEO of HouseFit Physical Therapy & Fitness in St. Louis, said walking speed can offer a broader look at how well the body is functioning.
A new study suggests that how fast a person normally walks could offer important clues about their overall health and longevity. (iStock)

"In physical therapy, we call walking speed the 'sixth vital sign' because it's a snapshot of how well many body systems are working together," Templin, who was not involved in the study, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Changes in walking speed can therefore offer clues about a person's health, according to the doctor.
"To walk briskly, you need strong legs, a healthy heart and lungs, good balance, and a brain and nervous system that can coordinate it all," she said.
Researchers found that faster walking speed was associated with a lower risk of death among more than 4,000 older adults in the U.K. (iStock)
"When walking speed starts to slip, it's often an early warning sign that one of those systems is declining, sometimes before anything shows up on a lab test," Templin added.
For older adults who want to improve their walking speed and overall fitness, simply taking more steps may not be enough.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Build the engine, not just the habit," Templin advised. "Most people try to walk more, but speed comes from strength and balance."
The doctor suggested strengthening the legs with simple exercises, such as standing up from a chair without using the hands and doing heel raises while holding onto a counter.
Walking speed may reflect how well the heart, lungs, muscles and nervous system work together, experts say. (iStock)

She also recommended adding short bursts of faster walking. After warming up, a person could walk briskly for one minute, slow down for two minutes and then repeat, gradually increasing the faster periods.
The findings do not mean that simply walking faster will make someone live longer, experts noted.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"This study shows an association, not proof that walking faster by itself adds years," Templin reiterated.

The participants included in the study were generally healthier than the larger group, the researchers noted. There is also no single standard method for measuring everyday walking pace with wrist activity trackers.
More research is needed to determine whether the findings apply to other groups.

title: Women's sex drive treatment linked to higher rates of heart attack and stroke
summary: A study of 6,000+ postmenopausal women links testosterone therapy to higher rates of heart attack, stroke and heart failure in new research.
story: OB-GYN Dr. Kudzai Dombo shares why interest in testosterone is rising among women, what evidence says about libido, and why access, dosing and insurance coverage can be complicated.
Postmenopausal women who use testosterone therapy could face a higher risk of heart attack, stroke and other cardiovascular problems, new research suggests.

The research, presented at the 2026 annual meeting of The Menopause Society last month in San Diego, looked at more than 6,000 postmenopausal women age 45 and older, comparing those who received testosterone therapy with those who did not. Women with a history of cardiovascular disease were excluded.
Among women receiving testosterone, 3.8% experienced a first-time cardiovascular event compared with 0.5% of women who were not receiving the treatment, according to The Menopause Society.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK
Those events included heart attack, stroke, heart failure and other cardiovascular problems.
Testosterone is a sex hormone produced by the ovaries and adrenal glands that plays a role in sexual desire, as well as muscle and bone health, mood and cognition, according to Cleveland Clinic.
Postmenopausal women who use testosterone therapy could face a higher risk of heart attack, stroke and other heart problems. (iStock)

Anna Cabeca, a Dallas-based board-certified OB-GYN and menopause expert, told Fox News Digital that the differences between the two groups — women who received testosterone and those who did not — deserve attention.

"The difference between 3.8% and 0.5% is certainly significant enough to warrant attention, but we need to be careful about what these numbers actually tell us," said Cabeca, who was not involved in the study.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
That amounts to about 38 cardiovascular events per 1,000 women receiving testosterone compared with five per 1,000 women who were not, the doctor noted.

For women considering testosterone therapy, Cabeca said doctors should look at the patient's overall health, including heart history, blood pressure, cholesterol, metabolic health, medications and family history.
Testosterone is a sex hormone produced by the ovaries and adrenal glands that plays a role in sexual desire, as well as muscle and bone health, mood and cognition. (iStock)

"Sexual health is an essential part of overall health, and women deserve to have their concerns about libido, arousal and intimacy taken seriously, particularly during and after menopause," she added.
While testosterone can improve sexual desire and satisfaction in appropriately selected postmenopausal women, the possible benefits should be weighed against potential risks, Cabeca advised.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
In cases when testosterone is appropriate, she favors careful dosing, monitoring and regular checks of a patient's symptoms and lab results.
There are important limitations to the new findings, the researchers acknowledged.
When testosterone therapy is appropriate, experts recommend careful dosing, monitoring and regular assessments of a patient's symptoms and lab results. (iStock)
The study was observational, meaning the researchers looked at outcomes among women who were already receiving testosterone rather than assigning the treatment in a controlled trial.
As a result, the study can show a link between testosterone use and cardiovascular events, but cannot prove that the treatment caused them.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Women who received testosterone may also have differed from those who did not in ways that affected their heart risk, including age, blood pressure, diabetes, cholesterol levels or other health factors, Cabeca said.
"This is an important safety signal that deserves further investigation, not definitive evidence of causation," she added.

title: 5 habits that could help keep you out of a nursing home, from an orthopedic surgeon
summary: Dr. Vonda Wright shares five daily habits that help older adults maintain independent living, starting with skeletal longevity and muscle strength.
story: Dr. Vonda Wright, a surgeon and longevity expert, reveals her top strategies for staying out of a nursing home and preserving mobility.
Three in four Americans aged 50 and older would like to remain in their homes as they age, according to the AARP — and preserving that independence starts with daily habits.

Dr. Vonda Wright, a double board-certified orthopedic surgeon, author and authority on active aging and mobility, who is based in Orlando, Florida, said there are three main problems that can make it difficult for older adults to age in place.
Those include difficulty getting up from a chair and caring for themselves, memory problems, and incontinence that makes it hard to manage personal hygiene.
FORGET THE GYM: A 30-SECOND TEST MAY BE ONE OF THE BEST INDICATORS OF LONGEVITY
"The missing piece in most conversations between mental health, physical health and independence is your skeletal longevity," Wright said.
Three in four Americans aged 50 and older would like to remain in their homes as they age, according to the AARP. (iStock)
Staying independent with age requires attention to the entire musculoskeletal system, including the muscles, bones and tendons, according to the surgeon.
Wright shared the following habits as most important for maintaining independence outside of a nursing home.
No. 1: Keep moving
The human body "craves mobility," Wright said.
"When you think about it, it's our first skill. We learn to walk when we're 1," she pointed out.
WEEKLY WEIGHTLIFTING SWEET SPOT MAY BE LINKED TO LONGER LIFE, STUDY FINDS

For older adults, staying active can help preserve the ability to handle everyday tasks independently. The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention suggests low-impact activities such as walking, cycling and water exercise.
"Even when your hips hurt, even when your knees hurt, you should move on the ground, or get in a pool in chest-high water," Wright suggested.
Staying independent with age requires attention to the entire musculoskeletal system, including the muscles, bones and tendons, according to the surgeon. (iStock)
While the doctor does not recommend exercising through a new injury or severe pain, she pushed back against the belief that rest is the best way to address pain.
PEOPLE LIVING PAST 100 IN ONE TINY VILLAGE SHARE 3 DAILY HABITS

"Rest doesn't cure anything. When you have, for instance, arthritic knees, do you know what can help? Building the muscles around your knees, building the muscles in your hips to support your knees," she said. "So rest is not the answer for feeling better — staying strong and mobile is."
No. 2: Build muscle
Strength training can help older adults maintain the ability to get out of a chair, climb stairs and carry groceries — everyday tasks that support independent living.
There is never an age or skill level when it’s too late to build muscle, according to Wright.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG

"Even if you feel like you've declined or your parents have declined, there is no age or skill level when we can't become more mobile, when we can't build muscle or reconnect the neuromuscular pathways," she said.

It’s even possible to build muscle sitting in a wheelchair, she noted. "Some of the very first research done by Dr. Maria Fiatarone at Tufts University showed that even at 90 years old, you can regain function."
"There is no age or skill level when we can't become more mobile, when we can't build muscle."

In that small 1990 study, nine nursing home residents who completed eight weeks of high-intensity resistance training increased their muscle strength by an average of 174%, and also showed improvements in muscle size and mobility.
For older adults, staying active can help preserve the ability to handle everyday tasks independently. (iStock)
The National Institute on Aging recommends that older adults perform muscle-strengthening activities at least two days a week, targeting all major muscle groups, with recovery time between sessions.
Some options include resistance bands, hand weights and body-weight exercises. Beginners are advised to start gradually and seek guidance from a doctor or physical therapist as needed.
No. 3: Eat enough to support strength
Older adults tend to eat less, which can undermine efforts to maintain energy and build muscle, Wright warned.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"It’s something I see even happening to my 86-year-old parents; they're just eating less and less," she said. "And we cannot fuel the muscle we want to build [and] the energy we need without a protein-forward, adequate-calorie diet."
"The most common mistake I see seniors making as they age is assuming that aging is an inevitable decline from vitality to frailty."
Although older adults may require fewer calories, they still need enough nutrients to support their health, according to the National Institute on Aging.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

To help maintain muscle, the agency recommends that older adults consume protein-rich foods throughout the day, including seafood, dairy, fortified soy products, beans and lentils. Specific calorie needs will vary based on each person’s weight and activity level.
No. 4: Drop the mindset that decline is inevitable
Wright urged older adults to challenge assumptions about what they can and can’t do as they age.
The surgeon urged older adults to challenge assumptions about what they can and can’t do as they age. (iStock)
"The most common mistake I see seniors making as they age is assuming that aging is an inevitable decline from vitality to frailty," she said.
"They just assume that a certain number of birthday candles predisposes them to sitting on a couch the rest of their life. The reality is that there is no age or skill level when you're done."
No. 5: Have open conversations
Wright suggested that people should start working toward future independence during their busy working years.

"We need to start thinking about that in our busiest times of life, in our 30s, our 40s, our prime times of working," she said. "It’s part of a long-term, lifetime plan to live where you want to live, with whom you want to live, when you want to live there."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The doctor recommends that adults directly ask their aging parents what assistance they need and to explore available support, including community programs.
Although older adults may require fewer calories, they still need enough nutrients to support their health, according to the National Institute on Aging. (iStock)
In many cases, she said, parents do not want to be a burden to their adult children, so they never ask for anything.
"I think this is a time for really open, frank conversations," Wright said. "What do you want help with? How can I help you? How could we get help for you if possible?"
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

As an example, Wright said her elderly parents live with her family. When she noticed their meals started to suffer while she was traveling, she arranged for support to help them continue managing their lives.
"I have half of their meals delivered every week because I'm not going to be home to shop or cook," she said. "They remain independent, but with assistance. And that's what works for us."

title: Paper straws could be doing more harm than good, study suggests
summary: A South Korean government-commissioned life cycle assessment found paper straws scored 6.33 times higher than plastic on a cancer-related measure.
story: 'Fox & Friends' co-hosts react to a new study raising concerns about the environmental impact of paper straws while revisiting President Donald Trump's decision to bring back plastic straws.
Paper straws have been marketed as a more environmentally friendly alternative to plastic, but a new South Korean assessment suggests they may carry a greater pollution-related health burden.
South Korea’s Ministry of Climate, Energy and Environment commissioned the assessment from the Korean Society for Life Cycle Assessment, according to news reports.
Researchers compared how paper, plastic and other disposable straws could affect human health and the environment, from production through disposal.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK
Paper straws scored 6.33 times as high as conventional plastic straws in an estimate of cancer-related harm from pollution generated during production and disposal, according to South Korean reports.
The score estimates potential harm from pollution generated from production through disposal — not chemical exposure or cancer risk from drinking through a straw, the researchers noted.
The assessment compared how paper, plastic and other disposable straws could affect human health and the environment, from production through disposal. (iStock)
The assessment reportedly compared four straw types: paper, conventional plastic, biodegradable plastic and bio-based polyethylene, or bio-PE.
Researchers assessed 16 environmental impacts, assuming about 74% of discarded straws were incinerated and 26% went to landfills, based on South Korean waste statistics.
MICROPLASTICS DETECTED IN MOST HEART ATTACK PATIENTS' BLOOD IN STARTLING NEW STUDY
Conventional plastic straws performed best in 10 of the 16 environmental categories, but no straw type came out ahead in every category.
The study did not measure whether chemicals leach from straws into drinks and did not assess health outcomes among people who use them.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Researchers recommended that stores provide disposable straws only upon request, according to The Korea Herald.
Paper straws scored higher than conventional plastic straws on one modeled measure related to cancer-causing effects, according to reports. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Lawmaker Kim Wi-sang, whose office received the report, later criticized plastic straw restrictions, arguing that alternatives had failed to deliver their promised environmental benefits.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
President Donald Trump has also criticized paper straws, calling them ineffective and arguing that they may pose health risks.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

In February 2025, he signed an executive order directing federal agencies to stop buying and providing paper straws and to develop a national strategy to end their use, according to a White House press release.
"I was tired of having straws melt in my mouth," Trump previously said.
The study’s findings do not prove that drinking through a paper straw increases a person’s cancer risk. (iStock)

Fox News Digital previously reported on health concerns raised by Florida lawmakers, including a 2023 University of Antwerp study that detected PFAS, or "forever chemicals," in 27 of 39 straw brands tested, most often in paper straws.

Separately, 360° Foodservice, a European food-service packaging association, previously said its member companies have a no-PFAS clause and set requirements for food-contact safety.
Fox News Digital reached out to the Foodservice Packaging Institute and 360° Foodservice for comment.
