title: One industry faces multitrillion-dollar reckoning after historic midterm election reshuffle
summary: Donald Trump backed AI data centers, but Texas Democrats' historic midterm sweep now threatens billions in planned projects across the state.
story: Alpha Compute CEO Brittany Kaiser argues that common-sense regulations, not sweeping bans or moratoriums, are the key to unlocking economic growth while protecting local communities.

President Donald Trump has thrown the federal government's weight behind massive data center build-outs needed to power the country's artificial intelligence (AI) boom. But a historic Democratic sweep in Texas has put one of the nation's biggest AI infrastructure hubs under new political leadership, raising questions about the future of billions of dollars in planned investments.

The victories marked a historic midterm night for Texas Democrats, who captured the governor's mansion for the first time in more than three decades and won a U.S. Senate seat for the first time since 1988.

Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. data center power capacity through 2030. With at least 248 projects planned across the state, investment bank Jefferies estimates that 13.3 gigawatts of announced developments could be at risk under a moratorium backed by Gov.-elect Gina Hinojosa.
ONE STATE IS GROUND ZERO AS TRUMP'S MULTIBILLION-DOLLAR TECH AMBITIONS FACE A MIDTERM TEST
Texas is poised to overtake Virginia as the nation's largest data center market and is projected to account for roughly a quarter of new U.S. capacity through 2030. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Texas was hardly alone in facing growing opposition to data center development. In Ohio, voters weighed 21 data center-related ballot questions across 18 communities in the midterm elections, more than any other state, highlighting the mounting resistance to America's rapidly expanding AI infrastructure.
The results this week are now forcing some developers to reconsider where to invest billions of dollars in future projects as political power shifts.

"It makes us and our investors pause and think if we should be investing somewhere else," Brittany Kaiser, CEO of Alpha Compute, told Fox News Digital following the Republican bloodbath in Tuesday's election.

Kaiser warned that political shifts in traditionally Republican states could push billions of dollars in planned investments elsewhere, including overseas, as companies weigh growing opposition to data center development — especially within the Democratic Party.
"There's new decision making that needs to come into play and a lot more to think about than there was before the election," she said.
IT TOOK 3 MONTHS TO GET INSIDE THIS MASSIVE TEXAS DATA CENTER — HERE’S WHAT WE SAW
A data center stores and processes the digital information that powers services people use every day. (Nathan Howard/Getty Images)
But relocating projects already underway is far more complicated, particularly when developers have secured land, negotiated power agreements and committed substantial capital.
"It's not very easy to pivot after you've already made contractual and financial commitments to these types of builds," Kaiser said.

For projects still in the pipeline, however, companies have more flexibility. Kaiser said Alpha Compute has already invested in data centers in Canada, Europe and Mexico, where regulatory approvals are more straightforward.
The backlash highlights growing tensions between Washington's push to accelerate AI development and voters' concerns about electricity costs and the impact of data centers on their communities.
Kaiser urged incoming lawmakers to strike a balance between addressing community concerns and preserving what she called "the biggest economic opportunity of our generation."
The AI boom is accelerating demand for data centers across Texas as companies seek more space, power and infrastructure to support increasingly intensive computing needs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's really important, yes, to make sure that data center companies are good actors and are doing things the right way," she said, calling for "common sense legislation and regulation" that allows developers to work with lawmakers and local communities.

"If we can abide by those rules, then bans and moratoriums should not be the answer," Kaiser said. "It's just let's sensibly regulate and move forward in a way that is positively impactful for communities."
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Somali daycare owner tied to fraud wins Minnesota House race sparking online fury: 'Lost state'
summary: Abdi Daisane's Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud received millions in state and federal funding and has faced multiple violations.
story: Abdi Daisane was elected to represent the St. Cloud area in the Minnesota House. (Abdi Daisane for State Representative)

ST. CLOUD, Minn. — The owner of a Somali daycare center that has faced scrutiny over state and federal funding and is linked to a massive fraud settlement won a seat in the Minnesota legislature Tuesday night.

Minnesota Democratic–Farmer–Labor Party (DFL) candidate Abdi Daisane defeated a Republican incumbent to win Minnesota’s House District 14A seat in St. Cloud, Minnesota, becoming the first Somali-born lawmaker in the statehouse from St. Cloud, MPR News reported.

Daisane, who delivered part of his victory speech in Somali, is the CEO of Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud, which has received $7.29 million from the state-run Child Care Assistance Program since 2018.

His childcare business also received $598,251.62 from the federally-funded Child and Adult Care Food Program (CACFP) since 2020. A nonprofit called Partners in Nutrition, which recently had to pay an $18.5 million civil settlement for fraud, was the center's sponsor for CACFP funds.

A press release from the settlement says Partners in Nutrition "knowingly defrauded the State of Minnesota out of millions of dollars in federal child nutrition funds during and after the COVID-19 pandemic, in violation of the Minnesota False Claims Act."
MINNESOTA OFFICIAL'S VOTER GUIDE MESSAGE ON SOMALI TV TRIGGERS VIRAL BACKLASH: 'NOT AN ACCIDENT'

Fox News Digital visited Blooming Kids Child Care Center on Thursday and found a quiet scene. The childcare center is situated along a main road in St. Cloud's small downtown. A paper sign on a wooden front door that faces the street directs visitors to a different entrance. The floor-to-ceiling glass windows next to the door are covered with a tinted and mirrored film.
The building is flanked by a parking lot that was mostly empty on Thursday afternoon.
Behind the building is a tiny fenced-in playground, anchored by two children's jungle gyms that appear to fill most of the area.
Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud, Minn., on Nov. 5, 2026. The center is owned by state Representative-Elect Abdi Daisane. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)

Alpha News reported on the funding in late October, and spoke with a nearby worker who said they never saw children entering or exiting the childcare facility. The outlet also reported that Blooming Kids Child Care Center has been cited for over a dozen violations.

Additionally, questions about the immigration status of Daisane's wife, Ayaan Aydid, have circulated online after a video surfaced of her detailing to the BBC how she crossed into the United States at the southern border.
CULTURE CLASH LAID BARE AS VIOLENT SOMALI GANGS GRIP SUBURBAN COMMUNITIES: ‘THESE KIDS ARE DIFFERENT’
Daisane did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment.

A small outdoor play area at the Blooming Kids Child Care Center in St. Cloud, Minn., on Nov. 5, 2026. The center is owned by state Representative-Elect Abdi Daisane. (Peter D'Abrosca/Fox News Digital)
News of Daisane’s victory quickly sparked pushback on social media.
"We are a lost state," Red Ax Strategies President Matt Brodsky posted on X. "We should cede it to Canada."
"MINNESOTA IS SO FREAKING COOKED," conservative commentator Eric Daugherty posted on X.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Minnesota is done," conservative personality Gunther Eagleman posted.

ACT for America founder Bridgette Gabriel flagged a post about Daisane's election — and his purported illegal immigrant wife — to the Department of Homeland Security (DHS) and DHS Secretary Markwayne Mullin on X.
"[G]reat opportunity to do something about this," she said.
Andrew Mark Miller is a reporter from Pasadena, California, who has been with Fox News Digital since 2021. You can reach him at AndrewMark.Miller@fox.com.

title: Vance, Cruz and DeSantis diagnose GOP's midterm disaster as battle over party's future begins
summary: JD Vance's 600-word postmortem blamed the Iran war for GOP midterm losses, putting striking daylight between himself and Trump on foreign policy.
story: Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis discusses how his state avoided a Democratic electoral wave and lays out where the GOP should go after the midterms on ‘The Ingraham Angle.’

The 2028 Republican White House race may be getting its first battle lines, as Vice President JD Vance, Sen. Ted Cruz and Florida Gov. Ron DeSantis quickly offered competing assessments of the GOP's devastating midterm election losses, potentially previewing their visions for the party's future.

The three high-profile Republicans, all viewed as potential contenders for the party's presidential nomination, used their postmortems to weigh what went wrong and what Republicans must do differently — a debate that could help define the GOP's direction heading into 2028.

"I think everybody's trying to figure out where to position themselves in the aftermath. Where were you on the day after," longtime Republican strategist and presidential campaign veteran David Kochel told Fox News Digital. "I think these are all moves designed to look towards 2028."

Oil drilling CEO and prominent Republican donor and bundler Dan Eberhart told Fox News Digital that "the early moves have started" in the 2028 Republican presidential nomination race. "These guys are going to go a couple of rounds before Christmas."
HEAD HERE FOR FOX NEWS LIVE UPDATES ON THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport, Monday, Nov. 2, 2026, in Rome, N.Y. (Tom Brenner/Pool Photo via AP)

Vance kicked off the debate Wednesday morning with a roughly 600-word postmortem on X, blaming President Donald Trump's war with Iran for Republicans' worst ballot-box drubbing in decades as they lost control of Congress, along with a slew of governorships and state legislatures.
Fueled by anger over high costs and the war with Iran, voters delivered a repudiation of Trump and his agenda, boosting Democrats to large majorities in the House and Senate.

"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote as he appeared to put daylight between himself and his boss on foreign policy and America's relationship with Israel. "Any honest conversation about where we go from here must start there."

Vance, in what some pundits viewed as an early pitch to eventually claim the MAGA and America First mantle, argued that defections from the party's successful 2024 coalition of voters, rather than a lack of GOP turnout, fueled the Republican collapse in the midterms.
CLICK HERE FOR THE LATEST MIDTERM ELECTION RESULTS AS THE VOTES CONTINUE TO BE COUNTED

Kochel called Vance's assessment "the most striking because it appears to say 'hey, we made a mistake with the war in Iran,' and that's about as far as I've seen a vice president go, not as a criticism of Trump but as a criticism in the policy."
Asked about Vance's post, Trump told reporters, "I know how he feels about it. I think it was fine. I thought it was good."
The president acknowledged that the war and the high gas and diesel prices it spurred hurt his party at the ballot box but insisted it was worth the cost.
"If I had to do it again, I'd have to do it again," he said. "As far as that war is concerned, I would have done nothing different."
Donald Trump Jr., the president's eldest son and a prominent figure in the MAGA movement, quickly gave Vance's postmortem a thumbs-up, writing on X, "Every word of this is 💯 💯 💯."
Hours after Vance posted his assessment, Cruz posted his own scathing take on the midterms.
POLLSTERS MISSED THE MARK, BUT THIS TIME IT WASN'T REPUBLICANS THEY UNDERCOUNTED
Sen. Ted Cruz, R-Texas, speaks during a campaign rally with Republican nominee for U.S. Senate Mike Rogers in Grosse Pointe Woods, Mich., on Oct. 28, 2026. (JEFF KOWALSKY/AFP via Getty Images)

The conservative firebrand senator from Texas, who was runner-up to Trump in the bruising 2016 Republican presidential primaries and has made no secret that he may run for the White House again, described the midterms as a "blue tsunami" and warned that his party had lost touch with voters, particularly in the Lone Star State.
"2026 was not simply a blue wave; it was a blue tsunami. It was an a-- kicking," Cruz wrote. "It was not simply a bad 2006 midterm election. It was a Watergate-level repudiation."
"Nowhere are the consequences of this election greater than Texas," Cruz wrote. "In the Lone Star State, we lost every single statewide election...Texas is blue. That is a hard sentence to utter."
FLORIDA'S DESANTIS DESCRIBES GOP MIDTERMS WIPEOUT AS 'CLOSE TO AN EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' FOR REPUBLICANS
Cruz blamed the losses on the high cost of living and pointed to Trump's tariffs and the war in Iran.

"Food is too high, gas is too high, diesel is too high, insurance is too high, life is too high," he wrote. "Understandably, people were pissed off, and elected Republicans didn't do enough to address their very real pain."

DeSantis, the term-limited conservative governor who ran for the 2024 Republican presidential nomination before being decisively defeated by Trump, held a news conference Wednesday morning where he called the midterm election results "close to an extinction-level event for Republicans across the country."

"Let’s just be clear, that is going to hurt — not just for the next two years... That is something that can reverberate for the next decade or more," he said. "We knew it could be worse. I don't think most of us thought it would be this bad."
But DeSantis repeatedly highlighted that "the one state that was able to hold the line and withstand that is right here in the free state of Florida."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
While most pundits view Cruz as a likely 2028 contender, the jury's been out regarding DeSantis.

But Eberhart, who's Florida-based, argued that "the first bullet in the 2028 contest was Ron DeSantis throwing cold water on Trump's $5,000 dividend," referring to the president's early September pledge at the GOP midterm convention to make a cash payment to every adult U.S. citizen if Republicans retained the House and Senate.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER

Looking at the postmortems, Kochel said, "I think that we're going to be digging through the rubble for a while...The party going to have through this post apocalyptic period here and figure out what's the message going forward."

He cautioned, "It's going to be really hard to hold the coalition together. I think Trump was uniquely able to do it with the power of his celebrity but I think there's going to be a lot of machinations here going forward."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Trump admin sues Penn State over in-state tuition policy for undocumented migrants
summary: The DOJ's lawsuit accuses Pennsylvania State University of offering undocumented students in-state tuition rates that discriminate against U.S. citizens.
story: The Justice Department sued Penn State over its policy allowing some undocumented students who meet Pennsylvania residency requirements to receive in-state tuition, arguing the practice violates federal law and discriminates against U.S. citizens.
The Trump administration is suing Pennsylvania State University over a policy that allegedly allows undocumented migrant students to qualify for in-state tuition.

In a lawsuit filed on Thursday, the Justice Department argued that in-state tuition for undocumented migrants discriminates against U.S. citizens because U.S. citizens living outside Pennsylvania are not eligible for the same reduced tuition rate.

"Congress made a deliberate policy choice that states and their public institutions may not grant tuition benefits to illegal aliens unless those same benefits are made to all U.S. citizens," Assistant Attorney General Brett A. Shumate of the DOJ's Civil Division said in a statement.
"This university has ignored that mandate. The Department will continue to challenge policies that unlawfully disadvantage American citizens," he continued.
JUSTICE DEPARTMENT SUES COLORADO OVER IN-STATE TUITION AND FINANCIAL AID FOR ILLEGAL IMMIGRANTS
The Trump administration is suing Pennsylvania State University over a policy that allegedly allows undocumented migrant students to be eligible for in-state tuition. (Getty Images)
The DOJ accused the university of violating federal law by "prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands."
Penn State's policy "unconstitutionally" discriminates against U.S. citizens who are not afforded the same reduced tuition rate as undocumented students, the department said.

The department seeks to enjoin the university from enforcing its policy that provides undocumented students, including illegal migrants who live in Pennsylvania, with in-state tuition rates, regardless of whether the students are lawfully in the U.S.
DOJ SUES NEW JERSEY OVER LAWS GIVING ILLEGAL ALIENS IN-STATE TUITION, SAYS CITIZENS TREATED AS 'SECOND-CLASS'
The Justice Department argued that in-state tuition for undocumented migrants discriminates against U.S. citizens. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)
The complaint also aims to enjoin the institution from adopting any new tuition policies that favor undocumented students over U.S. citizens.

According to Penn State's website, undocumented students with or without Deferred Action for Childhood Arrivals (DACA) status may be eligible for in-state tuition if they meet certain residency requirements.

"These requirements include attending an accredited Pennsylvania high school for at least four years and graduating from an accredited Pennsylvania high school or receiving a Pennsylvania General Educational Development (GED) certificate," the school's website reads.
FOX News Digital has reached out to the university for comment on the DOJ's lawsuit.

The DOJ accused the university of violating federal law by "prioritizing the needs of illegal aliens over U.S. citizens in defiance of Congress’s commands." (ANDREW CABALLERO-REYNOLDS/AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Thursday's lawsuit brings the DOJ's total to 27 lawsuits challenging in-state tuition for illegal migrants, including six lawsuits in Texas, Kentucky, Oklahoma, Nebraska, Illinois and Kansas that have resulted in favorable orders for the federal government.

"The Department of Justice today continues its efforts to ensure that no state law or university policy gives preferential treatment to illegal aliens over our Nation’s own citizens," Associate Attorney General Stanley E. Woodward, Jr. said in a statement. "Congress long ago made clear that states, through their public universities, cannot give reduced tuition to illegal aliens not available to all Americans."

title: Federal judge temporarily blocks construction of Trump's Arlington triumphal arch hours after approval
summary: The National Capital Planning Commission had approved construction for President Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., hours before the restraining order was issued.
story: The Trump administration is being challenged by a proposed arch that critics say will obstruct historical sight lines.

A federal judge early Friday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from breaking ground on President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch in Washington, D.C., just hours after a federal planning commission approved the project.
U.S. District Judge Tanya Chutkan issued a 14-day temporary restraining order halting construction of the proposed monument.

Chutkan granted a request from plaintiffs challenging the project in lawsuits filed by the District of Columbia and Virginia. The cases were consolidated with an earlier lawsuit brought by a group of Vietnam veterans and an architectural historian.
The National Capital Planning Commission approved the project hours earlier on Thursday with an 8-4 vote, clearing the way for construction before the court intervened.
SEN JIM BANKS: TRUMP’S NEW TRIUMPHAL ARCH IS A MONUMENT TO AMERICAN GREATNESS
A rendering of the Triumphal Arch slated to be constructed on Columbia Island in Washington, D.C. (Interior Department)

The federal panel approved construction of the 250-foot-tall structure, which is inspired by Paris' Arc de Triomphe and intended to attract visitors crossing the Memorial Bridge from Arlington National Cemetery into the nation's capital.
Mark Paoletta, the commission's Trump-appointed chairman, expressed support for the new structure during the panel's meeting.
"President Trump understands as president and a superb builder that it's important to our national identity to display who we are through grand monuments," Paoletta said.
Paoletta, who also serves as general counsel for the White House Office of Management and Budget, pointed to Trump's admiration for similar monuments around the world.
"As Trump has often remarked, the great cities around the world have arches: Paris, Rome, London," Paoletta said.
TRUMP SAYS NEW ARCH WILL ALSO DEPLOY DRONES, POSITION SNIPERS AND STORE AMMO

President Donald Trump holds a model of an arch as he delivers remarks during a ballroom fundraising dinner in the East Room of the White House Oct. 15, 2025, in Washington. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
The proposed structure would be clad in granite and topped with three golden statues.

Trump has previously said the triumphal arch would be converted into a military complex capable of rapidly deploying large numbers of drones, with snipers positioned on the roof and plaza areas. He also said the complex would store "large quantities of sniper ammunition."
The project has drawn criticism from preservationists, lawmakers and veterans, who argue that it could disrupt views of the Lincoln Memorial and Arlington National Cemetery.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

A model of President Donald Trump's proposed triumphal arch to commemorate the country’s 250th anniversary is seen on the Resolute Desk on Oct. 15, 2025 in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Dietsch/Getty Images)
Opponents have also questioned whether the project requires congressional approval under federal law.
The National Capital Planning Commission previously approved the site and preliminary plans.
Fox News Digital's Amanda Macias and The Associated Press contributed to this report.
Michael Sinkewicz is a writer for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to michael.sinkewicz@fox.com

title: Vance ‘privately’ blasts Netanyahu as Iran war divides Trump administration and 2028 ambitions loom
summary: JD Vance privately accused Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war as he positions himself for a 2028 presidential bid.
story: JD Vance uses clash with Benjamin Netanyahu to distance himself from the Iran war without directly criticizing Trump, Middle East Institute's Natan Sachs says.

Vice President JD Vance privately accused Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu of being "wrong on everything" about the Iran war, according to reports, as disagreements over the conflict expose tensions within the Trump administration and raise questions about Vance's potential 2028 presidential ambitions.

The clash, reported by Axios Nov. 4., comes after Republicans lost control of both chambers of Congress in Tuesday's midterm elections and Vance publicly blamed the war for the party's defeat while urging President Donald Trump to pursue a negotiated settlement rather than renewed military strikes.
"The reason we lost is the war," Vance wrote later on Wednesday on X.
VANCE'S SCATHING IRAN WAR POSTMORTEM PUTS POTENTIAL 2028 GOP SHOWDOWN IN FOCUS: 'EVERYONE KNOWS WHY'
"Low-level hostility between Vance and Netanyahu is beneficial for Vance," Natan Sachs, a senior fellow at the Middle East Institute, told Fox News Digital.

"It allows him to give some distance from the Trump administration, which has just taken a huge electoral beating, but also to position himself ... in a very different position than President Trump himself without attacking Trump."
Vice President JD Vance talks on his phone as he walks to the West Wing of the White House March 6, 2026, in Washington. (Alex Brandon/AP Photo)

Vance has also led a faction of senior administration officials urging Trump to negotiate an end to the conflict, warning that the unpopular war could cost Republicans control of Congress, according to reports.
Netanyahu had urged Trump to resume strikes against Iran ahead of the midterms, but Trump held off after endorsing Netanyahu for re-election in Israel.
Sachs said Vance's main concern appeared to be the prospect of overthrowing Iran’s government after Netanyahu presented Trump with a plan for regime change.

"Many opposition leaders in Israel, nonetheless, are very skeptical of the idea that you can bring about regime change through an air campaign," Sachs said, adding that such a campaign could have the opposite effect.
"You may strengthen the regime."

As previously reported by Fox News Digital, Vance had also declined to endorse Netanyahu’s re-election campaign and criticized Israeli government officials who opposed Trump's efforts to end the Iran war.

The Israeli election further complicated the relationship, Sachs said, leaving Netanyahu's political future uncertain and raising the possibility that Vance could have to work with a different Israeli leader.
NETANYAHU DEFIES EXIT POLLS AS VOTE SHIFTS IN HIS FAVOR, BUT MAJORITY REMAINS ELUSIVE
President Donald Trump welcomes Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu to his Mar-a-Lago estate Dec. 29, 2025, in Palm Beach, Fla.  (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"If Netanyahu is not the leader of Israel, Vance will find himself with another decision to make. Does he continue with a line that is confrontational with a new Israeli leadership, or does he say, 'Well, it was all Netanyahu; now we can see a different path forward'?" Sachs said.

"Netanyahu is a very easy target here, both because there are very real differences of opinion, and Netanyahu's role was important, but also because this way he can criticize the war, criticize Netanyahu, and not say any bad word about Trump."
Roughly six in 10 voters said U.S. military action against Iran was the wrong decision, according to the AP Voter Poll.

"I think what's remarkable here is that it's coming out now," Sachs said. "And it's part of the fact that about midnight Wednesday, the next presidential campaign in the United States began, and JD Vance is trying to position himself.
"He is breaking with the policy of President Trump, although he's doing so by criticizing Netanyahu, never Trump."
VANCE REVEALS THE TRUMP DILEMMA THAT COULD COMPLICATE HIS 2028 WHITE HOUSE AMBITIONS

Vice President JD Vance prior to a meeting between the United States, Iran, Pakistan and Qatar at the Burgenstock luxury hotel complex overlooking Lake Lucerne, Switzerland, June 21, 2026.  (Fabrice Coffrini/Keystone via AP)
Nonetheless, Vance has played a leading role in efforts to end the conflict with Iran, including direct outreach to senior Iranian officials.
Last month, he sent a letter through Qatari intermediaries to Mohsen Rezaei, secretary of Iran's Supreme National Security Council, proposing renewed peace negotiations.

According to Axios, the letter said any negotiations to prevent further U.S. military strikes must address Iran's nuclear program. A U.S. official said Trump backed the outreach. Rezaei later confirmed receiving the letter but said he had not responded.
"My suspicion is that JD Vance was operating on behalf of Trump on this," Sachs claimed.
"Trump, after the war sort of settled after the first few weeks, appointed Vice President Vance to try and negotiate the exit strategy, and Vance has been very keen on that."
Sachs also cited Vance's involvement in an earlier memorandum of understanding with Iran as further evidence of his preference for diplomacy.
"He agreed to the MOU, which has become quite notorious in the United States, giving quite a bit to the Iranians, much more than the administration is now considering reasonable.
VANCE TAKES LEAD SELLING TRUMP’S IRAN GAMBLE AS RUBIO, HEGSETH AND RATCLIFFE CEDE SPOTLIGHT ON FRAGILE DEAL
Vice President JD Vance speaks during a campaign rally at Griffiss International Airport Nov. 2, 2026 in Rome, N.Y. (Tom Brenner/Pool Photo via AP)
"Vance has certainly been on the side that has been trying to achieve a diplomatic breakthrough."
The White House is now weighing whether to resume major strikes against Iran, maintain economic and naval pressure or pursue a negotiated settlement.

On Thursday, Reuters reported that Tehran submitted a formal nuclear proposal to the United States through Qatari intermediaries, making further negotiations contingent on Washington addressing its seven demands.

"The real question is whether the Americans and the Iranians can approach some kind of agreement on the fundamentals, starting with freedom of navigation in the Straits of Hormuz and the cessation of hostilities," Sachs said.
For Vance, the dispute poses a political balancing act of distancing himself from a war he reportedly opposed while serving as vice president in the administration that launched it.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"He was against the war, so it would seem, but of course, he's vice president in the administration that went to war," Sachs said, describing it as a "very difficult balancing act for him electorally."

Emma Bussey is a breaking news writer for Fox News Digital. Before joining Fox, she worked at The Telegraph with the U.S. overnight team, across desks including foreign, politics, news, sport and culture.

title: Child molester's looming prison release reignites sanctuary showdown in wake of Dem election sweep
summary: DHS warns convicted child molester Leomar Zambrano could be released in Seattle as sanctuary city officials refuse to honor the ICE detainer.
story: Fox News Digital rides alongside ICE agents, capturing surveillance and high-stakes arrests of two migrants in Brooklyn.

A convicted child molester and illegal alien from Venezuela could soon be back on the streets unless authorities in Seattle ditch their sanctuary city policies and cooperate with federal immigration enforcement.

Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) has sent a detainer request to the liberal Pacific Northwest enclave for Leomar Alexander Lopez Zambrano, asking that he be turned over rather than be released back into the U.S. after his prison sentence concludes.

The clash between DHS and Seattle exacerbates longstanding tensions between President Donald Trump’s immigration officials and leaders in so-called sanctuary cities, which have thrown up roadblocks to law enforcement cooperating with federal enforcement authorities.

Going a step further, the outcome of Tuesday's elections are putting even more of a microscope on the agency at the center of much controversy during Trump's second term and is raising questions about which administration officials could face the wrath of a brand-new blue Congress.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin speaks during a news conference at the Eisenhower Executive Office Building July 17, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Jim Lo Scalzo/EPA/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"Sanctuary politicians in Washington are refusing to honor the ICE detainer and hand this disgusting criminal over to us after he finishes his prison sentence," Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said in a statement.
"This illegal alien has been convicted on TWO counts of child molestation."

After the 2026 midterms, the matter in Seattle raises new questions of whether sanctuary cities will feel emboldened to double down on their efforts to block Trump's agenda as Democrats prepare to retake a majority in the U.S. Senate and House of Representatives.

To those like Hans von Spakovsky, an immigration expert with Advancing American Freedom (AAF), the political tide turning in Washington, D.C., might encourage Democrat-run cities to go even further in stonewalling immigration enforcement agencies and making it harder for officials to do their jobs.
"I have no doubt that sanctuary jurisdictions will feel emboldened," Spakovsky told Fox News Digital in the days after the Republican bloodbath.

"I also would not put it past [Democrats] to try to impeach Tom Homan for imagined wrongs because he has been the most effective czar of immigration enforcement of any administration in the past 50 years," he said.
"I don’t think they would be successful, but, again, that will embolden defiance of federal immigration enforcement in sanctuary jurisdictions."
In many cases, sanctuary cities simply cut off communication with federal law enforcement, and DHS fears that will be the case with Zambrano, the convicted Venezuelan child molester.

Zambrano is now approaching the end of a 15-month sentence, the point at which he would normally face deportation. But Mullin noted DHS would have no way of knowing when he was out of jail without Seattle's cooperation.
ICE ARRESTS ILLEGAL ALIEN ACCUSED OF SEXUALLY ASSAULTING CHILDREN AFTER FAIRFAX COUNTY RELEASE: DHS

U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement (ICE) agents, along with other federal law enforcement agencies, attend a pre-enforcement meeting in Chicago, Illinois, US, on Sunday, Jan. 26, 2025. President Donald Trump has pledged to carry out the largest deportation effort in US history, vowing to ultimately deport all of the foreigners living in the country without permission. (Christopher Dilts/Getty Images)
"Sanctuary politicians care so much about illegal aliens that they’d rather release a convicted child molester than cooperate with federal law enforcement," Mullin said.
When asked about Seattle’s cooperation with DHS, the agency responded by similarly emphasizing local-federal partnership.

"The safest way to arrest and remove criminal illegal aliens from our streets is by lodging arrest detainers. Because some sanctuary jurisdictions refuse to work with ICE law enforcement, criminal illegal aliens are released from jails into American communities to perpetuate more crimes. Seven of the top 10 safest cities in the United States cooperate with ICE," the agency said in a statement.
In the wake of the election, some Republican onlookers believe similar concerns could emerge in other states, even red states like Texas.

Dan Bongino, a conservative commentator and podcast host, noted that the Lone Star State’s newly elected Democratic governor, Gina Hinojosa, voted against sanctuary city restrictions as a state legislator in 2017.
GOP SENATORS RALLY AROUND NEW DHS PROPOSAL TARGETING SANCTUARY CITIES: 'SHOULD PAY A PRICE'

"Folks, Texas shares a border with Mexico. Do we need to ChatGPT this for people?" Bongino said in a recent podcast. "The only message [voters] are sending is you want your state to become a sanctuary, sitting on the border with Mexico for illegals who come into the United States."

Spakovsky believes local resistance to immigration enforcement could coincide with congressional Democrats' legislative efforts. He believes Democrats will attempt to target immigration enforcement resources through the congressional appropriations process, although he cast doubt on their effectiveness.
The U.S. Capitol building Aug. 7, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Kevin Carter/Getty Images)

"Democrats will, no doubt, try to stop DHS from immigration enforcement and DOJ from prosecutions in the immigration area by trying to use the appropriations process to defund such enforcement at both agencies," Spakovsky said.
"I am not sure they will be successful … especially if they tie such punitive measures with must-pass government funding that the president signs."
Asked about whether DHS was concerned about an emboldened stance from sanctuary cities as Democrats retake control in the nation’s capital, DHS passed a statement along from Mullin.
"Deportations will continue," the DHS chief said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Officials from Seattle did not respond to requests for comment from Fox News Digital about Zambrano’s status.
Leo Briceno is a politics reporter for the congressional team at Fox News Digital. He was previously a reporter with World Magazine.

title: Trump signs proclamation to prevent changes to Oval Office, other White House rooms
summary: Trump signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room a national monument to prevent future presidents from altering them.
story: President Donald Trump offers an exclusive look at the White House ballroom project, discussing its innovative design and its role as a secure venue for formal events.

President Donald Trump signed a proclamation Thursday designating the Oval Office, the Outer Oval Office and the Cabinet Room as a national monument and federal landmark, a move intended to preserve the spaces and prevent future administrations from altering them.

"It won't be able to be taken down, destroyed, touched or anything else," Trump told reporters from the Oval Office. "It’s actually called a national monument. It’s a federal landmark. When completed … it'll make it impossible for anybody ever to destroy this incredible space. "
Fox News Digital has reached out to the White House.
DEMOCRATS SEIZE HOUSE CONTROL IN STUNNING BLUE TSUNAMI, VOW RETRIBUTION AGAINST TRUMP ADMIN

President Donald Trump speaks in the Oval Office at the White House in Washington, D.C. On Thursday, Trump signed a proclamation designating the Oval Office and Cabinet Room as a national monument and federal landmark. (Kylie Cooper/Reuters)
The announcement came two days after the midterm elections in which Democrats won enough seats to gain control of Congress.
The proclamation is part of a broader series of post-election public appearances highlighting White House construction initiatives.
TRUMP'S WHITE HOUSE BALLROOM CONSTRUCTION GETS ANOTHER LIFELINE FROM SCOTUS AMID HEATED LEGAL FIGHT

President Donald Trump, Vice President JD Vance and Secretary of State Marco Rubio meet with Micheal Martin, Ireland's prime minister, in the Oval Office. (Yuri Gripas/Abaca/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
On Monday, Trump detailed planned updates during remarks in front of the Reflecting Pool. On Wednesday, he held a press briefing at the construction site of a new White House ballroom.

Since returning to office in 2025, Trump has prioritized several high-profile architectural and cultural projects, including a proposed 250-foot triumphal arch near Arlington National Cemetery and proposals to rename and restructure the John F. Kennedy Center for the Performing Arts.
Louis Casiano is a reporter for Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to louis.casiano@fox.com.

title: Ex-Biden official projected to win bid to unseat Mike Lawler in high-stakes House race
summary: Republican Mike Lawler and Democrat Cait Conley clashed over sanctuary city laws and illegal immigration in a bitter fight for New York's 17th Congressional District.
story: Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., joins ‘Fox News Live’ to discuss his heated debate against Democratic challenger Cait Conley in the race for New York’s 17th Congressional District.
A former Biden administration aide is projected to defeat Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., in one of the most closely watched races of the 2026 election cycle.

Cait Conley, a military veteran who served on the White House National Security Council, will likely be coming to Congress next year after beating the two-term incumbent for the job, The Associated Press projected late Thursday.
Multiple forecasts suggested the seat would be a likely pickup for Democrats.
THUNE WEIGHS NIGHTMARE SCENARIO FOR GOP AS DEMOCRATS THREATEN TO FLIP HOUSE

The race between Rep. Mike Lawler and Democrat veteran Cait Conley could decide the fate of the House of Representatives for the next two years. (Eric Lee/Bloomberg via Getty Images; Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

Both parties poured enormous resources into the race for New York’s 17th Congressional District in the months before Election Day. It was widely seen as key to both parties’ quests to win the House majority.
The district, which sits just north of New York City, was won by Vice President Kamala Harris in 2024.
TENSION ERUPTS DURING HOUSE MIDTERM DEBATE AS LAWLER FACT-CHECKS NEW YORK DEMOCRAT OPPONENT ON IMMIGRATION
Lawler spent much of the race walking a political tightrope between supporting President Donald Trump and positioning himself as an independent voice.
And the race itself was marked by bitter divisions on issues like immigration enforcement and taxes.
Rep. Mike Lawler, R-N.Y., speaks with President Donald Trump at Rockland Community College Fieldhouse, May 22, 2026, in Suffern, N.Y. (Brendan Smialowski/AFP via Getty Images)
DHS BOSS REVEALS OVAL OFFICE PLAN TO 'WITHHOLD FUNDING' FROM SANCTUARY CITIES AFTER AGGRESSIVE NEW YORK BUST

Among Lawler’s backers were the parents of Sheridan Gorman, a college student from his district who was killed in Chicago while she was out with friends. Gorman’s accused killer is an illegal immigrant who was previously arrested for shoplifting, but was released without a federal immigration detainer because of Chicago’s sanctuary city laws.

Lawler and Gorman's parents have pointed to her killing as proof that Democrat-backed sanctuary laws — which are active in New York as well — are deadly for Americans. He argued that Conley would do nothing to mitigate the effects of illegal immigration.
ARMY COMBAT VETERAN CHALLENGING MIKE LAWLER CALLS HEGSETH NATIONAL SECURITY 'HAZARD,' BACKS IMPEACHMENT

The family of 18-year-old Loyola University Chicago student Sheridan Gorman of Yorktown Heights, N.Y., who was allegedly fatally shot in Chicago in March by an illegal alien, speaks about their daughter and sister during a speech by President Donald Trump in Suffern, N.Y. (Pool/Fox News)
Conley, for her part, condemned Gorman’s killing and has said she is against illegal immigration, but she has not spoken out against sanctuary laws specifically.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Conley served as counterterrorism director on the White House National Security Council from 2021 to 2023 and spent the remainder of former President Joe Biden’s term as a senior advisor on election security at the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency.
Fox News Power Rankings rated the district as "lean Democrat," while the Cook Political Report ranked it a toss-up.
Elizabeth Elkind is a politics reporter for Fox News Digital leading coverage of the House of Representatives. Previous digital bylines seen at Daily Mail and CBS News.

title: Hegseth expands National Guard operations in DC, authorizes police patrol cars, Humvees and boats
summary: Pete Hegseth authorized 60 marked patrol cars, Humvees and D.C. National Guard boats as a council hearing demands the military presence be removed.
story: Former D.C. homicide Det. Ted Williams discusses the Washington, D.C., City Council’s request that governors withdraw National Guard troops on ‘Fox Report.’

War Secretary Pete Hegseth has authorized National Guard troops in Washington, D.C., to use dozens of marked police cars, military vehicles and boats as local officials demand an end to the deployment.

Two Pentagon officials confirmed to Fox News Digital that Hegseth signed an Oct. 29 memo authorizing up to 60 marked patrol cars, Humvees, military tactical vehicles, D.C. National Guard boats and up to 20 light towers and generators.
Roughly 3,000 National Guard troops are deployed in the nation's capital as part of President Donald Trump's crime crackdown.
FBI TOUTS 6,000 ARRESTS, 44% HOMICIDE DROP ONE YEAR INTO TRUMP'S DC CRIME CRACKDOWN
Military police soldiers from the National Guard stand guard by Mine Resistant Ambush Protected All-Terrain Vehicles in Washington, D.C., Aug. 14, 2025. (Fox News Digital/Peter Pinedo)

"The secretary of war has authorized the continued use of National Guard personnel and capabilities in support of the Make D.C. Safe and Beautiful mission," a War Department official told Fox News Digital.

"The October 29, 2026, guidance authorizes the use of up to 60 marked patrol cars, military tactical vehicles, up to 20 light towers and generators and D.C. National Guard maritime boat assets in support of federal and local law enforcement operations."
Politico first reported the authorization, which follows Hegseth's decision last year to allow National Guard troops to carry service-issued weapons when required by their mission.
TRUMP’S DC LAW-AND-ORDER BLITZ MARKS ONE YEAR WITH EYE-POPPING HAUL OF SUSPECTS
Secretary of Defense Pete Hegseth speaks at the Association of the United States Army 2026 Annual Meeting and Exposition in Washington, D.C., Oct. 14, 2026.  (Jim Watson/AFP via Getty Images)
The move comes as D.C. Councilmember Brooke Pinto, chair of the council's public safety committee, held a hearing Thursday examining the federal law enforcement and National Guard presence.

"I am very hopeful and optimistic that we now have the partners we need at the state and congressional level to push back and demand that this unnecessary, harmful and unlawful military presence be removed from the district," she said during the hearing.
Pinto called on newly elected Democratic governors in Georgia, Iowa, Nevada, Ohio and Texas to withdraw the combined 628 troops she said their states have deployed to Washington.
National Guard vehicles were stationed in Washington, D.C., Tuesday amid the Trump administration's surge to combat crime in the capital. (WTTG)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Pinto also urged congressional Democrats to increase oversight of federal law enforcement operations in January, including requirements for identifying badges and body cameras.
Brittany Miller is a Fox News Digital breaking news writer and former Independent reporter who graduated from Syracuse University in 2023.

title: DeSantis nukes ‘tech guy’ Vivek after Ohio drubbing: ‘Not in tune’ with blue-collar voters
summary: Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis says Vivek Ramaswamy wasn't "in tune" with Ohio's blue-collar voters, citing his tech background and H-1B stance.
story: Vivek Ramaswamy addressed supporters at GOP headquarters in Columbus after the gubernatorial race was called for Democrat Amy Acton.

Florida Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis blasted failed Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and his GOP handlers, arguing on a podcast that he wasn't "in tune" with the working-class people of the state.

Biotech entrepreneur Ramaswamy lost his scandal-plagued race to Democratic candidate Amy Acton by 7.9 percentage points. Despite President Donald Trump’s endorsement and guidance from Vice President JD Vance’s top advisers, Ramaswamy lost amid a "blue wave" that produced major Democratic upsets across the country. The midterm elections were widely viewed as a referendum on Trump's presidency.
But DeSantis, who ran for president in 2024 and is term-limited after 2026, shared on the Sage Steele Show that Ramaswamy bore some responsibility for his loss.

"I don't know why they would have pushed him to be the candidate there. Oh, my mom's from Youngstown. Ohio is a working class state, very blue collar. You know Vivek, he's like a tech guy," DeSantis said.
RAMASWAMY OUTLINES KEY CONTRASTS WITH DEM OPPONENT LESS THAN 100 DAYS OUT FROM KEY GUBERNATORIAL ELECTION
Ohio Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy speaks during a campaign rally on February 25, 2025, at the Glass City Center in Toledo, Ohio. (Scott W. Grau/Icon Sportswire via Getty Images)

Ramaswamy, who previously ran for the Republican presidential nomination in 2024, is the founder of biotech company Roivant Sciences and anti-ESG investment firm Strive Asset Management. He also briefly co-led President Trump’s Department of Government Efficiency with Elon Musk.

He was warmly embraced by Trump, who endorsed him the same day Ramaswamy announced his candidacy. Trump had previously encouraged Ramaswamy to consider seeking Vance’s former Senate seat. Ramaswamy and Vance have known each other since their time at Yale Law School.

DeSantis criticized Ramaswamy’s support for a merit-based H-1B visa system, arguing that it likely further distanced him from Ohio’s blue-collar voters. Ramaswamy had said the current lottery-based system should be "gutted."
'He wants to bring in foreign workers on visas. That is not the type of person that's going to sell." DeSantis said.
Ramaswamy's own companies have used the H-1B program, with Roivant Sciences having 29 H-1B applications approved between 2018 and 2023.

Meanwhile, Strive Asset Management, the investment firm he co-founded, moved its headquarters from Columbus to Dallas in 2025, months before Ramaswamy launched his campaign for Ohio governor. Ramaswamy said he was no longer involved in the company’s operations, but remained a major shareholder.
FOX NEWS VOTER POLL: 2026 MIDTERM ELECTIONS USHER IN A BLUE WAVE AS DEMOCRATS WIN CONTROL OF CONGRESS
Gov. Ron DeSantis holds a press conference at the State Emergency Operations Center regarding Hurricane Isaias on Thursday, Oct. 8, 2026. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters)

"And I know he shot himself in the foot," DeSantis said. "I know he did a lot of other stuff to make it a real landslide against him. But even with that, it's like you know you got to meet the voters where they are on some of this stuff," DeSantis said. "I think we would have done better in Ohio had we had a candidate that was more representative or more in tune with the interests of kind of these blue collar people that make the backbone of Ohio."

Just weeks before the election, Ramaswamy’s campaign drew bipartisan outrage for using Democratic Gov.-elect Amy Acton’s estranged mother in an attack ad that called the Democratic candidate a "liar" and disputed her account of childhood poverty and homelessness.

The ad omitted that Acton had not seen or spoken to her mother since age 12, when her stepfather was arrested on charges of raping her. He pleaded not guilty but fled the area before trial, and court records show authorities continued seeking his arrest for years. Acton’s brother has said their mother remained married to him until his death in 2004.

Ramaswamy's loss, alongside Republican U.S. Senate candidate Jon Husted's loss to Democratic candidate Sherrod Brown by 4.9 percentage points, came just two years after Trump won the state by 11.2 percentage points.
DESANTIS CALLS GOP MIDTERM LOSSES 'EXTINCTION-LEVEL EVENT' — AND EXPLAINS WHY FLORIDA SURVIVED

Amy Acton, former director of the Ohio Department of Health and Democratic gubernatorial candidate, meets with local residents while campaigning at Bottoms Up Coffee in Columbus, Ohio, on Monday, April 6, 2026. (Stephen Zenner/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
In addition to criticizing Ramaswamy, DeSantis took aim at Congress, saying Republicans are now on the "defensive" and faulting lawmakers for failing to codify Trump’s executive orders into law.

"Last night's elections did not only kneecap the last two years of the Trump administration, it basically ensures the four years after that are going to either be Democrat years where they have a trifecta or where you have a Republican president that is hemmed in and limited," DeSantis said.
DeSantis also pushed back against any 2028 speculation.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"The only way that I would run for any office is if you can actually deliver big results," DeSantis said. "I don't want to just be a timepiece where I just sit there like a potted plant."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Fox News Digital reached out to Ramaswamy for comment.
Elaine Mallon is a writer for Fox News Digital and Fox Business covering national politics.

title: Ex-Alaska lawmaker details mystery recruiter as FBI, Congress widen 'Decoy Dan' scrutiny
summary: The FBI interviewed former Alaska Republican David Eastman after a Democratic operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter in the Senate race.
story: Article III Project attorney Will Chamberlain explains how an alleged effort to confuse Alaska voters by recruiting a second candidate named Dan Sullivan could violate federal conspiracy-against-rights law, potentially exposing those involved to felony charges carrying up to 10 years in prison.

A former Alaska Republican lawmaker told Fox News Digital the FBI interviewed him after an apparent Democratic political operative allegedly posed as a conservative recruiter and tried to persuade him to enter the state's U.S. Senate race amid an intensifying congressional investigation into the controversial "Decoy Dan Sullivan" ballot scheme.

The allegations raise questions about potential federal criminal liability. Article III Project attorney Will Chamberlain argued that a coordinated effort to deceive voters about a candidate's identity could violate 18 U.S.C. § 241, the federal conspiracy-against-rights statute.

The revelations come after former campaign staff for Democratic Senate nominee Mary Peltola spoke to the New York Times about their knowledge of a reported scheme to stack Alaska’s four-person ballot with other "Dan Sullivans" to help siphon votes from incumbent GOP Sen. Dan Sullivan.
MARY PELTOLA'S CAMPAIGN, DEMS BACKED COVERT SCHEME TO FIELD SPOILER CANDIDATES IN ALASKA SENATE RACE: REPORT
Sen. Dan Sullivan, R-Alaska, and former Rep. Mary Peltola, D-Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images; Nathaniel Wilder/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

The ballot ultimately included Peltola, incumbent Republican Sen. Dan S. Sullivan, Republican Gerald Heikes and retired Petersburg teacher Dan J. Sullivan. Whether the similarly named candidate diverted votes or affected the outcome remains unproven.
Chamberlain told Fox News Digital the alleged operation could constitute a federal felony if prosecutors establish that participants conspired to interfere with voters' constitutional rights.
PELTOLA CAMPAIGN'S ALLEGED DAN SULLIVAN SPOILER PLOT TAKES NEW TURN AS DOJ FACES MAJOR LEGAL HURDLE
Dan J. Sullivan, who filed to run for U.S. Senate in Alaska, poses for a photo in Petersburg, Alaska, on June 26, 2026. (Katie Holmlund/Associated Press)
"The basic concept is you're not allowed to conspire to injure or harm people's constitutional rights. And one of those rights is to vote for the candidate of your choice," Chamberlain said.

"These people conspired to put a fake ‘Decoy Dan’ Sullivan on the ballot in order to trick people who were going into the ballot box intending to vote for the incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan," he alleged. "There's a lot of good precedent on this that suggests that's a crime and a felony punishable by up to 10 years in prison."

Chamberlain cited historical cases involving ballot manipulation, while acknowledging that the precise circumstances of recruiting a same-name candidate have not previously been addressed in an identical case.

"Nothing exactly like this has happened before in the sense of recruiting a same-name candidate to trick people in the ballot box," he said, adding that a lot of slanted electoral messaging is not illegal.
ALASKA'S GOVERNOR ORDERS INVESTIGATION AFTER NYT REPORT ON ALLEGED DEM-LINKED SENATE ELECTION SCHEME

"If you want to pretend that another Republican is better than the current incumbent or pretend that the incumbent's not running and then persuade someone to vote for that candidate, that's not a ‘conspiracy against rights’ because the right to vote for the candidate of your choice has not been impinged upon," he said.

"It's the fact that when you're conspiring to put two people with the exact same name on the ballot to trick people who are going in there intending to vote for the incumbent and get them to vote for somebody else by deception."

Meanwhile, former state Rep. David Eastman, a Republican from the Matanuska-Susitna Valley, told Fox News Digital by phone from Wasilla that he was approached by an operative under what he later surmised were false pretenses to recruit him into the race. Eastman said he also received several "fake mailers" suggesting "Decoy Dan" Sullivan was the real or only Sullivan in the race.
The mailers, shared with Fox News Digital, are framed in a "meet the candidates" format and do omit Senator Sullivan.

Eastman told Fox News Digital he was approached in the Mat-Su by an operative he later identified in a blog post as Jerid Kurtz, who was named in the New York Times report. Eastman said the operative claimed to represent conservative donors and encouraged him to run for Senate.
"He approached me through a constituent. I sat down with him in April here in Wasilla," Eastman said.
"He pretended to represent conservative donors and was looking for conservative candidates to run for federal office; none of which was true," Eastman added.

Eastman alleged Kurtz "pretended" to represent conservative donors and used a false name, but said the operative never mentioned either Sullivan or disclosed an intention to confuse voters during their meeting.

Fox News Digital reached out to the DSCC, Peltola’s campaign and Wingspan Strategies — where Kurtz is named in congressional documents as a co-owner — for comment. Dan J. Sullivan reportedly "vanished" as investigators began knocking on doors in his remote community, according to the Wall Street Journal.

The allegations come as federal investigators examine whether Democratic political operatives improperly recruited Dan J. Sullivan in an effort to confuse voters who intended to support Senator Sullivan.

The controversy has also reached Capitol Hill. In an October 29 letter, House Oversight and Government Reform Committee Chairman James Comer, R-Ky., requested that Kurtz appear for an in-person transcribed interview on November 6 concerning allegations that operatives associated with Mary Peltola's campaign sought to recruit similarly named candidates to confuse voters.
"As a Democrat operative who was allegedly tasked with assisting in this effort, you have information that will assist the Committee's investigation," Comer wrote.
"If you do not voluntarily appear for the interview, we will be forced to evaluate the use of compulsory process," he warned.

Eastman said Kurtz did not mention either Sullivan or disclose an effort to confuse voters during their April meeting. He nevertheless questioned the operative's intentions after subsequent reporting connected Kurtz to the alleged candidate recruitment effort.

title: Gavin Newsom wipes out California's death row in historic mass commutation
summary: California Gov. Gavin Newsom will commute all 548 death sentences to life without parole, drawing sharp backlash from victims' rights advocates.
story: Decades after his daughter Polly Klaas was murdered, Marc Klaas speaks out against California Gov. Gavin Newsom's potential plan to commute California’s remaining death sentences, calling the move a betrayal of crime victims and voters.

California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced Thursday that he will spare the lives of 548 inmates currently on the state’s death row, effectively clearing capital punishment in the state years after issuing an executive moratorium on executions.
In a letter to constituents, Newsom, a Democrat, declared the state's capital punishment system fundamentally flawed, error-prone, and morally incompatible with California’s core values.

"After nearly 30 years in public office, I have come to understand the limits of what government can justly accomplish," Newsom wrote. "I take this action because I firmly believe that state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."
EX-CHIEF SAYS CHRISTA PIKE WAS 'ALMOST GIDDY' DESCRIBING MURDER AS GOVERNOR WEIGHS IN AFTER BOTCHED EXECUTION
California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced that he will commute the death sentences for all 548 of the state's death row inmates. (Fred Greaves/Reuters)

Under the executive action, all death sentences will be converted to life imprisonment without the possibility of parole. The move comes amid renewed national conversations surrounding capital punishment following a botched execution in Tennessee involving death row inmate Christa Pike.

California has not carried out an execution since 2006. Shortly after taking office in 2019, Newsom placed an official moratorium on executions and ordered the dismantling of the execution chamber at San Quentin State Prison.
The decision drew immediate criticism from victims' rights advocates, including Marc Klaas, whose 12-year-old daughter, Polly, was kidnapped and murdered in 1993.
Her killer, Richard Allen Davis, remains on death row.
CHARLES MANSON FOLLOWER TIED TO SHARON TATE MURDERS GETS RECOMMENDED FOR PAROLE AFTER 55 YEARS IN PRISON

The father of Polly Klaas, Marc Klaas, heavily criticized California Gov. Gavin Newsom amid reports that he is considering a mass commutation of the state's death row inmates. Richard Allen Davis, who was convicted for the 1993 death of Polly Klaas, was sentenced to death by a judge. (Polly Klaas Foundation; AP)

"He just gave the gift of life to [hundreds of] people who took the gift of life from their victims," Klaas told Fox News Digital, expressing disappointment over the decision. "I don't understand his rationale behind it… but it's probably the same old tired stuff that he said when he did his moratorium."
"He has definitely secured the serial killer vote now," he added.
POPE LEO DENOUNCES DEATH PENALTY AS 'INADMISSIBLE' AHEAD OF PENTAGON'S PLANNED LIVESTREAMED EXECUTION

Lt. Sam Robinson calls to open a door at San Quentin State Prison's death row in San Quentin, Calif., on Aug. 15, 2016. The prison is California's oldest penitentiary and houses the state's only death row for men with 700 condemned inmates. (Justin Sullivan/Getty Images)
Conversely, anti-death penalty advocates strongly praised the move.

"The silence after the very breath of a human is violently wrestled out of them is deafening," Rev. Jeff Hood, a spiritual adviser to death row inmates, said in a statement reported by The Sacramento Bee.

"I’ve heard it 14 times. Today, Governor Newsom has courageously chosen to break that silence. These commutations represent the height of moral leadership," he added. "Cruelty laid down. Now, I’m left with one prayer: God, don’t let any of the governors in the other executing states get any sleep until they find the ethical stamina to follow Newsom’s lead."
Despite the move, Los Angeles County District Attorney Nathan Hochman noted that it doesn't eliminate the death penalty.

"Only the Legislature or the voters can do that," he said in a statement. "Californians have been asked on two separate ballot initiatives to abolish the death penalty and both times they have chosen to keep it for the most serious crimes."
District Attorney Nathan J. Hochman speaks at a news conference at the Hall of Justice in Los Angeles, California. (Jim Vondruska/Getty Images)

"Until the law is changed, my office will continue to evaluate every death penalty-eligible case with the rigor, care and restraint these decisions demand. As always, we will be guided by the facts, the law and the evidence. If the Legislature or the voters remove the death penalty, we will follow that law just as faithfully," he added, noting that his thoughts "are with the families of victims, who deserve a justice system that honors the law as it is written and pursues it with fairness and due process."
Dan Dow, the district attorney for San Luis Obispo County, said framed Newsom's order as an insult to murder victims.

"Governor Newsom just told the families of Rachel Newhouse, Aundria Crawford, Kesha Gurke and every other innocent victim of California's 548 condemned killers that the killers' lives matter more," he said. "Juries chose justice case by case, voters chose it five times, and one outgoing governor tried to erase it all with a pen.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
California voters have consistently supported the death penalty.
In 2016, voters rejected Proposition 62, which sought to repeal the death penalty, while narrowly approving Proposition 66 to expedite the appeals process.

title: Democrats ‘divorced from voters’ as 5 states back citizen-only voting, bolstering GOP push
summary: Voters in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia approved noncitizen voting bans by wide margins, but a key Supreme Court case looms.
story: Honest Elections Project Action Executive Director Jason Snead says voters overwhelmingly support proof-of-citizenship requirements and urges the Supreme Court to clear the way for states to verify voter registrations.

Voters in five states overwhelmingly approved ballot measures barring noncitizens from voting, including Kansas, where Democrats scored a major Senate upset, and Alaska, where the Senate race remains uncalled.

Federal law already prohibits noncitizens from voting in federal elections, but measures approved in Kansas, Alaska, Arkansas, South Dakota and West Virginia clarify or explicitly codify citizenship requirements for voting in state and local elections, with support exceeding 60% in each state.

Election integrity advocates pointed to the results as evidence supporting President Donald Trump and Republicans’ argument that their push to require proof of citizenship for federal voter registration has "overwhelming bipartisan support."
REPUBLICANS SUFFER HISTORIC SENATE UPSET AS DEM FLIPS DEEP-RED STATE FOR FIRST TIME IN NEARLY A CENTURY
"I would absolutely agree that noncitizen voting bans are overwhelmingly popular," Jason Snead, executive director of Honest Elections Project, told Fox News Digital. "They enjoy bipartisan support."
A 2024 Gallup poll found that 83% of Americans, including 66% of Democrats, support requiring first-time voters to provide proof of citizenship when registering to vote.

A volunteer picks up a "Require Voter ID" sign at a news conference at the Riverside County Registrar of Voters March 2, 2026, as GOP lawmakers gather in support of placing a voter ID measure on the November ballot.  (Anjali Sharif-Paul/MediaNews Group/The Sun via Getty Images)

The ballot measure wins also come as the conservative-majority Supreme Court prepares to consider a related dispute over whether Arizona can require proof of citizenship on its state voter registration form and remove suspected noncitizens from the rolls before an election, a ruling that could affect how states enforce citizenship requirements.

Related election measures failed in California and Arizona. California’s Proposition 39 was defeated 58.5% to 41.4%, a margin of roughly 17 percentage points; the measure would have required voter ID and additional citizenship-verification procedures.

"I would note that the unique thing there is not only that California is openly hostile to the idea of trying to prevent noncitizen voting in terms of its elected leadership, but also the left poured more than $30 million into the ballot measure campaign to defeat that," Snead told Fox News Digital.
Snead said Arizona’s measure was broader legislation that included several provisions beyond noncitizen voting, which may have contributed to its defeat.

The victories for the measures barring noncitizens from voting follow the Trump administration and congressional Republicans’ failed efforts to pass the SAVE America Act, which would require proof of citizenship to register to vote.
ARIZONA VOTER LAW FIGHT REACHES SCOTUS AS ELECTION GROUPS WARN ‘ABSURD’ CONSEQUENCE COULD ENSUE
An election official sorts ballots during early voting Oct. 28, 2025, in Portland, Maine. (Robert F. Bukaty/AP)

The SAVE America Act also became a flashpoint in Congress, with Republicans and Democrats sparring over whether to attach it to a budget reconciliation package. Trump’s effort to tie the bill to Department of Homeland Security funding contributed to a prolonged standoff during the department’s shutdown.
Senate Majority Leader John Thune said Republicans lacked the votes to pass it, while Democrats argued it would disenfranchise eligible voters.
Hans von Spakovsky, a former member of the Federal Election Commission and senior legal fellow of Advancing American Freedom, said the Democratic Party is completely "divorced" from its voters.
Snead agreed, saying Democrats took a "90-10 issue" and turned it into a highly politicized fight.
"The left is far out of step with the American public, and they really should be answering the question, 'Why are you opposed to something that 90% of the public is in favor of?" Snead said.

"Only citizens should vote in our elections. And if you believe, as the left claims to, in democracy, well then, we should start by making sure that we have free and fair elections that are decided only by American citizens."
But while Spakovsky applauded the passage of the ballot measures, he warned they could prove ineffective unless states are allowed to verify voters’ citizenship.
"Look, I'm glad those states passed that referendum, but those provisions aren't going to be much good unless states are able to do two things," Spakovsky said.

Spakovsky pointed to Republican National Committee v. Mi Familia Vota, a case in which the Supreme Court will decide whether federal law prevents Arizona from requiring documentary proof of citizenship to register to vote in federal elections and from removing suspected noncitizens from its voter rolls.
He said the ruling could affect how effectively states can enforce citizenship requirements.
ELECTION EXPERT SOUNDS ALARM ON HOW NONCITIZENS ARE LANDING ON VOTER ROLLS
U.S. Senate Majority Leader John Thune, R-S.D., speaks to reporters in the U.S. Capitol on Aug. 8, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)
Snead said simply checking a box attesting to citizenship on a federal form has not been sufficient.

"As we have seen in a number of recent arrests by the Justice Department, with indictments going out against noncitizens, and with the failures of the automatic voter registration system in New Jersey, which added 6,600 noncitizens to the rolls, with almost 400 of them voting, we clearly have been let down by that check-a-box system," Snead said.
However, Spakovsky said a ruling in favor of Arizona would only go so far, arguing that proof of citizenship would only apply to future voter registrations.

"The only way for them to try to check the citizenship of people who are already registered is by using the SAVE database at the Department of Homeland Security, and with complete control of Congress, I have no doubt that one of the first things Democrats will do is try to defund the database so that states can't use it," Spakovsky said.

Snead applauded the Trump administration's efforts to expand states’ access to the SAVE database to clean up their voter rolls, arguing the previous process of tracking down ineligible voters was "cumbersome." He also voiced concerns that Democrats will gut the database.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
"I would not be surprised if they try to defund the entire safe system or pass legislation to prevent its use for cleaning up voter rolls," Snead said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"I think that we are fast approaching the point where it is fair to say, 'Why are Democrats actively pushing for noncitizen voting?'" Snead continued. "I think that's the direction that we are going."

title: Hegseth demands $350B for military, fires back at Dem impeachment push
summary: War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve $350 billion in military funding and vowed to fight Democratic impeachment efforts.
story: Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress to approve at least $350 billion in additional funding, arguing the investment is needed to rebuild the military and keep the U.S. ahead in a dangerous world. (Credit: @SecWar)
War Secretary Pete Hegseth urged Congress Thursday to approve at least $350 billion in defense funding while pushing back against efforts to impeach him.
In a video posted to X, Hegseth defended his Pentagon overhaul, including eliminating DEI initiatives, removing military leaders and rebuilding recruitment.
Hegseth dismissed the impeachment push as political theater while defending his efforts to overhaul the Pentagon and advance President Donald Trump's military agenda.
HEGSETH FACES BIPARTISAN IMPEACHMENT THREAT AFTER IRAN WAR GETS BLAME FOR GOP MIDTERM SLAUGHTER
Secretary of War Pete Hegseth testifies before the Senate Armed Services Committee on Capitol Hill, in Washington, D.C., April 30. (Cliff Owen/AP Photo, File)
"We need every vote from every patriotic member of Congress," Hegseth said, calling for a reconciliation bill of at least $350 billion to strengthen the military and defense industrial base.

The impeachment effort is being led by Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., who introduced eight articles against Hegseth in September, accusing him of violating congressional war powers during the Iran conflict and abusing his authority in other military operations.
Massie, who lost his Republican primary in May, plans to renew the effort when Congress returns next week. The House has not voted on the articles.
Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling ABC News he intends to keep him in his Cabinet despite the impeachment push.
GOP REP THOMAS MASSIE INTRODUCES 8 ARTICLES OF IMPEACHMENT AGAINST WAR SECRETARY PETE HEGSETH
Rep. Thomas Massie, R-Ky., introduced eight articles of impeachment against Hegseth in September. (Tom Williams/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images, File)
Hegseth dismissed the effort as politically motivated.
"A disgruntled, defeated congressman along with all his Democrat allies, has also dropped sham articles of impeachment against yours truly," Hegseth said.

He also took aim at former President Joe Biden and former Defense Secretary Lloyd Austin, accusing them of leaving the Pentagon in disarray and forcing the Trump administration to rebuild the military.
"We ended the weird and the woke and elevated patriots in strength," Hegseth said, defending his efforts to eliminate diversity initiatives and change military personnel policies.
HEGSETH'S LEADERSHIP QUESTIONED BY GOP MILITARY VETERAN AS DEMOCRATS TALK IMPEACHMENT
Trump defended Hegseth on Thursday, telling ABC News he intends to keep him in his Cabinet despite the impeachment push. (Aaron Schwartz/AFP via Getty Images, File)
Hegseth also defended the administration's military operations against Iran, describing the campaign as a historic effort to prevent Tehran from acquiring nuclear weapons.
The war secretary closed with a message to troops amid the political fight in Washington.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"Don't blink. Ignore the noise. Never hesitate," Hegseth said."We will not back down. We put America and the warfighter first, always and without apology."
