Cybercriminals can access online accounts without stealing passwords by hijacking login sessions, exploiting security approvals or abusing connected apps. (Felix Zahn/Photothek via Getty Images)
1. Stolen login sessions

When you sign in to a website, the service often creates a session that tells it you have already proved who you are. Your browser or app may keep that session active so you do not have to enter your password every few minutes. Criminals can sometimes steal the digital tokens or cookies associated with these sessions. If the service accepts the stolen information, an attacker may gain access without entering your password or completing another verification step.

How to protect yourself: Review the devices and active sessions connected to your accounts. Sign out of anything you don't recognize and check for suspicious login activity. We've previously explained how to check for unfamiliar devices and remove them from your Apple, Google and Microsoft accounts.

If you suspect unauthorized access, change your password using a trusted device and revoke other sessions when the service allows it. Remember that removing a device from an account list does not always terminate an active login session.
2. SIM swaps and phone account fraud

Your phone number is often connected to email, banking, payment and social media accounts. Criminals may try to convince a mobile carrier to transfer your number to a SIM card or eSIM they control. If the transfer succeeds, they may receive calls and text messages intended for you, including certain account verification codes. A sudden loss of cellular service can be an early warning sign, especially when there is no known local outage. Other signs include an unexpected carrier notification about a device change or a password reset message you did not request.

How to protect yourself: Ask your carrier about an account security PIN, number transfer lock and port-out protection. These protections vary by carrier. For sensitive accounts, use a passkey, security key or authenticator app when available. Unlike text verification codes, authenticator app codes generally do not depend on your phone number. If text messages are your only available second authentication method, keep them enabled. They still provide more protection than relying on a password alone.
ARE BANK TEXT CODES ENOUGH TO PROTECT YOU?
Stolen session cookies and malicious browser extensions can give hackers access to sensitive accounts, even when strong passwords are in place. (Britta Pedersen/picture alliance via Getty Images)
3. Fake login approvals and MFA fatigue

Multifactor authentication, or MFA, adds another layer of protection to your accounts. However, criminals sometimes target the person receiving the security request. One tactic is MFA fatigue, also called push bombing. An attacker who can trigger authentication requests repeatedly sends approval notifications, hoping you eventually tap "Approve" to make them stop. Criminals may also impersonate technical support or a financial institution and ask you to read aloud a one-time security code.

How to protect yourself: Never approve a login you did not initiate or share a verification code with someone who unexpectedly contacts you. If repeated prompts appear, deny them and check the account through its official website or app. Change your password if you suspect it has been compromised. When available, choose phishing-resistant authentication, such as a passkey or security key. App-based approvals that require number matching can also offer additional protection against accidental approvals.
4. Malware and risky browser extensions

An infostealer is malicious software designed to collect information from a device. Depending on its capabilities, it may steal browser-stored passwords, session cookies, payment information or other sensitive data. These programs can arrive through fake software updates, pirated applications, suspicious email attachments, malicious advertisements or compromised browser extensions. Some malware operates quietly, which means you may not immediately notice anything unusual.

How to protect yourself: Keep your operating system, browser and security software updated. Avoid downloading software from unfamiliar websites and review browser extensions regularly. If you suspect malware has compromised a device, use a separate, trusted device to secure important accounts. Run a security scan with strong antivirus software and remove suspicious software. For a serious infection, professional assistance or reinstalling the operating system may be necessary. Avoid signing back into sensitive accounts until you are confident the device is secure.
5. Malicious apps with access to your accounts

Some criminals do not need to steal your password or infect your device. Instead, they may trick you into giving a connected application permission to access your information. For example, a fake productivity tool might ask to read your email, access your contacts or manage files in your cloud storage. You may encounter a legitimate-looking permission screen asking you to approve those requests. If you grant access to a malicious app, it may be able to retrieve information through the permissions you approved. In certain cases, that access can continue even after you change your account password.

This technique is sometimes called OAuth consent phishing. In a September 2026 warning, the FBI explained that criminals can trick people into granting malicious applications access to their accounts. That access can remain active even after a password change unless the victim revokes the application's permissions.

How to protect yourself: Review the third-party applications connected to your Google, Microsoft and other important accounts. Look closely at what each application can access. Remove permissions for apps you no longer use or do not recognize. Be especially careful with applications requesting access to email, contacts, cloud files or account management features.
Passkeys can help, but they are not the whole answer

Passkeys can significantly reduce the risk of traditional password phishing. They use cryptographic credentials associated with your device, security key or password manager. Unlike a password that you type into a website, a properly implemented passkey is tied to the legitimate website or service. That makes it much harder for a fake login page to steal the credential. However, passkeys do not eliminate every security risk. Criminals may still target an already authenticated session, an infected device, a malicious connected application or an account recovery process.

How to protect yourself: Use passkeys when your important accounts support them. Protect your devices with a strong screen lock and keep recovery information current. If a service offers backup recovery codes, store them securely so you can regain access if your primary device is lost or damaged.
Why changing your password may not be enough

Changing a compromised password is important, but it may not automatically remove every form of unauthorized access. Some services revoke existing sessions after a password change, while others require you to sign out of devices separately.

A criminal might also have established another route into your account, such as an app-specific password, an unauthorized connected application or a new recovery method. Your email deserves particular attention. Someone with access to your inbox could create forwarding rules that quietly send copies of your messages elsewhere.

Review security settings for unfamiliar recovery addresses, connected devices, forwarding rules and app permissions. Remove anything you did not authorize. Also, check whether your password was reused elsewhere. If it was, replace those passwords with unique credentials. A password manager can make this easier without requiring you to memorize every login.
What to do if someone gets around your password
If you suspect an account takeover, act quickly. Start with the account that controls access to your other accounts, usually your primary email.
Here's where to focus:

Secure your email: Use a trusted device to change your password, revoke suspicious sessions and check recovery information.Review connected apps: Remove unauthorized permissions and app-specific passwords.Check your phone account: Contact your mobile carrier immediately if you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized number transfer.Protect financial accounts: Review recent transactions and contact your bank or card issuer about suspicious activity.Watch for identity theft: Examine your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze.Preserve evidence: Save security alerts, screenshots, transaction records, case numbers and dates of conversations with financial institutions.
Secure your email: Use a trusted device to change your password, revoke suspicious sessions and check recovery information.
Review connected apps: Remove unauthorized permissions and app-specific passwords.
Check your phone account: Contact your mobile carrier immediately if you suspect a SIM swap or unauthorized number transfer.
Protect financial accounts: Review recent transactions and contact your bank or card issuer about suspicious activity.
Watch for identity theft: Examine your credit reports for unfamiliar accounts or inquiries. Consider placing a fraud alert or credit freeze.
Preserve evidence: Save security alerts, screenshots, transaction records, case numbers and dates of conversations with financial institutions.

A credit freeze is free and can help prevent criminals from opening new credit accounts in your name. You must contact all three major credit bureaus — Equifax, Experian and TransUnion — to freeze your reports at each bureau. If you believe someone has stolen your identity, visit IdentityTheft.gov for a personalized recovery plan from the Federal Trade Commission.
The value of watching beyond the login

Strong account security is essential, but identity misuse can happen outside the original account. A criminal might use exposed personal information to apply for credit, take over a mobile account or attempt financial fraud without triggering a traditional password alert. That's where an identity theft protection service can provide another layer of monitoring.

These services can monitor certain financial accounts, credit activity and exposed personal information for signs of suspicious activity. Some also provide identity restoration specialists who can help you navigate the recovery process if your identity is stolen. Features vary by provider and plan, and no service can prevent every form of identity theft.

For additional peace of mind, consider a service that offers monitoring, timely alerts and recovery assistance. See my picks for the best identity theft protection services at Cyberguy.com to compare your options and find the right coverage for your needs.

Once a month, review active sessions for your main email and financial accounts. Remove devices you no longer use and check whether your recovery information or connected app permissions have changed. Pay attention to unexpected login alerts, changes to your mobile account and new financial activity. A short monthly security check can help you spot suspicious changes before they become a larger problem.
FAKE CHROME UPDATE SCAM COULD INFECT YOUR COMPUTER
SIM swap scams allow criminals to take control of phone numbers and intercept verification codes used to protect banking, email and social media accounts. (Donato Fasano/Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

For years, I've told people to use strong passwords and turn on two-factor authentication. I still stand by that advice. But what concerns me now is how criminals can get into accounts without ever knowing the password. Think about someone quietly reading your email through a connected app you forgot about or using a stolen login session to access information you've worked hard to protect. You might change your password and assume everything is fine, while that access remains open.

That's why I recommend checking which devices and apps have access to your most important accounts. Start with email and your mobile carrier, because losing control of either can create problems with your financial accounts. And while identity theft monitoring services can help alert you to certain suspicious activity, they work best alongside strong account security. A few minutes reviewing your settings today could save you a great deal of trouble later.

title: Elon Musk's Starlink could be your next cellphone carrier
summary: SpaceX is reportedly pursuing access to 80,000 cell sites to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier rivaling Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile.
story: President Donald Trump praised Elon Musk at the Golden Age of American Innovation Summit, recounting how the SpaceX founder rapidly deployed Starlink to hurricane-ravaged North Carolina. Trump says the technology restored critical communications and helped save hundreds of lives.

Ever look at your cellphone bill and wonder why you're paying so much when you still can't get a decent signal? Maybe calls drop inside your house or your phone loses service during a road trip. It's frustrating, especially when the big wireless companies keep promising better coverage.

Now, Elon Musk wants to give you another option. His company, SpaceX, is reportedly pursuing access to at least 80,000 cell sites across the United States. The goal is to turn Starlink into a major wireless carrier that could compete directly with Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile. If Musk pulls this off, the way you choose your cellphone service could change.

AMAZON LEO SATELLITE INTERNET TAKES ON STARLINK

You’ll learn how to secure your phone and personal information, find better travel deals, avoid common scams, save money on bookings and use technology to make your travels easier and less stressful. No technical experience is needed.

Elon Musk's SpaceX is reportedly seeking access to at least 80,000 U.S. cell sites as it explores turning Starlink into a nationwide wireless carrier. (Joan Cros/NurPhoto via Getty Images)
SpaceX wants 80,000 cell sites across America

SpaceX is reportedly negotiating with major cellular infrastructure companies to secure access to at least 80,000 sites nationwide. One company reportedly involved is Crown Castle, which owns and operates roughly 40,000 cell towers across the country. During an Oct. 21 earnings call, Crown Castle CEO Chris Hillabrant was asked about potential leasing discussions with SpaceX and other satellite providers. His response was revealing. "You can assume that we're talking to all parties," he said, although he declined to discuss specific customers. That's a significant development.

Cell towers provide the infrastructure that keeps our phones connected across the country. Wireless companies typically lease space on these towers rather than build every structure themselves. That approach helps them expand coverage without taking on the full cost of owning the infrastructure.

For perspective, the Wireless Infrastructure Association counted about 158,500 purpose-built cell towers nationwide in 2025. SpaceX's reported target of 80,000 cell sites would represent a substantial expansion, although cell sites and physical towers are not the same thing. A single tower can support equipment from multiple wireless networks, so the two figures are not directly comparable. Still, the reported discussions remain preliminary. SpaceX has not publicly confirmed agreements covering those 80,000 sites.
Why Elon Musk needs cell towers when Starlink has satellites

Here's something you might be wondering. If Starlink already has satellites orbiting Earth, why does SpaceX need thousands of cell towers? The answer comes down to how wireless coverage works. Satellites can provide connectivity in remote areas where traditional cell towers are scarce. However, signals from space can struggle to reach phones inside buildings or in places with an obstructed view of the sky.

That's where ground-based cellular networks come in. Traditional towers can provide stronger, more consistent service in areas where satellite connections face limitations. By combining both technologies, SpaceX hopes to create a network that keeps people connected across more locations.

There's another interesting piece to the strategy. SpaceX has also discussed adding small cellular base stations to equipment installed at Starlink customers' homes and businesses. Those stations could help provide mobile coverage without requiring the company to rely entirely on traditional cell towers.

However, there's a catch. Starlink customers install their equipment where they need home internet. Those locations may not line up with where a nationwide cellphone network needs additional coverage. That's why access to established cellular infrastructure could prove so valuable.
FCC CHAIRMAN CARR SAYS SPECTRUM AUCTION WILL MAKE WIRELESS FASTER, CHEAPER WHILE RAISING BILLIONS FOR TREASURY
SpaceX could challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile by combining Starlink's satellite technology with traditional cellphone towers across the United States. (Kirby Lee/Getty Images)
Starlink Mobile takes another major step forward

SpaceX has already made several investments that support its wireless ambitions. On October 8, investment firm Grain Management announced an agreement to sell its nationwide portfolio of 800 MHz wireless spectrum to SpaceX. The deal remains subject to Federal Communications Commission approval.

If you're unfamiliar with spectrum, think of it as the radio frequencies that carry wireless signals between your phone and a network. Different frequencies have different strengths. Lower-frequency signals generally travel farther and penetrate buildings more effectively than higher-frequency signals. That could help Starlink Mobile deliver coverage in places where satellite connections alone might struggle.

SpaceX also received FCC authorization in October to deploy a new constellation of up to 15,000 direct-to-device satellites. These satellites are designed to communicate with compatible phones and support a broader range of mobile services. However, that authorization doesn't mean all the satellites are already operating.

Together, those developments help explain why Musk is getting serious about the wireless business. SpaceX is assembling the pieces needed to connect phones through satellites and ground-based networks. During SpaceX's October earnings call, Musk said the company would expand its terrestrial networks to provide broader connectivity wherever SpaceX and Starlink are permitted to operate. He also said satellite launches and spectrum acquisitions would help Starlink Mobile become a major U.S. wireless carrier.
Could Starlink really challenge Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile?

The possibility has already caught Wall Street's attention. Following reports of SpaceX's cell tower negotiations, shares of major wireless companies fell on October 23. Meanwhile, cellular infrastructure companies saw their shares rise as investors anticipated potential business from SpaceX. But entering the wireless market won't come cheap.

Analysts at TD Cowen reportedly estimated that building a nationwide terrestrial network could cost more than $80 billion. The process could take years, even for a company with SpaceX's financial resources. And SpaceX would face established competitors with decades of experience. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile already operate extensive networks. They also have millions of customers and established retail operations.

Interestingly, SpaceX already works with T-Mobile through its T-Satellite with Starlink service. That partnership allows compatible phones to connect to satellites in certain areas without traditional cellular coverage. So, Musk's company currently helps support a wireless provider it could eventually compete against. That's an unusual position, but it also gives SpaceX experience delivering satellite connectivity to everyday phones. If Starlink Mobile becomes a standalone carrier, customers could eventually have another nationwide option beyond today's three dominant providers.
When could Starlink Mobile become available?

If you're already wondering when you can switch, there's an important detail to keep in mind. SpaceX has not announced a confirmed launch date for a fully independent nationwide cellphone service. The company expects to begin deploying its next-generation Starlink Mobile satellites in 2027.

However, building a terrestrial cellular network presents a separate challenge. SpaceX still needs access to suitable tower locations and the equipment required to operate them. The company also faces additional regulatory requirements. Its nationwide spectrum agreement with Grain Management, for example, still needs FCC approval.

Meanwhile, expanding coverage across the country will take considerable time. Even with thousands of satellites overhead, SpaceX would need a carefully planned ground network to deliver a reliable alternative to existing carriers. For now, Starlink's existing satellite partnerships should not be confused with the proposed nationwide cellphone service.
What this means to you

If you've been frustrated with your cellphone bill or unreliable coverage, another major wireless provider could eventually give you more options. More competition could mean better wireless deals. Verizon, AT&T and T-Mobile may face pressure to improve their plans if SpaceX introduces an appealing alternative. However, Starlink Mobile has not announced pricing for a standalone nationwide service. There's no guarantee it will cost less than what you're paying today.

Coverage could be the bigger selling point. By combining satellites with traditional cell towers, SpaceX could potentially reach places where existing wireless networks struggle. That could be especially appealing if you live in a rural community or frequently travel through areas with weak signals. However, actual performance will depend on where SpaceX installs its equipment and how well its satellite connections work.

The real test will come when SpaceX reveals its pricing and coverage plans. Can Starlink offer better service in places where other carriers struggle? And will it give people a compelling reason to switch? Those answers will determine whether Musk's wireless ambitions actually benefit cellphone customers.
GOV JEFF LANDRY: SPACEX BETS ON LOUISIANA AS AMERICA’S NEXT FRONTIER TAKES OFF IN THE SOUTH

Elon Musk's Starlink Mobile plans could give Americans another wireless option, although SpaceX has not announced pricing or a launch date for a standalone nationwide service. (Chandan Khanna/AFP via Getty Images)
Kurt's key takeaways

I've been covering wireless technology long enough to know that big promises don't always translate into better cellphone service. We've heard plenty about expanding coverage and improving connectivity. Yet there are still places where you can barely make a call. That's why I find SpaceX's plans interesting. Combining satellites with traditional cellular infrastructure could eventually give people more options, particularly in areas where the big carriers have struggled.

At the same time, I'm curious about the bigger picture. Musk already has an enormous satellite network, and now he reportedly wants to build a major wireless business on the ground. That could introduce some welcome competition. However, I'd like to know what the pricing will look like and whether Starlink can provide reliable coverage where people actually use their phones. If it can deliver on those promises, the established carriers may have a serious reason to worry. And frankly, a little more competition in the cellphone business wouldn't hurt.

If Elon Musk offered you cellphone service through Starlink, would you trust his company enough to leave Verizon, AT&T or T-Mobile? Or would you rather stick with the wireless provider you already know? Let us know by writing to us at Cyberguy.com

title: Florida Learjet crash investigators dig up engine piece after pilots warned of rough weather ahead
summary: NTSB crews recovered part of an engine from the Learjet 60 crash site in Greenacres, Florida, as the probe focuses on icing and turbulence reports.
story: Retired Navy fighter pilot Matthew 'Whiz' Buckley discusses the aircraft's damaged tail components, rapid descent and encounter with severe weather, as investigators work to determine what caused the deadly Florida Learjet crash.
Federal investigators have recovered part of an engine from the Learjet that slammed into the ground Sunday in Greenacres, Florida, killing all nine people aboard.

Crews started excavating the site Wednesday, once utility workers had drained water and cleared other hazards, the National Transportation Safety Board said Thursday. The Learjet 60 left Austin-Bergstrom International Airport around 10:37 a.m. Sunday, bound for North Eleuthera Airport in the Bahamas. Just before 1 p.m., it plunged into Palm Beach County, killing everyone aboard.
Once digging began, investigators uncovered a portion of one engine, officials said, noting that debris had also turned up on the roofs of nearby homes and buildings.
Earlier in the week, investigators recovered the left tail elevator, which controls the jet's pitch, in three separate pieces, one of them nearly four miles from where the Learjet 60 went down.

Adam Robinson and his wife, Helen Sharp, were traveling with their two young children when the Learjet carrying them from Texas to the Bahamas crashed in Palm Beach County, Florida, on Nov. 1. (Fox News)
National Transportation Safety Board member Thomas B. Chapman called the part a "very important piece of evidence" when he spoke to reporters Tuesday.
"Even small pieces of the wreckage may contain important evidence that could help investigators determine what happened," the agency wrote on social media.

title: Ex-MIT professor wins $6M after sex claims wrecked career, accuser joked about ‘#hetoo’
summary: David Sabatini's $6 million defamation win over Kristin Knouse now faces cross-appeals as both sides prepare to battle in Massachusetts courts.
story: Former MIT biologist David Sabatini won a $6 million defamation verdict against Kristin Knouse over sexual misconduct claims. Both sides now prepare cross-appeals.

A Massachusetts jury awarded former MIT biologist Dr. David Sabatini a $6 million defamation victory over sexual misconduct claims, setting the stage for cross-appeals as both legal teams prepare to take the case to a higher court.

Dr. Kristin Knouse, the former colleague whose sexual misconduct allegations dismantled Sabatini's American academic career, is challenging the October verdict. Her decision triggered a battle over legal consequences surrounding workplace misconduct claims and the authority of campus tribunals.

Knouse’s attorney, Ellen Zucker, believes that the $6 million verdict could potentially stop female scientists from reporting misconduct, claiming the jury's decision reflects a society that refuses to believe women who challenge powerful men.
David Sabatini listens to closing arguments in a pair of lawsuits on Oct. 14, 2026. (David L. Ryan/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
US OLYMPIC HERO NANCY HOGSHEAD WINS LEGAL BATTLE AFTER VOLLEYBALL COACH'S $250M DEFAMATION SUIT IS DISMISSED

"When someone can get sued for having spoken out, that kills the willingness of anyone to participate in an investigation," Zucker told Fox News Digital. "Daring to speak out will get you sued, [and] the likelihood that anyone would come forward goes down a lot."
Sabatini’s legal team rejected the narrative. His attorney, Lisa G. Arrowood, told Fox News Digital that the verdict poses zero threat to genuine victims.
"The jury verdict in this case should have no impact on women who truly have been harassed or abused and decide to report the misconduct," Arrowood said.

"What the jury found here, based on the contemporaneous documents written by Dr. Knouse herself, was that no harassment ever occurred and that her claims of harassment and rape were false and defamatory. This jury verdict, therefore, has no bearing on people who report truthfully."
The Maclaurin Buildings on the Massachusetts Institute of Technology (MIT) campus in Cambridge, Massachusetts, on Tuesday, Dec. 12, 2023. (Getty Images)
Arrowood also expressed confidence that the $6 million penalty would withstand appeal.
"This is her right," Arrowood said. "However, the judge was very careful in this case and frequently ruled in her favor on many close calls. We think her appeal will be unsuccessful."
FORMER CAL SOFTBALL PLAYER FILES LAWSUIT AGAINST UNIVERSITY, FEMALE EX-COACH OVER ALLEGED SEXUAL MISCONDUCT
Zucker argued that the verdicts will not stand, warning that penalizing accusers threatens future institutional investigations.

"We do not believe the verdicts will stand," Zucker said. "Our client came to court and told the truth about her experiences with Sabatini, as did multiple other women; investigators uncovered several violations of institutional policy."
The upcoming appellate fight will scrutinize the events that led to the lawsuit.
Consensual or coerced

The pair first met in 2012, when Knouse was a doctoral student in the Harvard-MIT M.D./Ph.D. program and Sabatini served on her thesis committee. By 2018 — after Knouse had been named a Whitehead Fellow — they began a relationship, according to court documents.
FORMER UCLA GYNECOLOGIST SENTENCED AFTER PLEADING GUILTY TO SEXUALLY ASSAULTING PATIENTS AT SCHOOL

Sabatini maintained the relationship was consensual. Knouse alleged it was coerced and that Sabatini created an inappropriate workplace dynamic. A 2021 Whitehead investigation found Sabatini violated its workplace relationship policy.
Text messages made public during the case showed Knouse wrote that she would "fixate on how I’m being held as a backup and competed against other women," Boston 25 News reported.
In one message about visiting Sabatini's hotel room one night on a work retreat, she wrote: "In hindsight, it was quite aggressive, #hetoo," according to the outlet.
Knouse launched a campaign against Sabatini that she called "Covert Operation Dethrone," Boston 25 reported, and joked in one message about buying a "Lambo" if she won a settlement.

Kristin Knouse, left, sits behind the bar with Lexi Foman, assistant to retired Judge Nancy Gertner. A motions hearing, in the cases of David Sabatini vs. Whitehead Institute and Kristin Knouse and Knouse vs. Sabatini, is held in Suffolk Superior Court in front of Judge Hélène Kazanjian. (Pat Greenhouse/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)

"Dr. Sabatini and his legal team do not criticize the MeToo movement or the right of women to complain of harassment," Arrowood added. "This case is unique in that the jury found that Dr. Knouse’s claims were fabricated and designed to cause harm to Dr. Sabatini."

After Knouse accused him of sexual misconduct, MIT administrators stripped Sabatini of his tenured position. The Howard Hughes Medical Institute (HHMI) dismissed him. The Whitehead Institute ousted him.
CBS NEWS FACES $20M DEFAMATION LAWSUIT AFTER MISIDENTIFYING MARYLAND TEENAGER IN REFLECTING POOL REPORT
Arrowood said that Sabatini’s team is launching its own counter-offensive on appeal, seeking to overturn the court’s earlier decision that dismissed the Whitehead Institute from the lawsuit.
MIT and HHMI were not defendants in the defamation lawsuit.

MIT declined to comment but referred Fox News Digital to a letter sent out to staff in 2022, when Sabatini resigned and the school said he was found to have "behaved in ways incompatible with the responsibilities of faculty membership."
HHMI did not respond to a request for comment.
BIDEN OFFICIALS CIRCUMVENTED COURT ORDER IN TITLE IX CASES, INCLUDING MALES IN GIRLS’ SPORTS, DOCS SHOW
Title IX Investigations

The universities based their firings on internal Title IX investigations, which concluded that Sabatini violated policies by entering into an undisclosed romantic relationship with a junior researcher.
The campus tribunals require a low burden of proof, which rarely allows the accused to cross-examine the accuser, according to the Foundation for Individual Rights and Expression.
Arrowood argued that the institutions rushed to judgment before the facts could be tested in a civil court.
"This verdict should send universities the message that all the facts and documents from both sides need to be obtained and analyzed before deciding to fire someone," she said.
SEND US A TIP

"Here, the investigators and the Whitehead Institute allowed one party and her lawyers to control what evidence they received and even what they could show to Dr. Sabatini. Had the full picture been shown to the institution and to the investigators, we believe the outcome would have been different."

Former MIT scientist David Sabatini, a biologist who once generated Nobel Prize buzz, is hoping for a comeback after he was abruptly ousted amid allegations of sexual harassment. (Jonathan Wiggs/The Boston Globe via Getty Images)
GOT A TIP?
When the legal battle reached a Suffolk County courtroom, the jury denied Knouse’s counterclaims of harassment and instead ordered her to pay Sabatini millions for defamation.

While Sabatini won the courtroom battle, the years-long ordeal destroyed his U.S. research operation. Activist billionaire Bill Ackman stepped in and funded a new laboratory for Sabatini in Prague, where Sabatini continues his life-saving cancer research.

"I lost everything. There was nothing left of my normal life," Sabatini previously told Boston 25 News. "I've been dreaming about this moment for all this time, but often thinking I might not make it, financially, emotionally or physically."

The case now moves to the Massachusetts appellate courts. The formal briefing schedule is pending.

title: Clash in the castle: Medieval Times dinner theater insiders allege animal cruelty, sexual harassment
summary: A former Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament queen alleges sexual harassment, cyberbullying and doxxing in a lawsuit targeting workplace culture.
story: Medieval Times faces lawsuits alleging animal cruelty, sexual harassment, gender discrimination, bullying, doxxing and retaliation from former employees at its castles.
For 43 years, Medieval Times Dinner & Tournament performers across North America have captivated audiences as jousting knights and bejeweled ladies on horseback.

But now the company’s own castle is under siege as former employees allege in lawsuits that the company shrouds a culture of animal cruelty, sexual harassment, discrimination, bullying and retaliation for reporting abuse.
At the shows, guests dine on what’s billed as a medieval-style feast, as they cheer on armor-clad knights, who participate in a tournament on horseback and battle with swords.
The chain established its first location in Kissimmee, Florida, near Orlando, in 1983. The company now employs more than 2,000 at 10 "castles" in the United States and Canada.

William Elliot III, 35, assistant head knight and former magician in Las Vegas, makes the grand entrance as the red knight, along with fellow knights during a show at Medieval Times in Buena Park on Friday, June 28, 2013. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
MEDIEVAL-THEMED LIVE SHOWS DRAW YOUNG WOMEN WHO ARE LOOKING FOR LOVE AND JADED BY MODERN DATING: REPORT
The theater’s show champions the "chivalry" of their knights. But some who work alongside those performers say the culture is biased against female cast members.
A former "queen" of the castle is now suing the company, alleging a workplace environment "rooted in gender discrimination and sexual harassment."
Another whistleblower alleged that she was fired for voicing concerns about animal cruelty.
FORMER DISNEY CHANNEL STAR ALLEGES SHE WAS SEXUALLY ABUSED AT 14 AFTER BEING TOLD TO ‘BOND’ WITH EMPLOYEE
Royal rivalry
A civil lawsuit was filed in June by a former cast member of the Buena Park, California, castle. She alleges a hostile work environment with widespread sexual harassment.

Kaitlyn Farrell resigned in February 2024 because of "intolerable" conditions after joining the company as a "queen" five years earlier, according to the lawsuit filed in the Superior Court of California, in Orange County.
The "two-tiered workplace culture" treats female cast members as "a lesser class of employee," she said in the lawsuit.
Farrell alleges that unwanted sexual advances toward female employees are "normalized" and "gender-based misconduct" and that complaints are "dismissed" with "indifference."
While working at Medieval Times, she was asked to be a witness in a workplace harassment investigation for another employee.
That made her the "target of open retaliation by the very employee she reported on," her lawsuit alleges.
Management stood by and did nothing, she said.

On another occasion, according to the lawsuit, a manager ordered someone to "remove stitching" from her costumes, what she calls a "calculated sabotage" that was "maliciously intended to cause wardrobe malfunctions in front of live audiences."

After employees unionized at the Buena Park location, and she participated in a strike in February 2023, Farrell said she became the "primary target of an extreme, sexualized cyberbullying and doxxing campaign."

Brandon Sanchez, who plays a knight, protests outside Medieval Times in Buena Park, California, on Wednesday, March 8, 2023. Performers picketed the Buena Park castle after launching an unfair labor practice strike against management. (Jeff Gritchen/MediaNews Group/Orange County Register via Getty Images)

Anonymous social media accounts with "obvious indications" of employee or management involvement posted content such as her dating history, sexually derogatory captions and photoshopped images with her face "on the bodies of semi-nude cartoon characters depicted in simulated sexual positions," the lawsuit alleges.
DISNEYLAND, ACTORS' UNION CLASH OVER PARENTAL LEAVE, BENEFITS AS UNION NEGOTIATES FIRST CONTRACT

The harassment escalated to physical stalking when Medieval Times employees "traveled to Ms. Farrell's secondary workplace" at another theme park "to physically intimidate her while she was working" to entertain guests, the lawsuit alleges.
When she made formal complaints about the behavior, an attorney for Medieval Times issued a written letter dismissing the cyberbullying and stalking as "weird allegations."
"We look forward to proving these allegations in court," Farrell’s attorney, Charles Ludd Jr., told Fox News Digital.
‘False claims’
Medieval Times did not respond to a request for comment on the lawsuit. But former employee Bill Elliot calls Farrell’s allegations "false claims."
Elliot worked at the same Medieval Times location as a knight until leaving after 12 1/2 years in 2015. He had no complaints with the company, he told Fox News Digital in a text message.
"The company took care of us," he said. "We had decent pay; full-time hours with overtime … full medical, dental and vision insurance; and 401K."

William Elliot III, 35, assistant head knight and former magician in Las Vegas, prepares to throw a flower to an audience member as he performs as the red knight during a show at Medieval Times in Buena Park on Friday, June 28, 2013. (Allen J. Schaben/Los Angeles Times via Getty Images)
He believes that people making claims against the company are part of "the-rich-need-to-pay-their-fair-share group" and want to cash in, he said.
"They have no responsibility in running a company that employs thousands of people and no risk in doing it, but believe they deserve more of the profit," he said.
"If it was such a toxic environment and company, they could have immediately removed themselves, but didn't," he said.
It was common for female cast members to seek "attention from the knights and [they] did everything to try and get that attention," Elliot said.
"Now, because those females didn't get their way or what they wanted, they started making false claims and screaming ‘toxic masculinity’ or any other buzzwords to get attention."
Animal-cruelty allegations
Farrell’s lawsuit isn’t the first to make concerning claims against the dinner theater company.

In her 2019 lawsuit, Bethany Regan tells about how she joined the Buena Park castle in 2013. During her employment, she was treated "less favorably" than male cast members, according to court documents.
When she became increasingly concerned about the welfare of the equine performers, she made reports to management, the lawsuit alleges.
The head trainer had a "volatile temper" and would whip horses "unnecessarily" until they had "large welts" over their body, according to the lawsuit.

Some horses were trained in ways that made them bleed from their mouths and in various places on their bodies, she alleged. Horses were "overworked" and sometimes weren’t allowed to rest until they were dehydrated, according to her complaint.
One horse died as a result, she alleged.
Regan had been warned that the head horse trainer was a close friend of the owner of the company and that any complaints could result in "retaliation." She brought up her concerns anyway.
She also reported "dangerous and unsafe working conditions" for female cast members.
After she made formal complaints, the company suspended her for "starting rumors," her lawsuit alleges. Later, her job was terminated.
The lawsuit was settled in 2020. The conditions of the settlement were not made public.
Regan’s attorney did not respond to a request from Fox News Digital for comment.
Horses in the spotlight

Yvonne Barteau was principal trainer and director of entertainment operations for six years at Arabian Nights Dinner Attraction. Minutes away from a Florida Medieval Times castle, the horse-themed dinner theater operated from 1988 until 2014.
Barteau now runs a horse rescue in Florida called Horses without Humans. She founded the operation after making a documentary about theater horses in the United States.
Over the years, she worked with many Medieval Times performers as they moved between dinner theater jobs in the Orlando, Florida, area, she told Fox News Digital.
It was common for young performers to get "way too into their role, like they're really medieval warriors," Barteau said. "I think they got too into the identity."
Yvonne Barteau performs with her grey stallion, Papi, at Spirit of the Horse. (Courtesy of Cheri Prill/Stunning Steeds Photography)
That led to men treating women in a "callous" way, she said, "and I think it was not frowned upon the way that it should be. So yeah, certainly back then, I saw it."
Dinner theater jobs "seemed to attract people like that. And then sometimes the upper management didn't shut it down like they should have," she said.
She met "good people" at Medieval Times. She met others that were not so good, she said.
And there’s never an excuse for abusing a horse, she said.
"Anybody that works with horses, or works with something that has no voice of its own—children, horses, any animal—you have to be the voice," she said.
But "in today’s culture," she said, people with little experience with horses assume that any performance with a horse should be considered cruel.

And that’s simply wrong, she said.

"They haven't seen how some horses really do light up, and they do love to be out there performing," she said. "They love the attention."
She has performed for years with a stallion named Papi.

"He's an absolute theater horse—he's a Brad Pitt.

"People see that horse, and they remember him, and it makes them love horses. And why wouldn't we want that, you know, as horse lovers? Why would we want somebody else to fall in love with horses?"

title: Colorado police officer killed, 3 more officers wounded after suspect opens fire near bus
summary: A suspect trying to board an RTD bus near Denver opened fire on Lakewood police officers, killing one and wounding three others Thursday evening.
story: One Colorado police agent was killed in a shooting in Lakewood on Thursday night, while three other agents were wounded, according to officials.
A Colorado police officer was killed, and three other officers were wounded in a shooting Thursday evening near a bus outside Denver, authorities said.

Lakewood police said officers responded to a report of a suspicious person near the intersection of Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m., where they encountered a suspect attempting to board a bus.
The suspect opened fire on officers, striking four of them, Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero said during a news conference.
"We are very sorry to report that one of those agents has been pronounced dead of their injuries," Romero said.
FOUR DEAD, INCLUDING WASHINGTON DEPUTY, FOLLOWING DOMESTIC CALL SHOOTING; ANOTHER DEPUTY ON LIFE SUPPORT
Lakewood Police Public Information Officer John Romero confirmed that one officer was killed, and three others were wounded during a gunfight with a suspect Thursday evening. (KDVR)
The suspect was shot by police and pronounced dead at the scene, Romero said.
A civilian was also injured and transported to a local hospital.
Police did not immediately provide details about the extent of the injuries or the conditions of the three surviving officers.
Authorities said the suspect was attempting to board a Regional Transportation District (RTD) bus when officers approached.
CHICAGO HOSPITAL SHOOTING LEAVES 1 OFFICER DEAD, OTHER 'FIGHTING FOR HIS LIFE'; SUSPECT IN CUSTODY
A Lakewood police agent has died after a shooting Thursday evening and three others were injured. (KDVR)
"Within seconds of agents approaching the suspect, the suspect opened fire on our agents," Romero said.
Romero also delivered an emotional message to the fallen officer's family:
"We just want the family to know that we love them, that we're here for them, and Lakewood Police Department is a family, and we will be here for each other."
Colorado Gov. Jared Polis released a statement following the deadly shooting.
"Law enforcement put their lives on the line for our safety everyday and I am heartbroken to learn that a Lakewood Police Agent was killed in the line of duty this evening," Polis wrote.

"My heart goes out to their family and friends," he continued. "My thoughts are also with the three agents who are still receiving care at area hospitals, as well as the civilian who was wounded, and I wish them a full and speedy recovery. Thank you to law enforcement who run into danger to keep us safe and to protect our communities."
Polis said the Colorado State Patrol was assisting at the scene and participating in a procession from the hospital honoring the fallen officer.
The Jefferson County Critical Incident Response Team is leading the investigation into the officer-involved shooting, with support from the Colorado Bureau of Investigation.
RTD also released a statement saying it was "deeply concerned" by the shooting.

Lakewood police responded to a report of a suspicious person near Colfax Avenue and Wadsworth Boulevard around 6:30 p.m. Thursday before a gunfight erupted. (KDVR)
"Our thoughts are with those affected directly by this incident," the statement read. "The safety and well-being of our customers, employees, and partners remain our highest priority."

title: Indiana, Florida and Alabama carry out rare US triple execution day
summary: Three inmates were executed by lethal injection in Indiana, Florida and Alabama on the same day, the second time that has happened in 2026.
story: Three states carried out executions on the same day, while California Gov. Gavin Newsom announced plans to commute all 548 of his state’s death sentences.
Indiana, Florida and Alabama each put a man to death Thursday, the second time this year that three inmates were executed in the U.S. the same day.

The first triple execution this year took place Aug. 13, when Oklahoma, Tennessee and Alabama executed inmates within hours of each other. Before Aug. 13, the last time three executions were carried out in the U.S. on the same day was Jan. 7, 2010.

On Thursday, Indiana officials put to death the first inmate of the day when it executed Jeffrey Weisheit, 50, for setting a 2010 house fire that killed his girlfriend's two children, ages 8 and 5, as the couple's relationship deteriorated. He was pronounced dead at 12:45 a.m. at the Indiana State Prison in Michigan City after receiving a lethal injection.

His attorneys sought permission for additional brain scans, arguing that his history of head injuries and mental health problems warranted further examination. Republican Gov. Mike Braun denied the request. Braun also rejected appeals to commute Weisheit's death sentence to life in prison.
INDIANA EXECUTES MAN CONVICTED OF KILLING 2 CHILDREN AS MORE US EXECUTIONS LOOM THURSDAY
Jesse Guardado, Michael Taylor and Jeffrey Weisheit were executed the same day Thursday. (Florida, Alabama and Indiana Departments of Corrections)
Weisheit's lawyers had also raised separate concerns about Indiana's planned use of execution drugs obtained from a pharmacy facing a disciplinary hearing before the Indiana Pharmacy Board next week.

But the Indiana Department of Correction maintained it was confident in its ability to carry out the execution "humanely." After the execution, Braun said Weisheit's case had undergone repeated reviews in state and federal courts.
"These reviews have never resulted in an overturned sentence," Braun said in a statement. "Today, Weisheit's sentence has been carried out as ordered by the court."

The execution provided "long-awaited justice for Alyssa Lynch and her brother Caleb, two innocent children whose lives were stolen in an act of unspeakable cruelty," Indiana Attorney General Todd Rokita said.

In Florida, Jesse Guardado, 64, was executed after confessing and pleading guilty to fatally stabbing a 75-year-old woman who had helped him find a job and housing in 2004. Guardado killed Jackie Malone inside her home before stealing her jewelry box, $80 and other items to fund his drug addiction.
Guardado was pronounced dead at 6:13 p.m. following a lethal injection at Florida State Prison near Starke.
Florida's latest execution matched last year's state record total of 19 inmates put to death in a single year.

Florida has ramped up executions after Republican Gov. Ron DeSantis signed a series of death warrants since 2025. The state's 19 executions last year was more than under any other Florida governor in a single year since the death penalty was reinstated in 1976. Those executions accounted for roughly 40% of the 47 carried out nationwide in 2025.
FLORIDA PUTS 77-YEAR-OLD MAN TO DEATH FOR DEPUTY'S MURDER AS STATE CLOSES IN ON EXECUTION RECORD
Florida's latest execution matched last year's state record total of 19 inmates put to death in a single year. (AP Photo/Curt Anderson, file)

The Sunshine State has also accounted for more than half of the 35 executions carried out nationwide, which includes Thursday's executions. In July, Florida executed two prisoners on the same day, the first double execution by a single state in nearly a decade.

Alabama capped off the triple execution day by putting Michael Taylor, 54, to death for the 1991 murders of an older couple who were beaten to death with a metal bar during a robbery inside their home. Authorities caught Taylor in Birmingham, about an hour away, with the victims' Cadillac.

Taylor was executed by lethal injection after a judge ruled against his attorneys' objections to the method. Taylor had previously requested execution by nitrogen gas, and his attorneys sought to preserve that choice.

His attorneys said he "knew the depth of the harm he caused" and "grieved it for the rest of his life." They also said he became a changed man while behind bars, saying, "Michael’s life was proof that God isn’t finished with any of us. Tonight we pray that both families find peace, and we deeply mourn the loss of Michael."

Death penalty opponents had urged Republican Gov. Kay Ivey to commute Taylor's sentence to life in prison, arguing that he was too young and immature at 19 to fully understand the consequences of his actions.
But the governor declined to stop the execution. Ivey issued a statement on Thursday night describing his actions as "reprehensible."

"Thirty-five years ago yesterday, Ivan and Lucille Moore kindly opened their home to Michael Taylor. Mr. Taylor repaid the Moores by beating them to death with a metal bar, all to rob them for money to buy clothing and jewelry," she said.
The victims' family thanked the state attorney general's office for bringing closure to the case but expressed disappointment for having to wait 35 years to see the death sentence carried out.
The first triple execution this year took place Aug. 13, when Oklahoma, Tennessee and Alabama executed three inmates within hours of each other. (AP Photo/Kim Chandler)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"We know that a person has the right to appeal, but there should come a time when the jury’s decision is final. For all these years, our family has had to live with the waiting, the delays, and the uncertainty," the statement read. "We have never forgotten our loved ones or what was taken from us."

The executions come amid renewed scrutiny of lethal injection procedures following a failed execution attempt in Tennessee, where death row inmate Christa Pike survived two doses of pentobarbital and was rushed to a hospital in late September. She has since been released from the hospital and returned to prison.

Thursday's executions came on the same day California Democratic Gov. Gavin Newsom announced he is seeking to commute all 548 death sentences in the Golden State to life without parole, though 382 of the commutations require a recommendation from the California Supreme Court, saying he believes "state-sanctioned killing is incompatible with California’s values, undermines the foundations of our legal system, and diminishes each of us."

Newsom, who put a moratorium on executions in the state in 2019, said he "knew we cannot execute people in our imperfect legal system and remain true to our core values, the first among them justice and human decency."
The Associated Press contributed to this report.

title: Escaped Tennessee killer hid in Illinois shed with beer and garlic bread before capture: Sheriff
summary: Jacob Allen Morley hid in an Illinois shed near Marion, drinking beer and making garlic bread before FLOCK cameras helped track the Tennessee escapee.
story: Former federal prison warden Cameron Lindsay says Jacob Morley’s escape raises serious questions about staff failures after video showed the convicted murderer moving through the facility seemingly unimpeded.
A convicted killer who broke out of a Tennessee prison spent his time on the run hiding in a shed, drinking beer and making garlic bread, officials said.

Jacob Allen Morley broke out of the Northwest Correctional Complex in Tiptonville, Tennessee, on Oct. 25 and was recaptured by authorities on Tuesday. He was arrested without incident after authorities used FLOCK cameras to help track him down, according to the Missouri State Highway Patrol.

"On November 3, 2026, at approximately 9:30 a.m., the Patrol’s Missouri Information Analysis Center and Troop A Communications received information from the Tennessee Bureau of Investigation that Morley may be traveling westbound on Interstate 70 near Independence," the Missouri State Highway Patrol said in a statement. title: Marine veteran working security hailed as hero after stopping active shooter at Florida Citibank campus
summary: Florida Marine veteran John Fraley took a tactical position in a restroom and shot the Citibank Center campus gunman five times, the sheriff said.
story: The suspect, 35-year-old Jacob Pearson, died from his injuries after the encounter. (Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office via X)

A Florida Marine veteran was credited Thursday as a hero for fatally shooting a gunman who drove onto a Citibank Center campus and began hunting down workers in anger over a delinquent $2,500 credit card bill, officials said.

During a press briefing detailing the tragedy, Hillsborough County Sheriff Chad Chronister identified the security officer as John Fraley, who confronted 35-year-old Jacob Pearson inside the corporate setting just after he shot and killed a female Citibank employee.

"He is an individual that's afforded an opportunity to carry a firearm because the ones who were either previous law enforcement or military and have that training. Citibank empowers them to carry a handgun," Chronister said.
"He didn't have to stop. He could have run and protected his own life, too. He took up a tactical position when he saw the suspect coming and made a decision."
ARMED SECURITY GUARD HAILED AS HERO AFTER FATALLY SHOOTING GUNMAN AT MASSIVE TAMPA CITIBANK SITE
Newly released body camera footage shows Hillsborough County deputies responding to a deadly shooting at a Citibank campus in Brandon, Fla., Wednesday. (The Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office)
"That decision put his own life at risk to stop that shooter from harming anyone else," he added.
Pearson was married and had a 7-year-old child, the sheriff said.

He became violent upon receiving a court summons regarding a $2,500 delinquent debt owed to Citibank, the sheriff said. Furious over the court notice, Pearson called an attorney's office contracted by the bank for collections around 9 a.m. Wednesday.
He allegedly made violent threats to the attorney's office over the phone before leaving his Orlando home.
"Unless you want me to go over there with my AR-15, my bulletproof vest and my insanity, you m------------ cancel this court case," he allegedly said, Fox 13 reported.
"Do you understand me? They are only an hour and three minutes away, so the last thing you want to do is f--- with me."
Authorities converge on a Tampa-area business park where an active shooter was reported Wednesday, resulting in one suspect and one victim dead. (Fox News)

Citibank’s head of security, a retired Secret Service agent, recognized the severity of the threat, and contacted both the Orlando Police Department for a welfare check and the Hillsborough County Sheriff's Office to request deputy presence on campus.

Despite those steps, Pearson drove to the Brandon campus, crashing through a gate into the courtyard where employees were gathered.
Once inside, he got out of his sedan with a rifle and immediately shot 41-year-old learning advisor LeAnne Selmon three times before his weapon malfunctioned, according to Chronister.
ARMED SECURITY GUARD HAILED AS HERO AFTER FATALLY SHOOTING GUNMAN AT MASSIVE TAMPA CITIBANK SITE

"As he shoots her, his rifle begins to malfunction," he said. "This suspect goes back … returns back to his car, retrieves his handgun, walks back over to the victim who's trying to crawl away with her life and executes her.

"He was there intent on one purpose, and that purpose was to hunt any human being he could find and kill," the sheriff said. "Because of the heroic actions of this Citibank security officer, vice president of operations, his reign of terror ended before it even began."

Pearson then walked into a cafeteria intent on finding more victims before encountering Fraley, the sheriff said. Fraley, a Citibank security guard, took a tactical position inside the men's restroom and opened fire, striking Pearson five times, according to the sheriff.

title: MICHAEL RUIZ: 'Today' segment may explain key Apple Watch detail in Nancy Guthrie ransom note, expert says
summary: A retired detective says Savannah Guthrie's "Today" show Tucson segment may have sparked her abductor's interest in Nancy Guthrie before her kidnapping.
story: Retired FBI profiler Jim Clemente says there's a likelihood that whoever is behind the disappearance of Nancy Guthrie had a fixation on her famous daughter.  "It's not logical. It's not something you can anticipate."

A year after "Today" co-host Savannah Guthrie highlighted her hometown roots and introduced viewers to her mother and favorite haunts, the broadcast is drawing new scrutiny over whether it could have helped make Nancy Guthrie a target in her still-unsolved kidnapping.
According to several experts who have been following the case, the same segment could have provided information that influenced the kidnapping — or allowed someone to fake inside knowledge afterward.

"There's nothing about the house, but you could easily infer that she would still be wearing that watch two months later," said Morgan Wright, the CEO and founder of the National Center for Open and Unsolved Cases and an expert on digital forensics. "And again, it's not an unreasonable assumption to think that elderly people would take their watch off at night."
As Fox News Digital has reported previously, investigators were divided over whether the two early ransom notes were authentic and have not publicly identified their sender.
NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM DEMANDS RELEASED BY PIMA COUNTY SHERIFF'S DEPARTMENT IN BID TO IDENTIFY SENDER
From left to right, Annie Guthrie, Savannah Guthrie and Nancy Guthrie pictured at a popular Tucson restaurant, El Charro, in a "Today" show segment that aired on Nov. 5, 2025. (NBC/"Today")
But Savannah Guthrie's prominence, combined with the personal details included in the segment, could also have caught the attention of someone with malicious intent, according to experts.

"I think the segment is worth considering as a very possible spark for someone’s interest in Nancy," said Lisa Miller, a retired detective and law enforcement executive at the Colorado Attorney General's Office who has been following the case. "Whether this involved a kidnapping for ransom, someone fixated on Savannah, or another motive, that broadcast could have introduced a potential offender to Nancy and planted the seed of an opportunity."
She called the segment's influence on her abductor or abductors "a strong possibility to investigate" while noting the motive remains unclear.

"I want to be very clear — none of that places responsibility on Savannah," Miller said. "She shared her love and pride in a strong woman who raised a family, spent part of those years parenting alone and built a successful career."
NBC BEEFS UP SECURITY AT 'TODAY' STUDIO AFTER NANCY GUTHRIE KIDNAPPING, INTRUDER INCIDENT

Jim Clemente, a retired FBI supervisory special agent and profiler, separately told the "Crime & Justice with Donna Rotunno" podcast that Savannah Guthrie's fame may have caught the perpetrator's attention.
Savannah Guthrie and her mother Nancy discuss how the family settled in Tucson in the 1970s in a "Today" show segment that aired on Nov. 5, 2025. (NBC/"Today")

"Whether it actually caused I can't say that, but certainly Savannah's popularity and the fact that Nancy was on her shows and the relationship between them could have caused some sort of, some type of jealousy or some type of feeling that they belonged to this person, and they wanted to get back at her for not feeling the same way," he said. "It's not logical. It's not something you can anticipate. But it could be possible."
What the segment revealed — and what it didn't

"Until that story, I didn’t even know she was from Tucson," said Bob Krygier, a retired SWAT commander with the Pima County Sheriff's Department, which is headquartered in the city. "I’ve always had a bit of a feeling that there was some connection."

I want to be very clear — none of that places responsibility on Savannah. She shared her love and pride in a strong woman who raised a family, spent part of those years parenting alone and built a successful career.

NANCY GUTHRIE RANSOM NOTES MAY BE FAKE AS RENOWNED PROFILER SAYS CASE LOOKS MORE LIKE BURGLARY GONE WRONG
The watch detail could have been used by whoever wrote the notes, said Wright, the expert on digital forensics — even if they had no connection to the abduction.

One of the notes included references to the crime scene that may not have been public at the time they were sent — including details about the location of Guthrie's Apple Watch and the smashed floodlight in her backyard. Fox News Digital first learned about the watch on the morning of Tuesday, Feb. 3. According to authorities, the note had been sent the day before, on Monday, Feb. 2, indicating the sender knew about it before the information began to seep out into the public sphere.
But it could also have been a lucky guess, Wright said.
"So I believe none of the ransom notes are credible, and that, that information could have been easily obtained from just watching a video," he said.
The first purported Nancy Guthrie ransom demand was sent on Feb. 2, a day after her suspected abduction in Tucson, according to authorities. (Pima County Sheriff's Department)
Krygier said public figures should be cautious about what they share online in today's environment.
"You need to be careful, but I also don’t think they need to go into a complete shell," he said. "It’s a balance, but being careful is incredibly important."
The 'evolved wrench attack' theory

Visit Tucson, a local nonprofit created to attract tourists and business to the city, sponsored the segment, which remains visible on YouTube. It featured some of Savannah Guthrie's favorite locations in her hometown — and the Sonoran Desert's iconic saguaro cactuses.

"People ask me, 'Where are you from?' I'm always proud when I say, 'Tucson, Arizona,'" Savannah Guthrie said in a segment that aired on Nov. 5, 2025. "I grew up there, went to college there, my mom still lives there and honestly a part of me has really never left."

Guthrie was taken from her home in Tucson's Catalina Foothills neighborhood in the early hours of Feb. 1. After she missed a gathering with friends for church, her family discovered she was missing and called police.
Savannah Guthrie and her mother, Nancy Guthrie. (Instagram/Savannah Guthrie)

The FBI and Google teamed up to recover home security video from her missing Nest doorbell camera, which showed a masked intruder wearing gloves and carrying what appears to be a gun on her front porch. But nine months later, his identity remains unknown — as do her whereabouts.

"From what we know publicly, I see little that would explain Nancy becoming a target apart from her connection to Savannah," Miller told Fox News Digital. "I also have difficulty reconciling her removal from the home with a straightforward burglary gone wrong."
Her abduction required planning and a "consequential decision," Miller told Fox News Digital.

"That does not establish the motive, but it is a central reason I believe Nancy herself was the target, a pressure point to reach Savannah," she said.
Savannah Guthrie and her mother, Nancy Guthrie. (Instagram/Savannah Guthrie)

In a prior interview with Fox News Digital, Miller floated the idea that the abduction may have been an "evolved wrench attack" — an effort to extort money out of the wealthy and famous Savannah Guthrie by threatening her mother.

"The question is whether someone recognized that targeting a vulnerable family member could create leverage over Savannah," Miller said Wednesday. "But the segment’s potential significance isn’t limited to that theory. Someone with a fixation on Savannah could also have redirected that attention toward her mother."

Where the case stands now

"Behind every theory is a woman who deserves to be brought home and a family living with an anguish most of us cannot comprehend," Miller said. "I have grave concerns about Nancy’s fate, but the evidence must answer that question. My sincere hope is that evidence and tips lead investigators to those responsible, bring Nancy home and give her family answers. Every family deserves no less than that."

title: 3 injured in shooting at Des Moines, Iowa post office, suspect detained: Police
summary: Police in Des Moines, Iowa, said multiple people were injured and a suspect is in custody following a shooting Thursday at a United States Postal Service facility.
story: Police respond to a shooting at a U.S. Postal Service office in Des Moines, Iowa, on Thursday, Nov. 5, 2026. (Credit: WOI/AP)
Police in Des Moines, Iowa, said three people were injured and a suspect is in custody following a shooting Thursday at a United States Postal Service facility.
The incident unfolded at the post office at 1165 Second Ave. Multiple law enforcement agencies, including the ATF and FBI, have responded to the scene.

"ATF Special Agents are responding to reports of a shooting at the main U.S. Post Office in Des Moines, Iowa, to assist our law enforcement partners. Public safety remains our top priority," ATF Kansas City said.

Des Moines Police Sgt. Paul Parizek told reporters that "right about 9:10, we started receiving multiple phone calls from inside of the post office reporting that there was an active killer situation going on, someone shooting on the second floor.

"We've had three victims right now that we are aware of. We don't have their life status right now, initially they were believed to have non-life threatening injuries, they're all at the hospital they're being cared for right now," he added.
